column36: Urban local bodies (ULBs) across Maharashtra continue to send large volumes of dry, recyclable waste particularly plastics, e-waste, cloths to landfill because collection remains informal, unsegregated, and disconnected from any organised processing chain. This overburdens landfill sites, while adding to municipal transport and disposal costs. These recyclables are sought after by waste pickers who then scavenge through the dumpsite to retrieve them. SORT IT addresses this by building decentralised Reduce, Reuse, Recycle (RRR) centres, run by trained local women from Self Help Groups, that intercept recyclable dry waste at source, segregate it, sell it for reuse to locals or recyclers for further processing.  This specialised niche waste solution, creates a convergence of waste management and womens economic empowerment for a resilient urban ecosystem. This can be scaled for a larger impact using Digital operational intelligence. The model is anchored on three core pillars:   Livelihood Generation: Formalizing women SHGs into specialized service providers.   Circularity and traceability: Promoting resource efficiency by closing the loop on specialized waste streams, turning recyclables into valuable market commodities. Aggregating the quantities recycled across geographies on a platform to provide traceability and potential for valuation.  Landfill Diversion: Implementing decentralized source segregation and collection to reduce the volume of dry recyclable waste requiring long-haul transport. The digital "intelligence layer" will ensure transparency, scale, aggregation of benefits and institutional trust. It will create a replicable and scalable model that can be rolled out across ULBs without depending on a single site's infrastructure.
column37:
Digital transparency serves as the "trust layer" required to scale social enterprises within the complex waste management value chain. For ULBs and companies looking to comply with thier Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) credits, data is the currency of accountability. The SORTT IT central portal will provide a standardized architecture for multi-center management and aggregation. It will consist of two modules:
The Training & Onboarding Module: Focuses on skill acquisition and financial literacy. It disseminates Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) and Entrepreneurship Development Program (EDP) modules to ensure uniformity across geographically dispersed SHGs. It also records the number of SHG women onboarded and trained, and livelihoods generated.
The Operational & Management Module: Facilitates real-time tracking of daily collection, secondary sorting, sales, and accounts. This module allows for centralized reporting and data-driven troubleshooting. It gives ULBs a live, auditable record of waste diverted from their landfills it allows SORTT and its SHG partners to monitor unit-level performance (collection efficiency, sales) and intervene quickly when a centre under-performs and it builds the traceable impact record of waste.
The digital operational platform will track the entire RRR-centre value chain in real time.  Critically, this digital traceability is not merely a monitoring tool but a strategic prerequisite for accessing high-level revenue streams. By aggregating data across centers, we establish the verifiable "environmental proof" required to participate in Carbon Credit markets and Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) frameworks, while simultaneously providing the scale needed to negotiate superior market rates for recycled products.
column38:
Traditional municipal waste management is characterised by high economic leakage, with significant expenditure on waste transportation and limited value recovery. SORTIT offers a decentralised alternative through RRR Centres, addressing key gaps including high transportation costs, landfill dependency, loss of recoverable resources and livelihoods, and the carbon footprint of waste management.

While the SWM Rules 2026, Swachh Survekshan and Garbage Free Cities promote circularity and RRR Centres, many ULB-operated centres remain focused on compliance and scoring rather than financial sustainability. SORTIT builds on KIFs pilot experience with four RRR Centres to develop revenue-generating, self-sustaining models that can achieve viability through scale.

Existing informal systems, including scrap shops and traditional barter networks, often lack quality control, price transparency and stable livelihoods for waste pickers. SORTIT addresses this gap by combining decentralised, SHG-led RRR Centres with a digital aggregation platform. Centres operate closer to the source, with trained women managing collection, sorting and quality control, while recovered materials are linked to recyclers and buyers. The digital platform aggregates material volumes, enables traceability and provides operational and market support, helping centres improve revenues, strengthen livelihoods and achieve measurable waste diversion.

column43:
Based on our experience of operating four RRR centers the major challenges we have encountered:
Turnover of women in operating the RRR centers  Due to personal or financial reasons, women do not stay committed to the livelihood model, to accrue the benefits of increased income. Training at least 20 women per ULB, provides us with a pool of trained women to substitute as well as creates a competitive spirit.
Variation in recyclable waste quantities and quality The size and socio-economic nature of the ULB determines the quality and quantity of recyclable waste from each town. Thus integration of several centers under one portal can provide an opportunity to cross-subsidise other towns. 
Market Risk  Price fluctuations of the recyclables if localised. We thus propose doing secure offtake agreements or MoUs with buyers and diversify buyer base across multiple ULBs. Providing scale to the operations with supporting data will work to mitigate this risk.
Dependency on ULB for space: Our current models are dependent on the ULB for space for the RRR center.  Completing the administrative formalities for the same takes time. However, once the centre achieves financial stability, it can afford to rent a space.
Membership to the IT Portal: There is a risk that centers that become financially successful quickly may choose to not remain members. A MOU at the start of the formation of the centers have to make this a conditionality to start the center.

The primary beneficiaries are women members of Self-Help Groups (SHGs) and independent waste pickers working in the various ULBs in Maharashtra.  These are largely, women from low-income families, who have been a member of the local SHG for a few years, under the cities National Urban LIvelihood Mission. They are currently engaged either in informal or domestic work, or pursue some income generating activity such as tailoring, food service or beautician. They are looking for opportunities that provide increased income, flexibility and stable work. A structured, skilled role at an RRR centre offers a significant improvement in income stability, safety, and social standing. Beneficiaries are onboarded through the SHG federation structure and awareness session on business opportunities, and trained progressively so that over time a core group of women can take on supervisory or entrepreneurial roles within each centre.
A secondary beneficiary group is the ULB itself, which gains a measurable reduction in landfill-bound waste and a formal, accountable partner for its recyclable dry-waste stream. 
The third is the companies that have to comply with EPR regulations, the digital platform provides them a one source quantity to comply with their requirements.

column36: Across India, used water from municipal STPs and industrial CETPs is typically treated only to the point required for regulatory discharge, not to a standard that allows reuse. Once water meets that threshold, it is released into drains, nallahs, creeks or coastal outfalls and is permanently lost to the system, despite a substantial share of that volume being suitable for reuse in flushing, gardens, road washing, construction or industrial cooling with one additional treatment step. This is a structural gap, not an isolated one. India operates more than fifty thousand industrial STPs and ETPs, together with thousands of municipal STPs, and the majority stop at compliance rather than proceeding to reuse, since the additional treatment required is costly, operationally complex, or generates a secondary waste stream of its own. The consequence is twofold: cities and industries continue to draw fresh water that could have been substituted, while the treated water that could have replaced it is discharged instead, frequently carrying residual colour, odour and organic load visible at the point of release. In dense wards across Mumbai, Thane and Mira Bhayandar, where drainage infrastructure runs directly through residential areas, this burden is borne most directly by the communities with the least capacity to address it. This is the specific gap Exposome's technology is engineered to close, by making reuse the outcome rather than compliance alone.
column37: Exposome's core technology is a molecularly engineered filtration media is designed to combine multiple removal mechanisms within a single engineered particle, integrating adsorption, ion exchange and controlled redox reactions rather than relying on separate processes for separate pollutants. This design enables a single media to address colour, COD, odour, heavy metals, hardness and reactive silica concurrently, in place of requiring a dedicated unit for each parameter. Because pollutant removal occurs within the material itself, the media is installed directly into an fiber-vessel , no civil works, and no interruption to plant operation. Most tertiary treatment technologies currently in use, including membranes, ion exchange resins and standard activated carbon, are designed for single use, which is the principal driver of their operating cost and servicing burden at municipal scale. Exposome's media is differentiated by its capacity for in place regeneration, through a defined service, rinse and regeneration cycle, extending its operational life to four to five years in place of three to six months for conventional alternatives. This regeneration capability is the technological foundation of Exposome's platform, converting a consumable requiring continuous replacement into a durable asset that a municipal body can own and operate over an extended period.
column38: The specific need is a treatment step engineered to enable reuse, rather than one designed solely to satisfy a discharge limit. The tertiary stage currently deployed, where one exists, is typically a biological filter or an MBBR type process, both of which are designed to bring a plant into compliance and are not intended to produce water suitable for reuse. Where reuse is pursued, reverse osmosis is the conventional choice, though RO rejects a significant proportion of throughput as brine, commonly in the range of thirty percent, and that reject stream requires its own disposal pathway, effectively substituting one waste management problem for another while adding considerable capital cost. Ion exchange resins are used in some installations but offer limited selectivity across the mixed pollutant loads typical of real waste water streams and require frequent, costly replacement. Evaporation and advanced oxidation processes are available as well, though both are energy intensive, generate substantial sludge volumes, and require more space than most existing STPs can accommodate. None of these approaches were designed with reuse as the primary objective. For a ULB specifically, the practical alternative today is to forgo reuse entirely, which is the exact constraint Exposome's drop in media is designed to remove, without requiring new civil infrastructure.

column42: Exposome delivers treatment and reuse as a complete solution, sized to the requirements of each site, rather than as a fixed equipment sale. For smaller and mid sized installations, such as the CETP Tarapur plant, Exposome designs, installs and services the deployment directly, supplying media and maintaining an annual regeneration and monitoring contract with the site. For larger municipal and industrial scale deployments, Exposome partners with established EPCs and process majors, led by Thermax WWS as its exclusive channel partner in India, ensuring the offering is delivered through an infrastructure relationship the customer already trusts, rather than as a standalone product introduced through an unfamiliar vendor. Revenue is generated through two linked streams: media, supplied by weight and replaced on a four to five year cycle rather than every few months, and an annual service contract covering on site regeneration, monitoring and operator support. For a ULB, this model translates into media installed directly within the fiber-vessel at the pilot site, with an annual regeneration and monitoring contract as the ongoing revenue line following conversion to commercial deployment, consistent with the asset light structure Exposome operates across more than fifty installations nationally.
column43: Customer hesitation toward adopting a new material category is addressed through pilots that generate independent performance data at the customer's own site, resulting in a conversion rate above ninety percent across fifty completed pilots. Municipal procurement and payment cycles are typically long and tender bound, a constraint mitigated through established channel partnerships and through precedent, as MSInS issued an INR 15 lakh work order for the Tarapur plant, demonstrating that a Maharashtra state body has evaluated and funded this technology directly. Variability in influent quality at municipal sites is addressed through a two to four week characterization process conducted prior to media selection, rather than assuming industrial parameters will apply. Regeneration discipline at plants operated by third parties is managed through operator training and Exposome run service contracts, ensuring the regeneration cycle is not left solely to the customer. Manufacturing scale up is addressed through the ongoing Series A round, structured specifically to fund multi tonne annual production capacity. For a municipal pilot specifically, the primary additional risk is greater variability in influent quality relative to an industrial CETP, a risk Exposome manages consistently across all site types through characterization prior to media selection.

column47:
The most directly relevant reference is the CODe reduction pilot plant commissioned in October 2023 at CETP Tarapur, a shared industrial effluent treatment cluster in Palghar district. This project was jointly enabled by the Maharashtra State Innovation Society and the Maharashtra Industrial Development Corporation, following Exposome's recognition at Maharashtra Startup Week 2022 in the water management category. MSInS issued a formal work order for a 10 cubic metre per hour capacity plant, installed with two identical media units operating in a lead and lag configuration for continuous operation, incorporating service, rinse and regeneration modes from commissioning. The plant operated continuously from 27 October 2023 through 10 May 2024, delivering a consistent 60 to 90 percent reduction in COD and 50 to 90 percent reduction in colour and odour, verified through before and after water quality testing jointly released by MSInS and Exposome. While Tarapur serves an industrial cluster rather than a ULB operated STP, it establishes three relevant facts: a Maharashtra state government body has evaluated, funded and endorsed this technology the plant has demonstrated sustained operational reliability over an extended period and the reported performance figures are independently verified rather than self reported.

Exposome's broader deployment base further supports its readiness for this pilot. The technology is TRL 9 and commercially deployed across more than fifty installations nationally, serving more than twenty paying enterprise customers, with a record of over one hundred and ten completed paid pilots converting at above ninety percent to commercial contracts. In 2025, Exposome also delivered a UP government enabled installation treating colour and COD at the Kumbh Mela, a mass public gathering context requiring rapid deployment, reliable operation under variable load, and coordination with a public sector authority, all directly applicable to a municipal STP pilot in Mumbai, Thane or Mira Bhayandar.

Exposome's position for T-MAP is that of a company with a state government validated technology and an actively developing relationship with Mumbai's municipal ecosystem, seeking its first pilot within a Maharashtra ULB's own STP rather than its first pilot in any environment. This represents a lower risk proposition for both Exposome and the participating ULB, as the underlying media, the twelve week characterization to validation methodology, and the operator training model have already been proven at Tarapur and require only deployment within a municipally operated facility to complete the record T-MAP requires. Exposome welcomes T-MAP's support in identifying the appropriate ULB and site to establish this first Maharashtra municipal deployment.
column48:
In the short term, within the twelve week pilot phase, expected impact includes a validated reduction in COD, colour and odour at a single Maharashtra ULB site, benchmarked against the 60 to 90 percent COD reduction and 50 to 90 percent colour and odour reduction already demonstrated at CETP Tarapur. Alongside this water quality outcome, the pilot generates a defined volume of treated water available for reuse at the site, whether for flushing, gardens or road washing, and produces the first independently observable evidence of Exposome's performance within a genuine ULB operated STP rather than an industrial CETP alone.

In the medium term, over the twelve to twenty four months following a successful pilot, expected impact includes conversion of the site into a commercial annual service contract, consistent with the conversion rate exceeding ninety percent that Exposome has achieved across its national pilot programme. This is expected to be followed by replication across additional STPs within the same ULB, or across the other T-MAP geographies of Mumbai, Thane and Mira Bhayandar, with each retrofit capable of meeting the daily water needs of nearby residents. At this stage, the Tarapur precedent and the T-MAP pilot together are expected to provide Maharashtra's other ULBs and CETPs with a second, municipally specific reference point, complementing Exposome's existing industrial reference sites.

In the long term, expected impact includes the establishment of regenerable tertiary treatment as a standard reuse layer across Maharashtra's municipal STPs, functioning as routine infrastructure rather than an exceptional retrofit. At scale, this translates to freshwater draw reductions in the 40 to 60 percent range already observed at Exposome's existing deployed sites, applied across a broader base of municipal facilities, alongside elimination of the hazardous sludge stream generated by conventional activated carbon based tertiary treatment at comparable scale. This positions Exposome, and the ULBs it partners with, as an early and credible reference point as reuse mandates and zero liquid discharge norms extend further into India's municipal sector, providing Maharashtra's cities an established position ahead of a transition expected across municipal water management nationally.

Project Description. Exposome proposes a twelve week pilot deployment of its regenerable filtration media within an existing STP operated by a Maharashtra Urban Local Body, most likely in Mumbai, Thane or Mira Bhayandar, the three geographies identified in the T-MAP program brief. Exposome manufactures molecularly engineered, regenerable filtration media that removes COD, BOD, colour, odour, heavy metals, hardness and reactive silica from waste water, integrating adsorption, ion exchange and controlled redox reactions within a single engineered material. In contrast to single use activated carbon or ion exchange resins, this media is regenerated in place through a defined service, rinse and regeneration cycle and remains operational for four to five years, rather than requiring replacement every few months. Because the pollutant removal mechanism resides within the material itself rather than in separate equipment, the media is installed as a drop in tertiary stage directly within an FRP vessel, requiring no civil works, no additional tankage, and no interruption to ongoing plant operation.

The technology holds TRL 9 status and is commercially proven, with more than fifty installations nationally and more than twenty paying enterprise customers, including Unilever, Reliance Industries, Tata Group and Aditya Birla Group. The most directly relevant reference project is the PureCODe pilot plant commissioned in October 2023 at CETP Tarapur, under a Maharashtra State Innovation Society and Maharashtra Industrial Development Corporation initiative, which delivered a consistent 60 to 90 percent reduction in COD and 50 to 90 percent reduction in colour and odour, independently verified through before and after testing jointly released by MSInS and Exposome. T-MAP represents the opportunity for Exposome to apply this validated methodology, for the first time, within a ULB operated STP rather than an industrial CETP.

Geography. The target deployment is within the Mumbai Metropolitan Region, at an STP operated by the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation, Thane Municipal Corporation or Mira Bhayandar Municipal Corporation, the three ULBs identified in the T-MAP brief. Final site selection will depend on the ULB and facility identified through the T-MAP program, and Exposome's characterization first methodology is designed to adapt to site specific influent conditions rather than requiring a particular starting profile.

Timelines. Weeks 1 to 2 comprise wastewater characterization and media selection, based on laboratory analysis of the site's actual influent for COD, colour, surfactants, silica, metals and total suspended solids, ensuring the media specification reflects real operating conditions. Weeks 3 to 4 comprise drop in installation, conducted in parallel with the plant's existing operations to avoid downtime or disruption to the ULB's ongoing treatment obligations. Weeks 5 to 12 comprise live performance validation, with bi weekly reporting on inlet and outlet COD, colour and odour, alongside tracking of the volume of treated water made available for reuse. This phased structure mirrors the methodology Exposome has applied across more than one hundred and ten completed paid pilots nationally, adapted for a municipal rather than industrial operating environment.

Funding amount required. The specific figure will depend on the scale and influent characteristics of the assigned ULB site, as pilot cost is a function of flow rate and the corresponding media volume required, consistent with the sizing basis applied to the 10 cubic metre per hour Tarapur plant. Exposome will confirm an exact figure with the T-MAP program team once a ULB and site have been identified, drawing on the cost basis established across its completed pilots to date, in order to provide an accurate figure rather than a provisional estimate that may not reflect the assigned site's actual requirements.

Partnerships associated. On the government and municipal side, T-MAP is administered by Villgro and Cisco under Cisco's 40 Communities initiative, with the participating Maharashtra ULB serving as Exposome's direct implementation partner once assigned. Exposome brings an established, demonstrable relationship with Maharashtra state government bodies to this partnership, through the MSInS and MIDC backed Tarapur deployment, evidencing the company's capacity to execute within a Maharashtra public sector process from initial engagement through to a delivered, independently verified result.

Expected impact description. In the short term, a successful T-MAP pilot validates that Exposome's media performs to the same standard within a genuine ULB operated STP as within an industrial CETP, generating the first independently observable proof point of municipal performance in Maharashtra, alongside a defined volume of water made newly available for reuse at the specific site. In the medium term, the anticipated path is conversion of the pilot site into a standing annual service contract, consistent with the conversion rate exceeding ninety percent that Exposome has achieved across its national pilot programme, followed by replication across further STPs within the same ULB or across the other T-MAP geographies, with each 1 to 3 MLD retrofit capable of meeting the daily water needs of approximately 5,000 to 21,000 residents, based on the benchmark of one MLD of reused water meeting the daily needs of 5,000 to 7,000 people. In the long term, the opportunity is to establish regenerable tertiary treatment as a standard reuse layer across Maharashtra's municipal STPs generally, reducing freshwater draw at the 40 to 60 percent rate already observed at Exposome's existing deployed sites and eliminating the hazardous sludge stream generated by conventional single use tertiary treatment, while providing Maharashtra's ULBs an early, credible position ahead of reuse mandates expected to extend further into India's municipal sector.

Beyond Maharashtra specifically, Exposome is concurrently scaling this drop in, regenerable model into new geographies and sectors, including data centre cooling circularity applications under discussion through a Cleveland Water Alliance partnership in the United States. A well documented ULB pilot under T-MAP would provide Exposome with a second substantive reference case, alongside Tarapur, supporting this broader scaling effort and extending the value of this pilot beyond its immediate Maharashtra deployment, while positioning Maharashtra's ULBs among the first anywhere to gain direct experience with a technology Exposome is actively deploying globally.

Urban local bodies face a critical gap in the safe and effective management of faecal sludge and sewage from septic tanks and sewer systems. Cleaning these systems can still involve hazardous manual interventions, while conventional mechanised equipment may be unable to effectively remove accumulated sludge or operate in difficult-to-access spaces.

This exposes sanitation workers to toxic gases, biological hazards and confined-space risks, while limiting the efficiency and consistency of municipal sanitation operations. It also creates challenges for the safe handling and management of this specialised sanitation waste stream.

HomoSEP addresses this gap through robotic, mechanised cleaning that enables septic tank and sewer cleaning without human entry into hazardous confined spaces. The solution helps ULBs transition from hazardous, labour-intensive cleaning practices towards safer, more efficient and technology-enabled sanitation operations.

The innovation therefore addresses both the municipal waste-management challenge and its critical human dimension: enabling ULBs to manage sanitation waste more effectively while contributing to the elimination of hazardous manual cleaning and improving the safety and dignity of sanitation workers.
column37:
Technology is the core enabler of HomoSEPs ability to transform hazardous sanitation work into a safe, mechanised and scalable municipal service.

HomoSEP combines robotics with specialised sludge-removal mechanisms to perform desilting, grabbing and suction/jetting from above ground, eliminating the need for workers to enter septic tanks or manholes. Its homogenisation/blade mechanism helps break down and loosen compacted sludge that conventional suction systems may struggle to remove, while integrated gas sensing and a display unit provide real-time operational visibility during cleaning.

The technology consolidates multiple cleaning functions into a single robotic system, reducing dependence on multiple assets and enabling deployment across varied urban environments, including difficult-to-access locations.

Beyond replacing a hazardous manual task, HomoSEP enables a technology-led operating model for municipal sanitation: sanitation workers can operate the system remotely, shifting their role from hazardous manual cleaning to safer, skilled robotic operations. This creates a pathway for ULBs to improve worker safety, operational efficiency and the scalability of specialised waste-management services.
column38:
The innovation addresses the need for safe, effective and efficient mechanised cleaning of septic tanks, manholes and sewer systems, while eliminating the need for workers to enter hazardous confined spaces. Despite policy mandates for mechanised sanitation, ULBs continue to face challenges in removing compacted sludge and debris, particularly where conventional equipment is ineffective. Maharashtra has specifically directed ULBs to undertake septic tank and sewage-line cleaning entirely through mechanised means.

The primary alternatives today are manual cleaning, conventional suction/desludging vehicles, and separate mechanical equipment. Manual entry is hazardous and undermines the objective of eliminating hazardous sanitation work. Conventional suction systems are effective for removing liquid sludge but can struggle with the dense, settled sludge at the bottom of septic tanks.

HomoSEP addresses this gap through an integrated robotic system combining sludge homogenisation/blade cleaning, desilting, grabbing and suction/jetting. This allows difficult sludge to be loosened and removed without human entry, while consolidating multiple cleaning functions into a single system.

The resulting need addressed is therefore not just mechanisation, but a safer and more capable technology-enabled model for municipal sanitation operations that protects workers while improving cleaning effectiveness and operational efficiency.

Direct sale of robotic units to ULBs, sanitation agencies and service providers.

Training and capacity building, enabling sanitation workers and municipal teams to transition to robotic operations.

The key challenges to scaling HomoSEP are primarily related to municipal adoption, field-level implementation and operational sustainability, rather than technology readiness.

1. Municipal procurement and adoption: ULB procurement processes can be lengthy, and adoption of new technology requires demonstration of operational effectiveness and value for money. We mitigate this through pilots, direct engagement with ULBs, and deployment models that generate evidence for larger-scale procurement.
2. Diverse field conditions: Septic tanks, manholes, sludge characteristics and access conditions vary significantly across cities. HomoSEP has therefore been designed as a compact and adaptable system, with modular components and multiple cleaning functions to address varied operating environments.
3. Operator adoption and capability: Transitioning from manual practices to robotic operations requires training and changes in existing workflows. Solinas addresses this through operator training, field support and ongoing operations and maintenance.
4. Sustained utilisation and O&M: For municipalities to realise the full value of the technology, robots need to be integrated into regular sanitation operations rather than treated as standalone assets. Solinas works with deployment partners to establish operating protocols, maintenance systems and trained local operators.
5. Affordability and scalability: Municipalities may face budget constraints despite the need for mechanisation. Flexible procurement/service models and evidence from deployments can help reduce adoption barriers and demonstrate the economic value of improved productivity and safer sanitation operations.

Our focus is therefore to convert proven technology into a repeatable municipal deployment model that can be adopted and scaled across cities.

Solinas is seeking approximately ?80 lakh in T-MAP support for a 12-month municipal deployment of HomoSEP, aimed at demonstrating and establishing a scalable model for safe, mechanised and technology-enabled sanitation operations.

Importantly, the project is not intended as a technology-development exercise. HomoSEP is a field-deployable technology with existing deployments and ULB experience. T-MAP support will enable Solinas to demonstrate how the technology can be systematically integrated into municipal operations and generate the operational, social and environmental evidence required for wider adoption.

* Field deployment and integration with municipal sanitation operations.

Geography

Funding Required
Approximately ?80 lakh, covering the manufacture and supply of HomoSEP, deployment, 12-month O&M, worker training and capacity building, field support, monitoring, impact measurement and documentation.

Partnerships

3. Municipal impact: Demonstrate a practical and financially viable model for integrating robotic sanitation into routine ULB operations, with measurable productivity, operational and safety outcomes.

The ultimate objective is to create a replicable municipal sanitation model: demonstrate the intervention in one priority zone, generate credible evidence, and use the results to enable the participating Municipal Corporation to expand HomoSEP deployment to additional zones. The model can then be replicated across other ULBs in Maharashtra.

This makes T-MAP a catalyst not simply for deploying one robot, but for demonstrating how robotics can enable a systemic transition from hazardous manual sanitation to safer, more efficient and scalable municipal sanitation services.

Urban local bodies frequently manage drains, waterways, pumping assets and flood-prone locations through fragmented systems, periodic inspections and manual reporting. Water levels, drain flows, rainfall, pump status, water quality and field incidents are often monitored independently, preventing officials from seeing a reliable, real-time operating picture.

This results in delayed identification of rising water levels, drain blockages, pollution events, equipment failures and localized flooding. Response teams may receive information only after citizen complaints or physical inspection, while senior officials lack a unified record of alerts, actions, response times and unresolved risks.

AquaSense addresses this gap through an integrated urban water intelligence platform for continuous monitoring, early warning and coordinated municipal response. The platform connects strategically deployed sensors, existing municipal assets and field observations to a GIS-enabled Mobile/Cloud SCADA dashboard. It supports drain and waterway monitoring, flood-risk alerts, visual verification, asset-health monitoring, incident escalation and historical analysis.

For the T-MAP pilot, the solution can be configured for selected drains, waterways, culverts, underpasses, pumping locations or other vulnerable urban zones identified jointly with the participating ULB.
column37:
Technology converts periodic inspection and fragmented operational data into continuous, decision-ready municipal intelligence.

AquaSense deploys radar or ultrasonic level sensors, open-channel flow instruments, rainfall monitoring, selected water-quality sensors and AquaBrain IoT gateways at critical locations. Where required, AI-enabled cameras provide visual confirmation of water accumulation, blockage or overflow conditions. Existing municipal sensors, pumps and SCADA systems can also be integrated through APIs, Modbus, RS485 or other compatible interfaces.

Field data is transmitted to the AquaSense Mobile/Cloud SCADA and Digital Twin platform. Municipal users receive GIS-based visibility of locations and assets, configurable threshold alerts, trend analysis, equipment-health information, incident records and role-based dashboards. Officials can monitor conditions remotely, acknowledge alerts, assign field action and review response performance.

The system supports low-connectivity conditions through edge-based data logging and synchronization. Its modular architecture allows the ULB to begin with a focused pilot and later expand across wards, drains, waterways and pumping assets without replacing the initial platform.

The technology therefore strengthensnot replacesmunicipal engineers and field teams by enabling earlier detection, faster verification, accountable response and evidence-based planning.
column38:
The immediate need is for reliable, real-time visibility of urban drains, waterways and vulnerable flood locations, combined with a structured mechanism for alerting, verification and municipal response.

Current alternatives include manual inspections, citizen complaints, CCTV feeds, stand-alone sensors, rainfall information and conventional SCADA systems. These approaches provide partial information but usually remain disconnected. Manual inspection is labour-intensive and episodic. CCTV requires continuous human observation and does not independently measure water level or flow. Stand-alone sensors may generate data without integrating it into municipal workflows. Conventional SCADA is often limited to specific pumping or treatment assets and may not provide mobile access, GIS-based incident management or multi-location analytics.

AquaSense combines field telemetry, visual verification, GIS, Mobile/Cloud SCADA, Digital Twin capabilities and role-based response workflows in one modular platform. It can integrate existing municipal infrastructure rather than requiring wholesale replacement.

The platforms value lies not only in collecting data but in translating it into prioritized alerts, response actions, event histories and planning intelligence. This creates a scalable operating layer that can support both immediate monsoon preparedness and longer-term drain and waterway management.

AquaSense follows a business-to-government and business-to-business model, working directly with urban local bodies, utilities, industries, EPC contractors and implementation partners.

The initial engagement typically begins with a paid pilot covering jointly selected locations and measurable operational outcomes. After successful validation, the solution can scale through ward-wise, zone-wise or city-wide deployment. Scale-up revenue includes additional field devices, gateways, integration services, command-centre dashboards and customized analytics.

Recurring revenue is generated through annual platform subscriptions, connectivity, cloud hosting, software support, device-health monitoring, calibration, preventive maintenance and comprehensive operation-and-maintenance contracts. AquaSense can also integrate compatible third-party sensors and existing municipal systems, allowing the platform to scale without depending entirely on proprietary hardware.

For Maharashtra, AquaSense can work through local implementation partners, EPC contractors and municipal technology partners for installation and field maintenance, while retaining responsibility for platform technology, configuration, analytics and technical support.

The principal risks are long municipal procurement cycles, delays in site permissions, variation in field conditions, integration with legacy infrastructure, unreliable power or mobile connectivity, sensor fouling or calibration drift, and inconsistent maintenance after deployment.

Operational adoption is another risk. A technically functional platform will not create impact unless alert responsibilities, escalation procedures and response ownership are clearly defined within the ULB. Payment delays and dependence on annual municipal budgets may also affect the pace of scale-up.

AquaSense mitigates these risks through joint site surveys, modular pilot design, site-specific mounting and connectivity assessments, edge data logging, device-health alerts and integration with existing infrastructure wherever feasible. Sensor selection and maintenance schedules are determined according to the monitoring environment. Role-based dashboards, standard operating procedures and training help embed the system into municipal workflows.

The pilot will establish agreed baseline indicators, alert thresholds, response protocols and measurable success criteria before deployment. Local implementation and maintenance partners will support field coordination and service continuity.

Commercial risk is reduced through milestone-based deployment, clearly defined scope, annual platform and O&M agreements, and phased expansion based on demonstrated pilot performance.

Project Description

Urban water systems frequently depend on fragmented operational information, manual readings and disconnected monitoring systems. This limits the ability of municipal authorities to detect water losses, reservoir overflows, abnormal pressure, pump failures, excessive energy consumption and water-quality deviations in a timely manner.

AquaSense proposes to establish a real-time digital operating system for selected municipal water-supply assets and distribution zones. The proposed solution will combine field instrumentation, AquaBrain IoT gateways, Mobile/Cloud SCADA, operator applications and decision-support dashboards.

Depending on the selected ULB’s requirements and existing infrastructure, the system may include:

- Electromagnetic or ultrasonic flow meters
- Pressure transmitters
- Non-contact water-level sensors
- Pump-status and energy-monitoring devices
- Selected online water-quality sensors
- AquaBrain IoT gateways supporting digital, analogue and RS485/Modbus interfaces
- Solar or battery-supported telemetry at suitable locations
- Secure cloud-based data storage and processing
- GIS-enabled dashboards and automated reports
- Mobile applications for operators and engineers
- Alerts and maintenance workflows

The platform will provide live information on reservoir and tank levels, inlet and outlet flows, distribution pressure, pump operating hours, energy consumption, equipment condition and selected water-quality parameters. Configurable alerts will be generated for reservoir overflow, abnormal flow, suspected leakage, pressure deviation, pump failure, excessive runtime, communication failure and water-quality non-compliance.

Municipal field operators will be able to view assigned assets, acknowledge alerts, submit observations, upload supporting photographs and close maintenance tickets through a mobile application. Engineers and control-room personnel will receive live dashboards, historical trends, alarm status and device-health information. Senior officials will receive consolidated reports and performance indicators for operational and investment decisions.

The project will complement rather than unnecessarily replace existing municipal systems. Where technically feasible and formally approved, AquaSense will integrate its platform with existing SCADA, billing, grievance, laboratory or asset-management systems through APIs or controlled data exchange.

- Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation

- Thane Municipal Corporation

The first ULB, operational zone and assets will be selected based on municipal priorities, infrastructure readiness, data availability and potential for measurable impact. Priority may be given to areas experiencing intermittent supply, high water losses, reservoir overflow, pressure variations, recurring pump failures, water-quality risks or inadequate real-time operational visibility.

Following successful validation, the solution can be expanded to additional zones within the participating city and subsequently replicated across the other priority ULBs and additional Maharashtra cities.

Timelines

AquaSense proposes a 12-month implementation period.

Months 1–2: ULB engagement, site selection, infrastructure assessment, asset and data mapping, baseline establishment, user consultation and detailed system design.

Months 3–5: Procurement, device configuration, field installation, connectivity setup, software configuration, integration, calibration, commissioning and user-acceptance testing.

Months 6–10: Live operation, operator and engineer training, alert verification, maintenance workflows, performance monitoring and iterative system improvement.

Months 11–12: Outcome assessment, documentation, business-model validation, operations and maintenance planning, ULB review and preparation of the second-phase scale-up plan.

Funding Amount Required

AquaSense seeks ?50 lakh from Villgro/T-MAP to undertake the initial pilot.

The indicative utilisation of the ?50 lakh is:

- Sensors, AquaBrain IoT gateways, power systems and field enclosures: ?22 lakh
- Installation, calibration and commissioning: ?7 lakh
- Mobile/Cloud SCADA, dashboards and application configuration: ?8 lakh
- Baseline assessment, asset mapping and system design: ?4 lakh
- Training, operations and maintenance support: ?4 lakh
- Impact measurement, documentation and scale-up planning: ?5 lakh

Subject to successful pilot performance and approval by the participating municipal authority, AquaSense proposes a second-phase ULB contribution of ?50 lakh. This would support expansion to additional water-supply assets or distribution zones, integration with existing municipal systems and continuation of operations and maintenance.

The overall project and scaling opportunity is therefore estimated at ?1 crore:

- Phase 1: ?50 lakh requested from Villgro/T-MAP for pilot implementation
- Phase 2: ?50 lakh proposed from the participating ULB for expansion after validation

The ULB contribution is a proposed scale-up pathway and will not be represented as committed until formal municipal approval is obtained.

Partnerships Associated

AquaSense will serve as the technology and implementation partner. Its responsibilities will include technical assessment, detailed system design, hardware and gateway configuration, deployment support, software implementation, dashboards, mobile applications, system integration, training, maintenance and performance reporting.

The selected ULB—Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation, Mira-Bhayandar Municipal Corporation or Thane Municipal Corporation—will be the proposed municipal implementation partner. Its anticipated role will include:

- Identification of priority sites and operational problems
- Provision of site access and required permissions
- Sharing of available infrastructure and baseline information
- Nomination of operators, engineers and nodal officials
- Participation in system design, training and pilot reviews
- Verification of operational results
- Review of the scale-up and procurement pathway
- Consideration of a ?50 lakh second-phase contribution, subject to municipal approval

Villgro/T-MAP is expected to support municipal engagement, pilot structuring, sector mentorship, implementation review, business-model validation, market access and development of a scalable adoption pathway.

Additional local installation, civil, electrical, connectivity, laboratory or technical partners may be engaged where required. Any partnership or MoU will be presented as confirmed only after the relevant agreement or Letter of Intent has been formally executed.

Expected Impact

In the short term, the project will establish continuous visibility of selected municipal water assets and operating conditions. It will reduce dependence on manual readings and fragmented reporting while enabling faster detection and communication of overflow, leakage indicators, abnormal pressure, pump failure and water-quality risks.

The pilot will target at least 95% platform availability during agreed operating windows. Final targets for data completeness, alert acknowledgement, incident-response time, overflow reduction, pumping efficiency and water-loss identification will be established through the baseline assessment and agreed with the participating ULB.

In the medium term, the ULB will be able to use accumulated operational data to improve pumping schedules, identify avoidable water and energy losses, prioritise preventive maintenance, improve service reliability and allocate municipal resources more efficiently. Zone-level information can also help identify areas facing low pressure, intermittent supply or repeated service disruptions.

Residents served by the selected zones will be the principal social beneficiaries. Particular attention will be given to low-income and densely populated communities, women, elderly people, persons with disabilities and households dependent on unreliable or shared water services. Municipal operators and engineers will benefit from fewer manual inspections, safer operating procedures and improved information for daily decision-making.

In the long term, the project will establish a validated technical, institutional and commercial model for scaling Digital Operational Intelligence across additional zones and Maharashtra ULBs. The commercial model will combine equipment and commissioning revenue with annual software subscriptions, cloud services, operations and maintenance, analytics, training and technical support.

The intended long-term impact is to help Maharashtra ULBs transition from reactive and manually reported water operations to preventive, measurable and data-driven urban water management, contributing to improved water security, climate resilience, accountability and municipal service delivery.

column36:
Construction & Demolition (C&D) waste is one of the most difficult urban waste streams for ULBs to govern because generation is dispersed across thousands of construction sites, while collection, transportation, processing and disposal involve multiple independent stakeholders. Large volumes remain untracked or are illegally dumped, contributing to road dust, air pollution, flooding, land degradation and loss of recoverable construction materials.

While regulations place increasing responsibility on ULBs to monitor C&D waste, most cities still rely on fragmented, manual processes, spreadsheets, permits and point solutions. This limits visibility into how much waste is generated, where it moves, whether it reaches an authorized facility, and how much is actually recycled.

Trace Resource addresses this municipal operational gap through a specialized digital system that enables ULBs to monitor the complete C&D waste lifecycle, improve compliance, identify leakages and build a data-driven circular waste management system.
column37:
Technology is the core enabler of Trace Resource. We convert a fragmented, largely offline C&D waste ecosystem into a digitally traceable, multi-stakeholder network connecting ULBs, waste generators, transporters, recyclers and material buyers.

The platform digitizes workflows such as project registration, waste estimation, waste management plans, approvals, collection requests, transportation and final channelization. GIS, GPS/vehicle tracking, digital transaction records, dashboards and analytics provide visibility into waste movement and enable ULBs to identify exceptions and monitor compliance.

The architecture is modular and configurable, allowing the same core platform to be adapted to different municipal workflows and regulatory requirements without rebuilding the system for every city. API-based integrations can connect with existing municipal systems and construction-permit databases.

Technology also extends beyond waste tracking: our integrated marketplace connects recycled C&D materials with potential buyers, enabling the transition from waste management to material circularity.

Thus, technology is not merely digitizing paperwork it creates the operational intelligence and traceability layer required for a ULB to manage C&D waste as a measurable city-level system
column38:
The primary need is for ULBs to have a single, reliable digital system through which they can operationally manage and monitor C&D waste rather than relying on fragmented records and manual enforcement.

Today, cities typically use a combination of manual permits, spreadsheets, contractor systems, GPS/vehicle-tracking tools and locally developed IT applications. These may address individual steps but generally do not provide end-to-end visibility from waste generation to authorized processing and recycling. Generic waste-management and EPR platforms are also not designed around the unique workflows of C&D waste.

Trace Resource provides a specialized alternative: a configurable municipal platform combining C&D waste compliance workflows, stakeholder management, digital traceability, operational dashboards, analytics and a circular materials marketplace.

The need is therefore not simply another waste-management application, but a dedicated digital operating layer for a waste stream that is large, decentralized and increasingly regulated. For ULBs, this can improve operational efficiency and evidence-based monitoring for developers and contractors, it simplifies compliance and for recyclers, it improves visibility of material flows and potential demand.
column42:
Trace Resource will initially follow a ULB-specific B2G SaaS model for city-level C&D waste governance.

B2G: Urban Local Bodies will be the primary customers and beneficiaries. The initial deployment will require one-time financial support for platform design, workflow customization, technology development, integration and implementation according to the ULB's operational and regulatory requirements. This support will enable the platform to be adapted and deployed effectively within each city.

Following deployment, the platform's ongoing operational and maintenance costs can be recovered through user charges already collected by the ULB from relevant C&D waste generators, transporters, developers and other ecosystem participants. This approach keeps the recurring financial burden on the ULB minimal while creating a sustainable mechanism for continued platform operation, support and improvement.

The model therefore combines one-time deployment support with a recurring, user-charge-backed operating model. Once the initial design and customization are completed, the core technology can be replicated across cities with limited additional development effort, while city-specific workflows and integrations can be configured as required.
column43:
The principal risks are related to municipal adoption, procurement cycles, ecosystem participation and scaling execution.

Municipal adoption/procurement: ULB decision-making and procurement can have long cycles. We mitigate this by demonstrating working deployments, engaging multiple ULBs simultaneously and designing the platform to accommodate existing municipal workflows rather than requiring complete process replacement.

Stakeholder adoption: Generators, transporters and recyclers may initially resist digital processes. Assisted onboarding, simple workflows, training and phased implementation are therefore built into deployments.

Integration and data quality: Municipal systems and data formats vary across cities. Our configurable architecture and API-based approach reduce dependence on a single technology environment, while validation and reconciliation mechanisms improve data integrity.

Execution capacity: City-scale deployment requires both technology and field operations. We are progressively building dedicated implementation and partnership capacity.

Revenue timing/working capital: Government contracts can have longer payment cycles. We are diversifying through B2B subscriptions and marketplace revenues while maintaining a lean operating model.

Market development: C&D digital governance is an emerging category. However, increasing regulatory requirements and demonstrated ULB demand provide a strong structural driver for adoption.

Project Description: 
Trace Resource proposes to deploy and operationalize its specialized digital platform for Construction & Demolition (C&D) waste management with Mira-Bhayandar Municipal Corporation (MBMC). The project will establish an end-to-end digital system for managing C&D waste from generation through transportation, authorized processing/recycling and material recovery.
C&D waste is a highly decentralized and difficult-to-monitor waste stream. MBMC, like other rapidly urbanizing ULBs, requires greater visibility over project-level waste generation, transportation and final channelization. The proposed platform will provide MBMC with a digital operational layer to address this gap.
The deployment will include city-specific workflow configuration, stakeholder onboarding, digital waste-management and approval workflows, transporter and recycler management, GPS-enabled movement tracking, transaction-level traceability, ULB dashboards, exception monitoring, compliance reporting and impact analytics.
This will not only enable the corporation is efficienct facilitation, management, monitoring & governance of C&D waste, mitigate air polltuion, sporadice dumping, and indiscriminate movement of debris; but also help it comply with the new regulations, and directives of Hon. High Court and the High Power Committee. This multi-stakeholder digital public infrastructure will enable the ULB achieve multiple environmental objectives with minimal incremental load on its human and financial resources due to workflow digitization and automation.
The proposed deployment is not a technology-only pilot. It is intended to demonstrate a functional municipal operating model that can subsequently be replicated across other ULBs in Maharashtra.

Geography:
The project will be implemented in Mira-Bhayandar, Maharashtra, with MBMC as the principal municipal partner.
MBMC is strategically important as a demonstration geography because of its rapidly developing built environment and the resulting need for systematic C&D waste governance. The project will subsequently provide a reference model for replication across other Maharashtra ULBs, particularly municipal corporations in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region.

Timeline:
We propose an approximately 4-6 month accelerated deployment and validation period, structured broadly as:

Month 1 - Configuration & Integration:
MBMC workflow assessment, configuration of the platform, data/process mapping and preparation of deployment protocols.
Months 2-3 - Deployment & Stakeholder Activation:
Onboarding of municipal teams, generators/developers, transporters and authorized processors/recyclers; training and commencement of live operations.
Months 3-4 - Operational Monitoring:
Live tracking of waste movements, dashboard-based monitoring, data validation, exception identification and iterative product/process optimization.
Months 5-6 - Impact Validation & Scale Readiness:
Assessment of waste traceability and channelization, recycling/material recovery outcomes, environmental impact indicators and documentation of a replicable MBMC deployment model.

Funding Required:
We seek INR 60 lakh in T-MAP pilot/implementation support.
The funding will primarily support:
MBMC-specific platform customization and system configuration;
Integration with relevant municipal workflows/data systems;
Technology deployment and cloud infrastructure;
Stakeholder onboarding, training and field implementation;
Operational monitoring, data validation and optimization;
Impact measurement and documentation of the MBMC deployment;
Development of a replicable municipal deployment framework for subsequent Maharashtra roll-out.

Trace Resource will contribute its existing technology platform, core product/IP, management and technical resources and prior deployment experience as part of the overall project investment.

The proposed funding is therefore intended to accelerate and de-risk municipal adoption, rather than fund development of an untested technology from the ground up.

Partnerships:
Government / ULB: Mira-Bhayandar Municipal Corporation (MBMC) will be the anchor implementation partner and institutional user, providing municipal workflows, operational coordination, stakeholder access and validation of the deployment.

Construction ecosystem: Developers, contractors and project owners will participate as waste generators and users of the digital compliance and channelization workflows.

Logistics ecosystem: Transporters will use the platform for digital trip management and traceability of C&D waste movement.

Recycling ecosystem: Authorized C&D waste processing/recycling facilities will provide the final processing endpoint and support verification of waste received and processed.

Circular-material ecosystem: Buyers of recycled aggregates and other recovered C&D materials will be connected through the marketplace, creating downstream demand for recovered materials.

Trace Resource will provide the technology, product development, implementation and program-management capabilities required to bring these stakeholders onto a common digital operating layer.

Expected Impact: The project will generate impact across municipal governance, environmental performance and material circularity.

1. Improved municipal operational intelligence:
MBMC will gain a centralized digital view of C&D waste generation, movement and channelization instead of relying predominantly on fragmented/manual records. This will strengthen monitoring, planning, compliance management and evidence-based decision-making.

2. Increased waste traceability:
The platform will create transaction-level digital records linking waste generators, transporters and authorized processing facilities. This will allow MBMC to identify incomplete or anomalous waste journeys and improve accountability across the chain.

3. Increased authorized channelization and recycling:
By making the movement and final destination of C&D waste more visible, the project will support greater diversion from uncontrolled disposal towards authorized processing and recycling.

4. Air-pollution and environmental co-benefits:
Better traceability and channelization can reduce the risk of illegal dumping and uncontrolled handling of C&D waste, thereby contributing indirectly to reduced dust and associated urban air-pollution impacts. The project will quantify waste channelized/recycled and, where adequate data and accepted emission factors are available, estimate associated GHG benefits.

5. Material circularity:
The integrated marketplace will help create a connection between C&D waste processors and users of recycled construction materials, supporting greater utilization of recovered materials and reducing dependence on virgin resources.

6. Replicable municipal model:
The most important outcome of the T-MAP engagement will be a validated, deployment-ready model for digital C&D waste governance that can be adapted to other Maharashtra ULBs. The MBMC implementation will generate operational learnings, standardized workflows, impact metrics and implementation protocols that reduce the time and cost required for subsequent deployments.

Why T-MAP is strategically important

Trace Resource already has demonstrated market validation, including a ?1.1 crore work order from BMC, and has experience deploying its C&D waste technology across multiple cities. The MBMC project therefore represents an opportunity to move beyond individual deployments and establish a repeatable Maharashtra municipal deployment model.

T-MAP's support would provide the catalytic capital and municipal implementation environment required to validate this model in a second major Maharashtra ULB. Successful implementation in MBMC, combined with the existing BMC experience, can create a strong foundation for replication across the Mumbai Metropolitan Region and subsequently across Maharashtra.

The proposed project therefore seeks to demonstrate not merely that Trace Resource's technology works, but that a specialized digital C&D waste governance model can be rapidly adopted, operationalized and replicated by Maharashtra's ULBs.

Indias waste management ecosystem operates largely in silos, with waste generators, collection teams, transporters, processing facilities, waste workers and recyclers functioning through disconnected systems. This creates significant gaps in data, visibility, accountability and traceability across the waste value chain.
Most cities lack a unified digital layer that can map and continuously track where waste is generated, what type of waste is generated, how it is segregated and collected, where it moves, and how it is ultimately processed or recycled. As a result, operational decisions are often based on fragmented records, manual reporting and limited real-time intelligence.
This gap is particularly relevant under the SWM Rules, 2026, which place greater emphasis on digital registration, online reporting and monitoring, geo-tagging of waste-management infrastructure, documentation of waste flows and stronger accountability of waste generators and local bodies. The Rules therefore create a clear need for reliable digital systems that can support both day-to-day operations and compliance.
The absence of technology-enabled coordination makes it difficult to monitor segregation, optimize collection and transportation, verify processing and manage specialized waste streams. Valuable waste can consequently be lost, mixed or diverted.
Our solution addresses this gap by creating a digital intelligence and coordination layer for the waste ecosystem. It connects fragmented stakeholders and data onto a common platform, enabling end-to-end visibility, traceability, digital evidence and operational intelligence. This allows cities to move from siloed waste management to a connected, data-driven and accountable ecosystem, while enabling specialized solutions and supply chains for specific waste streams.
column37:
Technology is the core layer that integrates and connects the fragmented processes of waste management into a single, operationally intelligent ecosystem.
The solution uses mobile applications, GIS-based mapping, dashboards and integrated digital workflows to connect waste generators, collection teams, supervisors, transporters, processing facilities and recyclers. This enables information captured at one stage of the waste value chain to flow seamlessly into the next, creating a connected ecosystem rather than isolated systems.
A key component is the creation of a digital twin of the city, where waste-generating premises, collection points, routes, vehicles, workers, processing facilities and other relevant assets are digitally mapped and GIS-tagged with high location accuracy. This creates a continuously updated digital representation of the city's waste management infrastructure.
Technology also creates digital evidence at the point of activity. Mobile applications enable field teams to capture geo-tagged images, location data, activity records and other operational information, creating verifiable evidence rather than relying solely on manual reporting.
The platform integrates these data points to provide real-time operational visibility, monitoring and analytics, helping identify gaps, improve resource allocation, optimize processes and strengthen accountability.
Thus, technology is not merely being used for digitization it acts as the connective infrastructure between multiple stakeholders and processes, creating a single source of truth for the city's waste management ecosystem.
column38:
The primary need addressed by the solution is to help cities and waste generators meet the evolving requirements of the SWM Rules, 2026, particularly around segregation, accountability, monitoring, traceability and digital management of waste.
The solution addresses these needs through:
End-to-end traceability: Tracks waste from generation and collection through transportation to the appropriate processing facility.
BWG compliance: Creates a digital record of Bulk Waste Generators, their waste generation, segregation, collection and processing arrangements, enabling better monitoring and compliance.
Segregation accountability: Documents segregation at source and provides digital evidence of compliance.
Collection and logistics accountability: Tracks collection activities, routes, movement and field operations through geo-tagged data and image-based evidence.
Processing and disposal monitoring: Digitally maps and monitors processing facilities and disposal points, helping ensure waste reaches appropriate destinations.
Unified data layer: Connects generation, segregation, collection, transportation and processing data within a common platform.
Transparency and operational intelligence: Provides ULBs with verifiable data for monitoring, enforcement, planning and performance management.
Alternatives
Technology solutions already exist for individual SWM functionssuch as fleet management systems, ERP/plant-management systems, collection applications or standalone survey platforms. However, these generally operate as silos and do not provide a unified view required for effective compliance and monitoring under the evolving SWM framework.
Our solution acts as the digital layer connecting these processes, creating one integrated ecosystem for the ULB and BWGs, with end-to-end visibility, evidence, traceability and accountability across the waste value chain.
column42:
Our current business and revenue model operates through two complementary streams:
1. City-level SWM Digital Infrastructure
The primary business model is to provide a technology-enabled Solid Waste Management solution to city administrations and Urban Local Bodies (ULBs). The platform integrates digitization, monitoring, collection, logistics, segregation, processing and operational intelligence into a unified city-wide system.
The engagement is structured as a tendered procurement by the ULB, with Recyclink providing the technology platform, implementation, field digitization and associated operational systems. Revenue is generated through the contracted implementation and ongoing platform/service fees, typically structured around the scale and requirements of the city.
2. Data-led Waste Supply Chains
The second revenue opportunity comes from using the city-level data and intelligence generated through the platform to identify and build specialized waste supply chains.
For example, the platform can identify the quantity and location of food waste generated by large restaurants, or the volume of tender coconut shells generated across a city. This provides visibility into where specific waste streams are generated, their volumes and the potential points of aggregation.
Based on this intelligence, we can forward-integrate into the aggregation and channelization of specific waste streams, connecting generators with appropriate processors and creating value from the movement of these materials through organized supply chains.
column43:
The primary challenges and risks identified in the business are largely associated with the nature of working with government and city administrations, rather than the underlying technology or market need.
Long sales cycles: City-level projects involve tenders, approvals, procurement processes and multiple administrative stakeholders, making government sales cycles significantly longer.
Administrative delays: Project initiation, data access, approvals, field mobilisation and operational decisions can be delayed due to dependencies across departments.
Payment cycles: Government contracts can have extended payment timelines, creating working-capital requirements during implementation.
Operational adoption: Introducing a new digital system across an existing municipal ecosystem requires training, stakeholder engagement and change management. Acceptance can therefore take time, although it typically improves as users experience the operational benefits.
Procurement dependency: A significant portion of the business depends on ULB budgets, tenders and project approvals, creating timing and revenue-visibility risks.
The key business risk is therefore execution and timing risk associated with government businessprojects may take longer to start, scale or generate revenue than initially anticipated.
We mitigate this through phased implementation, pilot-led adoption and a diversified city pipeline.
column44: We measure social impact through multiple, digitally documented indicators across the waste management ecosystem. Quantitatively, we track the number of premises moved towards source segregation, number of citizens and waste-generating premises trained, number of waste workers documented and integrated into the system, and the number of training and capacity-building sessions conducted for waste workers and other stakeholders. Qualitatively, we assess improvements in segregation practices, participation and awareness, as well as the formal documentation and integration of waste workers into municipal operations.
column46:
The beneficiary group comprises a diverse urban population across upper-, middle- and lower-income segments, reflecting the socio-economic diversity of cities in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region (MMR). These cities have relatively high population density and significant vertical development, with a mix of high-rise housing societies, established neighbourhoods, informal settlements and commercial areas.
The programme will cover residential households, housing societies, commercial establishments, institutions and Bulk Waste Generators (BWGs) across both residential and commercial categories. This diversity creates varying patterns of waste generation, segregation and collection requirements.
The beneficiary ecosystem also extends to municipal teams, waste workers, collection and logistics operators, transporters, processing facilities and recyclers. Connecting these stakeholders through a common digital platform will improve visibility, coordination and accountability across the waste value chain.
Given the density and scale of MMR cities, the intervention is particularly relevant for managing high-volume waste generation within concentrated urban clusters, while enabling more efficient collection, processing and recovery.
column47:
Recyclink has conducted large-scale digital Solid Waste Management programmes in Mira Bhayander Municipal Corporation (MBMC) and Thane Municipal Corporation (TMC). These programmes have focused on creating a digital and operational foundation for a connected, accountable and traceable waste management ecosystem.
1. Mira Bhayander Municipal Corporation (MBMC)
The MBMC programme began with a focused pilot in a single ward, designed to establish a digital baseline of the waste ecosystem and demonstrate how technology could connect waste generation, segregation, collection and logistics.
Ward-level pilot
The initial pilot covered approximately 20,000 households and 210 waste-generating premises, including around 2,000 commercial establishments.
Recyclink digitally mapped and tagged waste-generating premises, capturing information on:
Type and nature of waste generated
Segregation practices and standards
Collection arrangements and routes
Logistics and field operations
Waste workers and operational stakeholders
Relevant SWM infrastructure
The objective was not merely to create a database, but to establish a digital operating layer for the entire SWM ecosystem within the pilot geography.
The pilot continued for approximately six months. By connecting generation, segregation, collection and logistics within a common digital framework, the programme achieved an approximately 70 reduction in waste contamination and enabled the SWM operations of the pilot area to be digitally monitored and managed.
The success of this pilot provided the basis for scaling the model across MBMC.
City-wide digitization
The programme was subsequently expanded across Mira Bhayander, covering approximately:
240,000 households
6,000 premises
230 collection routes
Collection and logistics operations
Processing and treatment infrastructure
The programme created a digital representation of the city's SWM ecosystem, connecting waste generators with collection, transportation and processing infrastructure.
Multiple aspects of SWM were brought into a common digital framework, including b
The system also enabled the digital management of approximately 1.1 crore in fines, providing a structured mechanism for recording and managing compliance-related actions.
Waste diversion and specialized supply chains
A significant outcome of the MBMC programme has been the diversion of approximately 45,000 tonnes of waste from landfills through structured channelization and processing.
