For example, mapping large food-waste generators such as restaurants enabled identification and aggregation of food waste for appropriate processing. Similarly, mapping tender coconut vendors and their waste generation enabled the aggregation and downstream processing of coconut waste.
The MBMC programme therefore established a model in which the city could understand what waste is generated, where it is generated, how much is generated, how it is collected, where it moves and how it is ultimately processed.
2. Thane Municipal Corporation (TMC)
Recyclink subsequently implemented a similar digital SWM programme with Thane Municipal Corporation, initially focusing on four wards and approximately 100,000 households.
The programme created a comprehensive digital baseline of the selected areas, covering:
Household and commercial waste generators
Waste types and segregation practices
Collection infrastructure
Collection routes and logistics
Field operations
Waste workers and operational stakeholders
Relevant SWM assets and processing infrastructure
Mobile-based applications were used for field digitization, enabling the capture of location-based information, images and digital evidence. This created a more reliable and verifiable operational database for municipal monitoring.
As with MBMC, the objective was to move beyond standalone digitization and connect the different components of SWM into a common operational ecosystem.
The programme created the foundation for integrating waste generation, segregation, collection, logistics, processing and compliance into a unified city-level platform.
Relevance to the SWM Rules, 2026
The experience from MBMC and TMC is particularly relevant in the context of the SWM Rules, 2026, which increase the emphasis on segregation, accountability, monitoring, digital systems and compliance across the waste management chain.
The Maharashtra programmes have already established many of the foundational layers required for this transition: digitized waste generators, GIS-based mapping, collection routes, logistics, processing infrastructure, waste-stream data, operational information and digital evidence.
The next stage in both cities is therefore to move from digitization to an end-to-end SWM platform.
This platform will connect the complete chainfrom waste generation and segregation to collection, transportation, processing and final channelizationwithin a common digital ecosystem.
The objective is to provide the ULB with a single source of truth for its SWM operations while enabling stronger traceability, transparency, accountability, operational intelligence and compliance.
The MBMC and TMC programmes demonstrate that Recyclink's approach can operate at both pilot and city scale, and that digital SWM infrastructure can move beyond monitoring to deliver measurable outcomes in waste diversion, compliance, operational management and the creation of organized waste supply chains

Waste management transformation takes time because outcomes depend on multiple variables existing infrastructure, segregation practices, waste generation and processing capacity, operational systems, and ultimately, behavioural change among citizens and municipal stakeholders. Recyclink therefore builds impact progressively: from data to intelligence, operational transformation and measurable environmental and social outcomes.
Short Term  Establishing the Digital Foundation
The immediate objective is to create a complete digital baseline of the city's waste ecosystem. This includes mapping and quantifying waste-generating premises, understanding waste streams, documenting collection and processing systems, and mapping available infrastructure.
The platform creates a geographic and demographic understanding of the city, enabling the ULB to determine where waste is generated, what is generated, how much is generated and how it moves through the system.
The immediate impact is therefore visibility, facts and precisioncreating the foundation for informed planning and intervention.
Medium Term  Operational Intelligence and System Improvement
The digital baseline becomes the foundation for monitoring, planning and decision-making. The platform supports improvements in segregation, collection and logistics identifies infrastructure and processing gaps optimizes routes and resources and establishes SOPs, accountability mechanisms and digital workflows.
Data can be viewed from premise to ward to city level, enabling the ULB to move from reactive management to data-driven operations. It also enables targeted citizen and waste-worker training, monitoring of segregation adoption and measurable performance improvement.
Long Term  Connected Waste Intelligence and Circular Supply Chains
The long-term objective is a connected, traceable city-wide waste ecosystem, linking generation and collection through transportation to appropriate processing facilities using digital records and evidence.
This enables cities to measure waste actually diverted from landfills, rather than simply reporting waste collected. City-level intelligence can also support specialized supply chains for food, wet, dry and biomass/coconut waste, connecting each stream to appropriate recovery and processing infrastructure.
The resulting impact spans:
Environmental: Increased segregation, processing and landfill diversion.
Operational: Better collection, logistics, resource utilization and processing efficiency.
Social: Greater participation and integration of workers and communities.
Governance: Transparency, accountability and evidence-based decisions.
Economic: Organized waste supply chains and value recovery.
Intelligence: A continuously updated digital representation of the city's waste ecosystem.
Ultimately, digitization becomes a core layer of sustainable waste management. A city cannot effectively manage what it cannot see, measure or understand. Recyclink creates that visibility and progressively converts it into intelligence, action and measurable impact.

Recyclink is seeking support to scale and enhance its digital urban solid waste management platform, building on its existing implementation experience with Mira-Bhayander Municipal Corporation (MBMC) and Thane Municipal Corporation (TMC). The proposed project will strengthen the technology layer that enables cities to monitor, manage, optimise and ensure compliance across the waste-management chain.
The platform creates a connected digital foundation across waste generation, segregation, collection, transportation, processing and recovery/recycling. It combines city-level digitisation and GIS mapping with operational workflows, compliance monitoring, dashboards, analytics and decision-support tools.
The proposed ?90 lakh programme will be implemented over 12 months. It will use MBMC and TMC as real-world deployment environments to develop and validate enhanced capabilities in waste-flow intelligence, route and operational optimisation, BWG compliance, GPS/IoT-enabled monitoring and data-driven decision-making. Over the subsequent 24 months, the validated model will be positioned for replication across additional Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) in Maharashtra.
Problem and Scaling Opportunity
India’s urban waste-management challenge is no longer only about collection and processing capacity. A critical gap lies in the visibility, integration and intelligence needed to manage the system effectively.
ULBs often have aggregate waste data but limited granular visibility into where waste is generated, who generates it, what type of waste is generated, whether it is segregated, where it is collected and transported, and how it is ultimately processed or recovered. Collection, transportation, processing, BWG management, enforcement and citizen engagement also frequently operate as separate functions, limiting coordination and accountability.
Even where operational data is captured, it is not always converted into useful intelligence for route optimisation, performance monitoring, resource planning, compliance management or identification of service gaps. At the same time, the SWM Rules, 2026 place greater emphasis on segregation, BWG responsibilities, documentation, monitoring, accountability and digital reporting.
This creates a significant opportunity for a common digital layer that connects existing municipal systems rather than replacing them. Recyclink’s approach is to integrate existing infrastructure, stakeholders and workflows into a common digital framework and add capabilities for monitoring, analytics, compliance and decision support.
The project also addresses a second scaling opportunity: converting city-level intelligence into specialised waste-management interventions. Once the platform can identify where specific material streams are generated, their quantities and their downstream pathways, Recyclink can help organise aggregation and channelisation around those streams. This creates a bridge between digital operational intelligence and circular waste supply chains.
Building on MBMC and TMC, the project will therefore create a configurable technology architecture that can be deployed across cities with different operational models while retaining a common digital and intelligence layer.
Project Description
The proposed project will build the next technology layer on city-level digitisation already undertaken by Recyclink. Recyclink has created a substantial digital foundation across MBMC, covering approximately 240,000 households, and TMC, covering approximately 100,000 households. Rather than recreating this baseline, the programme will use the existing mapping, data and field workflows to develop enhanced technology capabilities.
The project will evolve through five interconnected layers.
1. Existing Digital City Foundation
The platform structures the city from City ? Zone ? Ward ? Area ? Premises. Existing digitisation covers households, housing societies/RWAs, commercial establishments, BWGs, collection infrastructure, routes, processing facilities and other relevant SWM assets.
This creates the base layer on which intelligence, monitoring and optimisation tools can be built.
2. Collection and Operational Intelligence
The programme will strengthen digital capabilities around collection coverage, segregation, routes, workforce activity and service performance.
The objective is to move beyond recording activities towards identifying operational gaps, improving resource utilisation and supporting data-driven municipal decisions.
3. Waste-Flow and Resident-to-Recycler Traceability
The platform will progressively connect waste generation and collection with downstream processing and recovery.
Different material streams can be linked to appropriate pathways, such as food/wet waste to biomethanation, dry waste to MRFs and recyclers, and biomass waste to appropriate processors.
This will improve visibility of material movement and strengthen Recyclink’s Resident-to-Recycler model.
4. Compliance and BWG Management
The platform will strengthen the identification, qualification and quantification of Bulk Waste Generators, along with compliance tracking, documentation, authorised vendor information and processing evidence.
This will provide ULBs with a structured digital mechanism to manage an increasingly important area of SWM compliance.
5. Intelligence, Analytics and Decision Support
The key technology advancement will be an intelligence layer over the digitised city.
This will include enhanced ULB dashboards, performance analytics, operational alerts, waste-flow analysis, compliance intelligence, trend identification, optimisation tools and structured reporting.
The progression is therefore:
Digitisation ? Monitoring ? Intelligence ? Optimisation
The approximately 340,000 households already covered across MBMC and TMC provide a significant real-world foundation for testing, refining and validating these capabilities before replication.
Geography and Scale
The funded programme will focus primarily on MBMC and TMC, using both cities as technology-development and validation environments.
MBMC: Mature Implementation Environment
MBMC represents Recyclink’s most mature city-level implementation, covering approximately 240,000 households.
The work has provided Recyclink with substantial on-ground experience across municipal operations, collection systems, waste flows, processing pathways and implementation challenges.
The project will use this foundation to demonstrate how an established city-level digital system can evolve into a more intelligent and scalable SWM platform.
TMC: Expansion and Validation Environment
TMC provides a second implementation environment, with approximately 100,000 households covered through digitisation.
This provides another municipal context in which enhanced technology capabilities can be tested, refined and validated.
Maharashtra-wide Replication
The wider scaling opportunity is Maharashtra. MBMC provides implementation depth, while TMC provides a second operating environment to test transferability.
Together, they create a foundation for standardising the product and implementation model before deployment across additional ULBs.
The approach is therefore:
MBMC as the mature implementation environment ? TMC as the validation environment ? Maharashtra as the immediate replication market.
Timeline and Implementation
The funded project will run for 12 months, followed by a replication and scale-up horizon over the subsequent 24 months.
Phase 1: Baseline Consolidation, BWG Mapping and Technology Design | Months 0–3
Existing premises, waste-generation, collection, processing and infrastructure data across MBMC and TMC will be consolidated.
Particular focus will be placed on the identification, mapping, quantification and qualification of BWGs. Technology and workflow gaps will also be identified to guide product development.
Phase 2: Operational Technology Integration | Months 3–6
Enhanced operational capabilities will be introduced and tested, including:
•	GPS-enabled collection monitoring
•	Route optimisation tools
•	Workforce and supply-chain integration
•	Improved ULB dashboards
•	Selected IoT-based monitoring at processing facilities, where technically and operationally feasible
Phase 3: Intelligence, Compliance and Optimisation | Months 6–9
Digitised and operational data will be converted into actionable intelligence through:
•	BWG compliance management
•	Performance analytics
•	Waste-flow intelligence
•	Operational alerts
•	Optimisation tools
•	Structured reporting
Phase 4: Validation, Standardisation and Scale Readiness | Months 9–12
The final phase will evaluate performance, consolidate learning across both cities, standardise workflows and refine the technology architecture for replication across additional ULBs in Maharashtra.
Over the following 12 months, Recyclink will pursue replication through ULB-funded contracts, government programmes and corporate partnerships.
Partnerships and Ecosystem Model
Recyclink will act as the technology and integration layer connecting ULBs, government stakeholders, technology companies and waste-management partners.
Government and ULBs: MBMC and TMC will provide the institutional and operational environments for implementation, coordination, field validation and product feedback.
Processing and Recycling Partners: These partners will support downstream integration of material streams, appropriate recovery and recycling pathways, and evidence of material diversion.
Corporate Partners: Corporate partnerships can support technology, infrastructure, sustainability and city-level programmes, including potential CSR-backed deployments.
Cisco Technology Partnership: Recyclink will explore a potential partnership with Cisco’s relevant business and government teams to assess technologies that can strengthen the platform. Areas for exploration may include IoT, connectivity, edge technologies, data infrastructure, cybersecurity, analytics and monitoring solutions, subject to technical and deployment feasibility.
Successful integrations can subsequently become reusable components of Recyclink’s broader platform rather than remaining one-off city-specific deployments.
Funding Requirement
Recyclink is seeking ?90 lakh for the 12-month programme.
The funding will support the following principal areas:
•	Manpower: Technology/product management, data management, field implementation and programme teams.
•	Technology and Software: Platform enhancement, new features, integrations, cloud and database infrastructure.
•	IT Hardware: Field devices, GPS-enabled systems, selected IoT systems and other operational technology required for testing and deployment.
•	Implementation and Management: Field coordination, travel, ULB engagement, administration and programme management.
•	IEC and Capacity Building: Training and engagement of ULB teams, BWGs, RWAs and other stakeholders.
•	Contingency: Technology integration requirements and field-level implementation variations.
Because substantial digitisation already exists across MBMC and TMC, the funding can be directed primarily towards technology enhancement, integration, field validation and deployment, rather than rebuilding the underlying city database.
The programme follows a clear pathway:
Build ? Demonstrate ? Validate ? Standardise ? Replicate
The grant-funded programme is intended to de-risk product development and validation in live municipal environments. Future deployments are expected to transition towards paid ULB contracts and other institutional funding channels.
The project is therefore not conceived as a standalone pilot, but as a product-development and market-validation programme that creates reusable technology, implementation protocols and evidence for subsequent commercial scale.
Expected Impact
The primary 12-month impact will be the conversion of existing city-level digitisation into stronger operational intelligence, compliance management and decision-support capabilities.
1. Enhanced Digital Infrastructure
The programme will deploy additional technology on the existing digital foundation, improve integration across collection, transportation, processing and recovery, and strengthen dashboards and analytical tools used by ULBs.
It will also test capabilities such as route optimisation, GPS-enabled monitoring and selected IoT-based processing monitoring in live municipal environments.
2. Improved ULB Visibility and Decision-Making
ULBs will gain more granular visibility into collection coverage, service gaps, waste flows, processing, BWG compliance and operational performance.
The objective is to move from periodic and aggregate reporting towards more continuous, evidence-based operational management.
3. Stronger BWG Management
The programme will strengthen the BWG digital layer through identification, mapping, quantification, compliance tracking, documentation and reporting.
This will help ULBs manage a critical component of SWM compliance using structured and verifiable data.
4. Operational Efficiency
Integration of field and operational data with digital tools will support better route planning, resource allocation, identification of service gaps and performance management.
Rather than relying only on static reports, municipal teams will be able to use operational data to improve decisions.
5. Waste-Flow Traceability and Recovery
By strengthening the connection between generators, collection systems and downstream processors/recyclers, the programme will improve visibility into where material moves after collection.
This will support stronger diversion reporting and organised supply chains for specific waste streams.
6. Replicable Technology Architecture
A critical outcome will be a common technology architecture that can be configured for different cities rather than rebuilt for every ULB.
The common layer will include:
•	Data model and platform architecture
•	Digital city and waste-generator mapping
•	Operational workflows and dashboards
•	BWG compliance framework
•	Reporting and analytics
•	Waste-flow architecture
•	Core technology integrations
The configurable layer will adapt to each city’s:
•	Geography and administrative structure
•	Collection and transportation model
•	Processing infrastructure
•	Vendors and ecosystem partners
•	Waste quantities and material flows
•	Local SOPs and operating practices
This distinction between common and configurable components is central to scalability. It reduces the time, cost and custom development required for each new city while preserving flexibility for different municipal contexts.
Impact Beyond the Programme
The larger opportunity lies in replication.
Once the enhanced platform has been validated across MBMC and TMC, Recyclink intends to deploy the model across additional ULBs in Maharashtra through municipal procurement, government programmes and corporate partnerships.
The longer-term impact can therefore extend beyond improved SWM performance in two cities. The project will create reusable digital infrastructure, standardised workflows, stronger compliance systems, improved waste-recovery pathways and a more evidence-based approach to municipal decision-making.
It will also strengthen Recyclink’s ability to use city-level waste intelligence to identify specialised waste streams and develop organised supply chains around materials such as food waste, dry recyclables and biomass waste.
This links Recyclink’s two core strengths: digital operational intelligence and specialised waste solutions.
Scalability and Replicability
The core scaling opportunity is to develop a common architecture that can be configured for different ULBs without creating a new system for each city.
The platform’s common components will include digital mapping, waste-generator registries, data architecture, operational workflows, dashboards, compliance systems, analytics, traceability and technology integrations.
City-specific configuration will account for geography, administrative structure, collection and transportation arrangements, processing assets, vendors, material flows and local SOPs.
MBMC and TMC therefore function as live validation environments for a repeatable technology and implementation model.
Each additional city can begin with an established architecture and configure it to local conditions, significantly reducing deployment complexity, time and cost.
Summary
India’s SWM challenge increasingly requires better visibility, accountability, traceability and decision-making, in addition to physical infrastructure.
Recyclink is building the digital intelligence layer that allows ULBs to see how their waste systems function, identify gaps, improve operations and track material flows more reliably.
The proposed ?90 lakh, 12-month project will use existing digitisation across approximately 340,000 households in MBMC and TMC to develop, deploy and validate enhanced capabilities in operational intelligence, BWG compliance, route optimisation, GPS/IoT-enabled monitoring, waste-flow traceability and decision support.
The immediate outcome will be stronger technology and operational capability in the two participating ULBs. The larger opportunity is to establish a standardised, configurable and replicable digital architecture that can be deployed across Maharashtra’s ULBs and, over time, across other Indian cities.

column36:
We through or patented TrashBot technology, address one of Indias most persistent environmental and public-health challenges: the safe and effective processing of mixed municipal solid waste (MSW).
A large proportion of municipal waste reaches collection and processing facilities in an unsegregated condition, containing food waste, plastics, paper, cardboard, sanitary waste, metals and other contaminants. Such mixed waste is difficult to recycle or compost and often ends up being dumped or burnt, contributing to landfill accumulation, air, soil and water pollution, greenhouse-gas emissions and health risks. Manual segregation is not only inefficient at scale but also exposes sanitation workers to hazardous and unhygienic conditions.
We address this problem through automated segregation of mixed waste with minimal or no direct human contact. TrashBot separates incoming waste primarily into biodegradable (having efficiency of minimum 85) and non-biodegradable streams, enabling the wet fraction to be directed towards composting or biogas and the dry fraction towards recycling, RDF or other recovery pathways.
The innovation therefore shifts waste management from a collect-and-dump model to a resource-recovery and circular-economy model, while improving worker safety, reducing landfill dependency and creating economic value from waste.
column37:
Technology is the core enabler of our innovation, transforming the conventional, labour-intensive approach to mixed-waste management into an automated resource-recovery process. TrashBot is a technology-driven automated mixed-waste segregation system designed to process fresh mixed municipal solid waste. Our technology can automatically sort mixed waste into wet, dry, inert (diapers, sanitary napkins, shoes, belts) and metal fractions, enabling subsequent recovery and recycling.

TrashBot integrates a combination of mechanical handling, conveyors, bag opening, magnetic separation, airflow-based separation and size-based sorting to identify and separate different materials from heterogeneous municipal solid waste. This reduces dependence on manual segregation and enables processing at significantly larger volumes.
Technology also plays a critical role beyond segregation. Once separated, the different waste streams can be directed towards appropriate value-recovery pathways: organic waste for composting or biogas, recyclables for material recovery, and difficult plastics such as multilayer plastics for recycling into products such as boards and lumber.
column38:
TrashBot addresses a critical need in municipal solid waste management: the safe, efficient and scalable segregation of mixed waste when source segregation is inadequate. Mixed municipal waste contains food waste, plastics, paper, cardboard, sanitary waste, metals and other contaminants. Manual segregation is difficult, unhygienic and exposes waste workers to health hazards. TrashBot is designed to automate this difficult stage, separating mixed waste into primarily biodegradable and non-biodegradable streams, with minimal or no direct human contact. The outputs can then be directed towards composting/biogas, recycling, RDF or other recovery pathways.

Available alternatives:
Manual segregation: Widely used but labour-intensive, unhygienic and difficult to scale for large quantities of mixed waste.

Source segregation: Separating wet, dry and other waste at household/commercial level reduces the need for downstream sorting, but depends heavily on consistent public participation and collection systems.

Trommel-based processing: Used for screening and separating waste by size, but we identifies limitations when handling highly mixed waste and frequent cleaning of clogged hoels.

The biggest challenge faced by us is the adoption of a new technology within a traditionally structured waste-management ecosystem. Municipal solid waste management has historically relied on conventional segregation and processing methods, and many stakeholders have become accustomed to accepting their limitations and relatively low efficiency. Introducing an innovative, automated and patented technology therefore requires a significant change in mindset, processes and procurement practices.
A major barrier is the municipal tendering and project-planning system. Municipal Corporations and Urban Local Bodies generally implement projects based on Detailed Project Reports (DPRs), technical specifications and tender documents prepared well in advance. In many cases, these DPRs specify conventional segregation equipment designed primarily for processing legacy or mixed waste. As a result, even when TrashCon demonstrates the superior capabilities and benefits of TrashBot, the technology may not be eligible for consideration if the prescribed DPR or tender specifications do not include or permit such technology.
This creates a technology-adoption and market-access risk, rather than merely a technology-performance risk. There is also a need to educate consultants, DPR preparation agencies, municipal decision-makers, contractors and operators about the technology and its measurable benefits.

Urban local bodies managing solid waste and water infrastructure routinely operate without real-time visibility into their own systems and hence lack the operational backbone to convert waste management from a collection-only service into a circular, accountable system. Three linked failures recur: source segregation is poorly enforced because there is no way to verify compliance at the household or establishment level, so contamination undermines everything downstream, including recycling and safe disposal of niche waste streams.
Collection vehicles run un-tracked routes, smart bins overflow undetected, weighbridge data is recorded on paper or in disconnected spreadsheets, and workforce attendance is self-reported.
And where multiple operators serve a city, there is no common, verifiable basis to compare performance on KPIs and compliance.
The compounding effect: without segregation compliance data, contamination keeps recyclable material out of the circular economy and drives more waste to landfill without service-linked billing, ULBs cannot fund improvements from user fees without comparable KPIs across vendors, poor performance goes unchallenged. Together, this keeps landfill diversion and recycling rates low and leaves the carbon and climate impact of poor waste management largely unmeasured.
For a city the size of Mumbai, Thane, or Mira Bhayandar, this translates into thousands of tonnes of waste moving daily through a system the municipality can only partially see: SLA violations go unflagged, route inefficiencies persist unnoticed, and citizen engagement takes a back seat.
column37:
Technology is central to converting waste operations from collection logistics into a verifiable, circular system. QR or RFID tags at the household/bin level link collection events to specific service points, enabling verification of source segregation and fee collection tied to actual, confirmed service rather than flat, unverified billing. Computer vision-based waste classification adds a further compliance layer, flagging contaminated loads at collection or MRF-processing points.
This same data feeds a KPI-based dashboard that benchmarks operator and vendor performance against defined service standards  pickup punctuality, segregation compliance rates, complaint resolution time, giving ULBs the tools to hold multiple vendors within a city to a common, transparent standard, and to introduce structured, healthy competition rather than relying on complaint-driven oversight.
Underlying this: GPS fleet tracking, smart bin sensors, weighbridge integration, and GIS mapping provide the real-time operational layer these KPIs are built on. Route optimization improves efficiency and reduces fuel-related emissions. Analytics translate this operational data into landfill diversion and recycling-rate tracking, and into estimated carbon impact - an evidence base for climate reporting, not just operational reporting.
A citizen engagement layer closes the loop, allowing residents to report issues or verify collection, which feeds back into the same operational dataset rather than existing as a separate complaint channel.
The design principle throughout is integration over addition: rather than layering another standalone tool onto a ULB's existing infrastructure, our technology connects what already exists into one coherent, real-time system of record.
column38:
ULBs need a way to make waste management circular and accountable, verifying source segregation, linking fees to service delivery, and creating comparable performance standards across vendors  rather than operating a collection-only, complaint-driven system with no feedback loop into recycling rates or carbon outcomes.
Available alternatives fall short. Manual, paper-based tracking offers no segregation verification and no way to link billing to service. Standalone GPS or RFID-only tools verify vehicle movement or occasional check-ins but don't connect to fee collection, segregation compliance, or cross-vendor benchmarking. Flat-fee municipal billing, which is still the norm in most ULBs, charges residents regardless of service quality, removing any incentive loop for improvement. Generic ERP/logistics platforms are built for private supply chains, not multi-vendor municipal accountability, and are priced beyond most ULB budgets. Global smart-city platforms may offer partial integration but are typically priced for larger city budgets and don't specifically target segregation-linked circularity or vendor benchmarking.
Our innovation sits in this gap: a municipal-first platform that ties QR/RFID-verified service delivery to fee collection, enforces segregation compliance through verifiable data, and applies a KPI-based system that lets ULBs compare and incentivize multiple vendors within the same city, turning operational data into a lever for landfill diversion, higher recycling rates, and measurable carbon impact.
column42:
We operate a B2B2G SaaS model, contracting with waste management operators, EPR-obligated brands, and municipal bodies rather than selling directly to residents. Revenue is structured as a recurring subscription, typically priced per household served or per tonne of waste processed through the platform, with tiered pricing based on the scope of modules deployed (fleet tracking, bin monitoring, weighbridge integration, analytics, citizen engagement).
This model aligns our revenue with the client's operational scale: as a city's household coverage or waste volume grows, platform fees scale proportionately, keeping pricing predictable for ULB budgeting cycles rather than requiring large upfront capital outlay.
Beyond subscription revenue, we see growing potential in circularity-linked revenue: in Indonesia, our data has supported a plastic credit generation pathway, converting verified recycling and diversion outcomes into a tradable environmental finance instrument. We see a similar model as a longer-term, complementary revenue stream in Maharashtra ULB pilots once source segregation and recycling-rate data reach sufficient verification maturity.
For pilot engagements with Urban Local Bodies such as those in Mumbai, Thane, and Mira Bhayandar, we propose an initial pilot-scope deployment covering a defined ward or zone, with pricing and terms structured to convert into a longer-term operator or ULB contract upon successful validation. This mirrors our current commercial approach across 13 cities in India, Indonesia, and Singapore, where pilot-to-contract conversion has been the primary path to sustained, recurring revenue rather than one-off project fees.
column43:
The primary risks are structural and behavioral rather than purely technical. ULB procurement and approval cycles are often slow and vulnerable to administrative or political turnover, which can delay pilot-to-contract conversion even where performance is demonstrated. Budget allocation for digital tools also competes with more visible infrastructure spending, making funding continuity beyond a pilot period a genuine risk unless outcomes are quantified early.
Behavioral risk sits at both ends of the chain: resident compliance with source segregation cannot be mandated by technology alone and requires sustained citizen engagement alongside enforcement and where multiple vendors are benchmarked, resistance from lower-performing operators is likely, particularly if KPI-based competition affects contract renewal or reputation.
Field-level risks include hardware durability - QR/RFID tags, sensors, and GPS devices deployed on public infrastructure are exposed to vandalism, theft, and tampering and inconsistent network coverage in denser or lower-income wards, which can affect data completeness.
We mitigate these through phased rollout starting with a defined ward or zone, citizen engagement campaigns tied to segregation compliance incentives, transparent KPI-setting processes that operators are consulted on rather than unilaterally imposed, ruggedized and tamper-resistant hardware based on prior deployment experience, and early evidence-building on cost savings and compliance improvement to support sustained budget commitment.

Project Description
We propose to deploy EcoSense's digital operating platform for municipal solid waste management as a Digital Operational Intelligence pilot within a defined ward or zone of an Urban Local Body in Mumbai, Thane, or Mira Bhayandar, to be finalized in scoping discussions with the host ULB. The pilot addresses three linked, currently unsolved problems within the chosen ward: the absence of verifiable source segregation compliance, the disconnect between user fee collection and actual service delivery, and the lack of a common, KPI-based basis to evaluate and compare vendor performance where multiple operators may be involved.

The pilot integrates four parallel data flows into a single platform, following an architecture already proven across our 13+ city deployments in India and Indonesia: collection fleet tracking via GPS devices and windshield RFID tags fitted to municipal or operator vehicles, giving real-time route adherence and coverage visibility; bin monitoring via IoT fill-level sensors, RFID tags, and proximity/movement sensors across a representative set of bins in the ward, flagging overflow risk and missed collections; workforce tracking in dual mode — wearable GPS for street sweepers and mobile-app-based tracking for collection crews — capturing attendance, task completion, and coverage without requiring new hardware for every worker category; and weighbridge integration, using UHF tag readers and ANPR (automatic number plate recognition) cameras at the ward's or ULB's existing weighbridge to digitize tonnage records by vehicle and, where the terminal supports it, by waste category, replacing manual logging at source.

Sitting above this data layer, our KPI dashboard converts these feeds into a single, auditable compliance and performance score for ULB officials — covering collection punctuality, bin servicing consistency, segregation compliance signals, and vendor SLA adherence. Where the ward is served by more than one operator, this dashboard is designed specifically to give the ULB a common, defensible basis for comparing performance and introducing structured, healthy competition rather than static, tenure-based vendor arrangements.

A citizen-facing layer, delivered through the existing EcoSense mobile app, extends the pilot beyond back-end operations: residents in the pilot ward receive collection schedule visibility, can lodge and track complaints, and receive Information, Education and Communication (IEC) content designed to build source segregation habits — directly supporting the segregation compliance data the platform is built to capture.

A near-free but high-value addition within this scope is a landfill-diversion percentage for the pilot ward, computed directly from weighbridge tonnage and waste-type data once that data is flowing — an analytics exercise on top of existing deliverables rather than new build scope. We would also explore, as an exploratory and clearly confidence-labeled stretch output subject to data quality and timeline, an estimated CO?e-avoided figure for the ward. We deliberately keep any carbon-credit monetization pathway outside pilot scope; our approach is to demonstrate this data foundation cleanly first; longer-term circularity-linked revenue mechanisms, of the kind we have supported in Indonesia through verified recycling data, are relevant only as a "what this unlocks" narrative for later scale-up, not a pilot deliverable.

The design principle throughout is integration over addition: the pilot connects data the ULB and its operators already generate — vehicle movement, bin status, weighbridge records, worker attendance — into one coherent, real-time system, rather than layering another disconnected tool onto existing infrastructure.

Geography
The pilot is proposed within one Urban Local Body among Mumbai, Thane, and Mira Bhayandar, with the specific ULB and ward to be confirmed jointly with the host city and T-MAP program partners during scoping. We recommend a single ward or a comparably bounded zone as the pilot geography — substantial enough to generate statistically meaningful, city-relevant performance data, but bounded enough to keep implementation timelines and cost realistic and to avoid the "sweeping ambition over focused plan" risk that undermines pilot credibility with evaluators and city officials alike.
This ward-first approach mirrors our deployment pattern in prior new-geography engagements (including our current Indian and Indonesian deployments), where a defined zone serves as both a proof point and the basis for city-wide or multi-ULB scale-up decisions.

Timelines
We propose a phased pilot running approximately 8 months from mobilization, structured as follows:
Months 1 (Baseline & Setup): Confirm the host ULB and ward; complete a multi-week operational baseline covering current collection coverage, missed-collection rates, and (where available) existing segregation compliance and weighbridge data; procure and install hardware (GPS units, bin sensors, RFID tags, weighbridge UHF reader and ANPR camera); onboard fleet, bin, and weighbridge data feeds into the platform; conduct ground staff and ULB official training.

Months 2–3 (System Live): Bring the full platform live across all four workstreams — fleet, bins, workforce, and weighbridge — with the KPI dashboard operational for ULB officials and the citizen app launched within the pilot ward, including initial IEC activity on source segregation.

Months 4–6 (Trend Visibility & Optimization): Generate a full, sustained data trend (rather than an early snapshot) across missed collections, bin servicing, route efficiency, and — where the weighbridge terminal captures waste-type granularity — landfill diversion percentage. Use this period to refine routes, address early operational friction identified through the dashboard, and begin structured vendor performance review where multiple operators are present.

Months 7–8 (Review & Transition): Consolidate pilot results into a documented performance report for the ULB, covering all committed KPIs and the financial sustainability pathway; present findings to municipal stakeholders; and structure the transition from pilot to an ongoing subscription or operator contract, consistent with our pilot-to-contract conversion approach across current deployments.
This timeline is intentionally realistic rather than compressed: a single-snapshot baseline understates real operational variation, while a full multi-month live period is what allows the ULB to see a genuine, defensible trend rather than an early and possibly misleading blip.

Funding Amount Required
The final pilot budget will be scoped jointly with the host ULB and T-MAP program partners based on confirmed ward boundaries, existing infrastructure (particularly weighbridge terminal capability), and hardware requirements. We anticipate this falling within a proportionate share of the programme's cumulative ?3 crore pilot pool, structured across hardware & installation, platform configuration & integration, training & program management, and contingency — consistent with the phased approach outlined above.

An indicative breakdown:
•	Hardware & installation (~30%): GPS devices for a representative fleet subset, bin fill-level sensors and RFID tags across the pilot ward's bin network, wearable GPS units for street sweepers, UHF reader and ANPR camera for weighbridge integration, and installation/mounting costs.
•	Platform configuration & integration (~35%): Configuration of the EcoSense platform to the ward's specific vendor, reporting, and data structures; weighbridge terminal integration (the most technically involved element, requiring mapping of existing data formats and handling of edge cases such as failed reads); KPI dashboard setup; citizen app deployment for the ward.
•	Training & program management (~20%): Onboarding and training for ULB officials, operator staff, and ground crews; on-ground program management across the pilot period; IEC content development and delivery for citizen segregation engagement.
•	Contingency (~15%): Covering hardware replacement (vandalism, theft, or damage risk on public infrastructure), connectivity gaps in denser wards, and any bin procurement needs if existing bins are not compatible with sensor retrofitting.
We would welcome T-MAP's implementation support in de-risking elements of this budget — particularly weighbridge integration and hardware procurement, where ULB-side infrastructure familiarity and program facilitation reduce both cost and delivery risk relative to a fully self-funded pilot.

Partnerships Associated
Urban Local Body: The host ULB (Mumbai, Thane, or Mira Bhayandar) is the anchor partner, providing the pilot ward, access to existing infrastructure (weighbridge, bin network, vehicle fleet), a designated nodal officer for coordination, and institutional buy-in for ground-level rollout, including staff training participation and support for citizen-facing IEC activity within the ward.

Government/Program Partners (Villgro, Cisco 40 Communities, LEAP Cities): As the program's architects, Villgro and Cisco provide the pilot pool funding structure, implementation support, and the direct relationship with ULB stakeholders that de-risks first-time deployment in a new state. We see this partnership extending beyond funding into program facilitation — particularly around introductions to ULB technical teams and any existing municipal digital infrastructure Villgro/Cisco's needs assessment has already identified as relevant.

Corporate/Operator Partnerships: Where the pilot ward is served by an existing waste management operator, that operator becomes a direct implementation partner — our B2B2G model is built around working alongside contracted operators rather than replacing them, using their existing fleet and workforce as the operational base the platform digitizes. This mirrors our current operator partnerships with Urban Enviro and 3R Waste Management elsewhere in India. Where the ULB manages collection departmentally rather than through a private operator, the ULB's own operations team serves this role directly.

Our own team and advisors: Our core technical team (led by our CTO) manages platform configuration and weighbridge integration; our carbon specialist supports the diversion-percentage and any exploratory CO?e analysis; and our advisory network, which includes South and Southeast Asian urban waste strategy expertise, supports context-appropriate implementation planning specific to dense Indian metro environments.

Expected Impact Description
Based on outcomes demonstrated across our current deployments, we expect this pilot to deliver measurable operational, environmental, and governance impact within the ward, reported as evidence-backed, conservative estimates rather than guaranteed outcomes:

Operational impact: A 25–40% reduction in missed collections through real-time fleet and bin visibility; a 5–8% improvement in route efficiency through data-driven route optimization; 2–5 hours per week of supervisor time saved through automated reporting replacing manual tracking; and a 15–25% reduction in bin overflow incidents through sensor-triggered servicing alerts.

Environmental impact: A landfill diversion improvement in the range of 5–15 percentage points for the pilot ward, computed directly from weighbridge tonnage and waste-type data; and, where the weighbridge terminal supports the necessary waste-category granularity, an exploratory carbon impact estimate potentially in the range of 500–1,500 tCO?e avoided per year, calculated using IPCC/DEFRA emission factors applied to ward-level operational data and clearly labeled as a conservative, confidence-rated estimate.

Governance and accountability impact: ULB officials gain, for the first time, real-time, auditable visibility into fleet, bin, weighbridge, and workforce operations within the pilot ward, replacing manual, self-reported compliance with verifiable data. Where multiple vendors operate in the ward, the KPI dashboard establishes a common, transparent performance benchmark that supports evidence-based vendor evaluation and structured competition, rather than reliance on complaint-driven oversight. JalSevak Solutions addresses the growing need for decentralized wastewater treatment and reuse, with a primary focus on greywater generated from residential, commercial and institutional activities. Greywater from bathing, laundry and washbasins forms a significant portion of wastewater, yet it is often discharged instead of being treated and reused, increasing freshwater demand and wastewater disposal.

Our flagship WARSHA system addresses this challenge at smaller residential scales by providing a compact, automated greywater recycling solution in 1, 2 and 5 KLD capacities. The broader product portfolio extends the same approach to larger and specialized applications through JalWASH, a scalable solution for 10100 KLD facilities, and GREEN, a movable system for construction sites and temporary facilities.

The systems enable treated greywater to be reused for suitable non-potable applications such as toilet flushing, gardening/landscaping and floor cleaning.

The innovation therefore addresses freshwater conservation, wastewater disposal, space constraints and the lack of practical decentralized treatment infrastructure through compact, scalable and application-specific greywater recycling products.
column37:
Technology is at the core of JalSevak's product platform, enabling conventional greywater treatment processes to be integrated into compact, decentralized and scalable systems.

Our flagship WARSHA integrates greywater treatment into a compact and automated product specifically designed for smaller residential applications. The same technology approach is extended through JalWASH for larger residential, commercial and institutional facilities and through GREEN for movable deployment at construction and temporary sites. The product portfolio therefore provides a common technology platform across different capacities and operating environments.

The treatment system integrates collection, multi-stage filtration, aeration, disinfection, storage and delivery within a modular configuration. The company's technology is designed for low space requirements, scalability, customization and automated IoT-enabled operation.

The modular architecture allows systems to be installed in both existing and under-construction buildings, reducing dependence on extensive civil infrastructure.

The technology therefore enables wastewater treatment to be brought closer to the point of generation and makes water reuse more practical across different customer segments.
column38:
JalSevak addresses the need for compact, affordable and scalable decentralized greywater recycling for locations that generate wastewater but face limitations of space, infrastructure, installation time or economics.

The primary need addressed by WARSHA is enabling households and smaller residential facilities to recycle greywater locally rather than relying entirely on freshwater for non-potable applications or discharging reusable greywater into the drainage system. For larger facilities, JalWASH provides a scalable solution from 10100 KLD, while GREEN addresses construction sites and temporary facilities where mobility is important.

Available alternatives include conventional STPs, site-built wastewater treatment plants, septic/disposal-based systems and continued dependence on freshwater or water tankers for non-potable requirements. Conventional systems can require significant space, civil infrastructure, capital investment and operational resources.

JalSevak's systems are designed specifically for decentralized greywater recycling, with low space requirements and modular configurations. The company's website states that its solutions can be installed in existing or under-construction buildings and are designed to be more cost-effective and easier to maintain than comparable STP-based approaches.

column36:
India generates approximately 70.73 lakh tonnes of textile waste annually, of which 58 is post-consumer waste. While a significant share is recovered, post-consumer textile waste remains difficult to sort and route to appropriate recycling pathways because it contains mixed fibres, blends, colours and fabric types. 

More than 95 of textile sorting in India is still manual, with fibre composition identification remaining a major gap. This limits sorting throughput and consistency, particularly for mixed and blended textiles, and reduces the ability of recovery facilities to generate clean, specification-based feedstock for recyclers. 

The challenge is therefore not only collecting textile waste, but making high-volume, accurate sorting economically viable. Existing FibreSENSE Go and Pro devices have validated KOSHAs fibre-identification technology in the market, but their application remains suited to smaller facilities and limited-volume or random testing because material handling is still manual. 

FibreSENSE Line addresses this scale gap through conveyor-based, high-throughput fibre identification and segregation for centralised recovery facilities. By increasing sorting throughput, reducing dependence on manual handling and improving fibre-level accuracy, the Line aims to reduce the cost of sorting, improve the quality and value of recovered material, and make more post-consumer textile waste viable for recycling.
column37:
Technology is the core enabler of KOSHAs innovation. FibreSENSE Line uses Near-Infrared (NIR) spectroscopy, photonics and proprietary AI/chemometric models to identify textile fibre composition rapidly and non-destructively. 

NIR light interacts differently with different textile fibres, generating a spectral signature. The Line captures this signal and processes it through trained models to classify fibres and blends, enabling accurate material-level segregation without damaging the textile. 

The key innovation is applying this validated fibre-identification technology in a conveyor-based, high-throughput system rather than relying on individual manual testing. FibreSENSE Line is designed for centralised recovery facilities to continuously identify and segregate large volumes of textile waste, targeting 5 tonnes per 8-hour shift. 

The technology therefore addresses both accuracy and economics of sorting: it reduces dependence on manual fibre identification, increases processing throughput and aims to bring sorting costs down significantly. The system also creates a pathway for trained workers to operate technology-assisted sorting systems, rather than replacing the human workforce. 

FibreSENSE Go and Pro have already validated the underlying fibre-identification technology in field and facility applications. The Line extends this core technology from small-scale identification and testing to scalable, high-volume sorting.
column38:
The key need is to make high-volume textile sorting faster, more accurate and economically viable, particularly for post-consumer waste. Mixed fibres, blends, and fabric types make manual identification difficult, while inconsistent segregation reduces the quality and value of material available for recycling. 

Current alternatives include: 

Manual sorting: Workers identify textiles through visual inspection, touch, labels and experience. It is labor-intensive, slower at scale, and inaccurate in identifying fibre composition and blends. Burn tests are hazardous relatively inaccurate and not scalable. 

Laboratory testing: Provides detailed material analysis but is slower, requires specialized equipment and trained personnel, making it unsuitable for continuous, high-volume sorting. 

Existing fibre-identification devices: Commercial NIR-based solutions can identify textile composition, but handheld/tabletop systems still require individual material handling and are therefore better suited to smaller facilities or random/limited-volume testing. Existing high speed identification systems are not affordable. 

FibreSENSE Line addresses the gap between accurate fibre identification,scalable sorting at value. It integrates KOSHAs validated NIR-based fibre identification technology into a conveyor system designed for continuous, high-volume segregation at centralised recovery facilities. This enables larger volumes to be processed with lower dependence on manual handling, improving sorting efficiency, material quality and the economic viability of textile recycling.

FibreSENSE Line  Revenue Model 

Machine sale: The Conveyor Line is priced at approximately Rs. 40 lakh, including deployment-related costs. TRFs can purchase and operate the machine directly. 

EMI / equipment financing: For organisations unable to make the full upfront investment, the machine can be offered through 23 year financing/EMI models, reducing the initial capital barrier. 

Rental / pay-per-use: Facilities with variable or project-based demand can rent the Line and pay based on utilisation or volume processed. 

Shared deployment: One machine can serve multiple TRFs, improving machine utilisation and allowing smaller facilities to access high-throughput sorting without purchasing the equipment. 

Customer ROI: The Line targets approximately 5 tonnes per 8-hour shift and aims to reduce sorting cost from the current 5/kg to approximately 2/kg, enabling TRFs to process substantially more waste without proportionally increasing manpower and improving their operating capacity and economics. 

Recurring software revenue: KOSHATrace provides traceability, material data and reporting services, creating an additional subscription/enterprise revenue stream. 

This creates a scalable model combining hardware sales, equipment financing, sorting-as-a-service and recurring software revenue, while improving the economic viability and capacity of textile recovery facilities.

The innovation addresses a critical gap in urban solid waste management: the absence of an integrated, data-driven system that connects waste generation, source segregation, onsite processing, recycling and final disposal.

Currently, waste collected from households, institutions and commercial establishments is often inadequately segregated at source, resulting in contamination of recyclable dry waste, inefficient recovery, higher quantities of mixed waste being transported to municipal facilities, and limited visibility of actual waste generation and treatment. While individual solutions such as awareness programmes, composting or dry-waste collection exist, they are rarely integrated into a single measurable system.

The proposed pilot will address this gap by digitising waste at the point of generation and collection, enabling waste quantities and segregation performance to be recorded and tracked. The resulting data will identify poor segregation and enable targeted interventions to improve source segregation through feedback and behaviour change. Segregated wet waste will be processed onsite through decentralised composting, while clean dry waste will be channelled to appropriate recycling/recovery streams, thereby improving material recovery and reducing contamination.

A key outcome will be quantification of the residual mixed waste actually handed over to BMC, providing an evidence-based measure of the waste diverted, processed and recycled at source.

The pilot therefore addresses the problem of fragmented waste management by creating a traceable, measurable and scalable model that can demonstrate improvements in segregation, decentralised processing, recycling efficiency and reduction of mixed waste requiring municipal handling.

Technology is the backbone of the proposed innovation, transforming waste segregation from a largely manual process into a measurable, traceable and behaviour-driven system.

At the point of collection, the waste picker will digitally record and photograph the waste presented by each waste generator and assign a segregation score on a 110 scale. This creates a real-time digital record of segregation performance and enables individual generators to be monitored over time.

The technology-enabled scoring system will trigger graded interventions based on actual behaviour. When a score falls below 7, photographic evidence will be captured and recorded. If a waste generator receives a score below 7 on five occasions in a month, the system will automatically trigger a communication encouraging improved segregation. If the score falls below 6, an in-person training intervention will be initiated on a chargeable basis. Where the score falls below 5, the digital record establishes accountability, with the waste generator responsible for consequences if improperly segregated waste cannot be collected.

The platform will aggregate data across generators and locations to identify recurring segregation issues, track improvement and quantify segregated waste, onsite processed waste, recyclable recovery and residual mixed waste handed over to BMC.

Thus, technology goes beyond digitising collection. It creates a continuous feedback loop of measurement  evidence  positive nudge  intervention  accountability  improvement, combining subtle behavioural nudges with proportionate corrective action to enable sustained behaviour change and generate reliable data for evaluating and scaling the model.

The innovation addresses the need for an integrated, measurable and accountable system that ensures waste is properly segregated, processed and recovered at source, while reducing the quantity of mixed waste ultimately handed over to BMC.

Existing waste-management systems often address individual stages independently. Source segregation is promoted through awareness campaigns, signage and periodic monitoring waste pickers collect segregated waste wet waste may be treated through onsite composting or other decentralised technologies and dry waste is transferred to scrap dealers, MRFs or recyclers. Digital solutions are also available for collection tracking, waste audits and reporting. However, these alternatives generally do not create a continuous feedback and accountability mechanism connecting the behaviour of the waste generator with the quality of waste presented, subsequent processing and the final quantity of mixed waste.

The proposed innovation integrates these components into one measurable service. Waste is digitally recorded and scored at the point of collection, with photographic evidence and automated interventions linked to segregation performance. Behavioural nudges and targeted training are triggered when performance deteriorates. Properly segregated wet waste is processed onsite, while cleaner dry waste is directed towards recovery and recycling. The system also quantifies residual mixed waste handed over to BMC.

The need, therefore, is not simply for another waste-processing technology, but for an end-to-end mechanism that converts waste segregation into a measurable behaviour, links behaviour with outcomes, and generates reliable data to demonstrate waste diversion and resource recovery.

The key challenges identified are behaviour change, operational consistency, technology adoption, willingness to pay and scalability.

1. Behavioural resistance: Waste generators may initially resist segregation scoring, photographic documentation and corrective actions. The model addresses this through positive nudges, feedback and graded interventions, with punitive measures used only when repeated non-compliance persists.

2. Subjectivity in scoring: Different waste pickers may assess segregation differently. Standardised scoring protocols, training, photographic evidence and periodic audits will improve consistency and credibility.

3. Technology adoption: Waste pickers may have varying levels of digital literacy or face connectivity/device constraints. The platform must therefore be simple, mobile-friendly and require minimal data entry, with offline functionality where necessary.

4. Willingness to pay: Some generators may view monitoring and training as an additional expense. Demonstrating measurable benefitsimproved recycling, reduced mixed waste, onsite processing and transparent reportingwill be important for customer adoption.

5. Operational scalability: Maintaining consistent service quality across multiple locations may become challenging as the network grows. Standard operating procedures, central dashboards, trained personnel and periodic audits will support quality control.

6. Financial and processing risks: Variations in recyclable-material value, compost quality and downstream recycling capacity may affect economics. Reliable processing protocols and multiple recycling partnerships will mitigate these risks.

The pilot will help validate these assumptions, refine the technology and service model, establish unit economics and develop a scalable implementation framework.

We have previously implemented and operated decentralised waste-management initiatives within Mumbai city limits, primarily in housing societies, using manual processes and without digital tracking.

These initiatives were undertaken around 2018, during the period when the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016 were being implemented more actively and housing societies were increasingly expected to undertake source segregation and decentralised processing of wet waste.

The model involved door-to-door collection of segregated waste, manual monitoring of segregation, and onsite treatment of wet waste using appropriate composting technology. Dry waste was separately collected for recycling, while the quantity of waste requiring onward disposal was reduced.

The experience demonstrated that even without sophisticated digital tools, consistent source segregation combined with effective onsite wet-waste processing can substantially reduce the quantity of waste leaving a housing complex for municipal disposal. Through these interventions and the use of appropriate composting technology, we are currently able to divert approximately 2.5 tonnes of waste from landfill every day.

However, the earlier model relied substantially on manual recording and operational supervision. There was limited ability to digitally capture individual waste-generator performance, track segregation scores over time, generate photographic evidence, automate corrective interventions, or produce consolidated data on waste diverted, recycled, processed onsite and handed over as mixed waste to the ULB.

The COVID-19 pandemic subsequently disrupted the implementation environment. During and after the pandemic, ULB waste-collection practices changed, and municipal systems in Maharashtra resumed collecting mixed waste from many housing complexes, reducing the effectiveness of decentralised source-segregation initiatives.

Our proposed TVARAAN 3.0 pilot builds on this field-tested operational experience while addressing its principal limitationthe absence of digital traceability and data-driven behaviour management.

The proposed pilot will therefore integrate our established experience in door-to-door collection, source segregation and onsite composting with digital waste tracking, photographic verification, segregation scoring, automated behavioural nudges, targeted training and quantification of residual mixed waste handed over to BMC.

This provides an opportunity to move from a manually monitored decentralised model to a measurable, data-driven and scalable integrated waste-management model, while building on an approach that has already demonstrated the ability to divert approximately 2.5 tonnes of waste per day from landfill.
