column50:
CarbonM FuelMax Technology is applying to scale its mixed plastic waste conversion and hydrocarbon upgrading platform through a pilot and demonstration facility in the **Chakan MIDC industrial cluster, Pune, Maharashtra**. The project is designed to address a major gap in industrial plastic waste management: large volumes of mixed, contaminated, multilayer and low value plastic waste are difficult to recycle mechanically and therefore often move toward co processing, low value recovery or disposal. At the same time, the same industrial ecosystem continues to consume fossil derived liquid fuels and petrochemical feedstocks.

Our proposed project converts this difficult plastic waste into standardized hydrocarbon products that can be used as industrial liquid fuel and, after appropriate qualification, as circular chemical feedstock. The project combines three core technology layers developed by CarbonM: a controlled pyrolysis system for converting mixed plastics into hydrocarbon vapours, **Alkanalyze**, our hardware and software adaptive process control platform for maintaining yield and product consistency despite feedstock variability, and **Oleum**, our downstream upgrading technology for improving the quality and contaminant profile of pyrolysis oil.

The proposed project is not intended to be only a laboratory demonstration. The objective is to build an operating industrial pilot that validates feedstock sourcing, process reliability, product quality, customer acceptance, operating economics and environmental impact under actual MIDC conditions.

### Project Description

The project will establish an integrated pilot facility of approximately **15,000 sq. ft. in the Chakan MIDC region**. The facility will receive difficult plastic waste generated by automotive, engineering, packaging and other manufacturing industries in and around the cluster.

Incoming material will first be characterized and preprocessed to remove incompatible contaminants such as metals and other unsuitable fractions. The acceptable mixed plastic fraction will then be converted through CarbonM's pyrolysis system into hydrocarbon vapours.

A key challenge in plastic pyrolysis is that industrial waste is not compositionally constant. One batch may contain more polypropylene, another more polyethylene, fillers, pigments or degraded materials. Conventional systems typically operate at fixed conditions, meaning changes in incoming waste can directly translate into changes in yield and oil quality.

CarbonM is developing **Alkanalyze** specifically to address this problem. A small representative sample of the reactor vapour is continuously withdrawn from the main process line and analyzed through a controlled sensing system. The resulting vapour signature is combined with reactor operating data and compared against a database of previously validated operating conditions. The system then recommends or automatically adjusts parameters such as temperature, feed rate, residence conditions and other process variables so that the reactor remains closer to the operating conditions associated with maximum useful liquid yield and a defined product quality window.

The resulting liquid hydrocarbon is subsequently processed using **Oleum**, CarbonM's proprietary downstream upgrading platform. Oleum is designed to improve raw pyrolysis oil quality by reducing undesirable contaminants and improving characteristics relevant to industrial use.

The final product pathway has two commercial routes. The first is **FuelMax**, an upgraded industrial liquid fuel intended for suitable boiler and process heat applications. The second is a circular hydrocarbon stream that can progressively be qualified for use as chemical and petrochemical feedstock.

This dual product strategy is important for commercialization. Industrial fuel provides a nearer term route to market, while circular chemical feedstock provides a longer term pathway to higher value material circularity.

### Geography

The proposed geography is **Chakan MIDC, Pune district, Maharashtra**.

Chakan is particularly suitable because it is one of India's major automotive and engineering manufacturing clusters and therefore generates multiple relevant plastic waste streams through packaging, rejected plastic components, trims, protective materials, logistics packaging and manufacturing residues.

CarbonM is already in discussions with **Mercedes Benz** regarding a potential pilot opportunity involving difficult automotive plastic waste. The Chakan location therefore provides the possibility of demonstrating the technology close to both waste generators and industrial consumers.

Locating the facility inside or near the MIDC ecosystem also reduces the need to transport difficult plastic waste over long distances and creates the opportunity to develop a local circular economy model in which waste generated by one part of the industrial cluster is converted into useful hydrocarbon products for industrial use.

Once validated, the Chakan model can be replicated in other MIDC clusters with large automotive, chemical, engineering, packaging and manufacturing footprints.

### Timelines

The proposed implementation period is approximately **15 to 18 months**.

During the first three months, CarbonM will focus on detailed waste mapping, feedstock characterization, engineering modifications, site planning and finalization of operating parameters for the Chakan waste streams.

The next three months will focus on installation and commissioning of the pyrolysis system, Alkanalyze hardware and control infrastructure, Oleum post processing equipment, storage systems, utilities and safety infrastructure.

Months 7 to 9 will focus on structured testing and optimization. Different industrial plastic waste streams and controlled mixtures will be processed to establish the relationship between feed composition, reactor conditions, yield and product properties. This phase will also be used to train and validate the Alkanalyze operating database.

Months 10 to 14 will focus on sustained pilot operation using actual waste streams sourced from participating industries. During this stage, CarbonM will undertake product validation, customer trials, repeated quality testing and operating cost measurement.

The final months will focus on performance assessment, environmental impact measurement, customer validation and preparation of the commercial scale up and replication model.

The expected outcome is that by the end of the pilot, CarbonM will have demonstrated not only that difficult mixed plastic waste can be converted successfully, but that the conversion can be performed repeatedly with controlled product quality and commercially relevant economics.

### Funding Requirement

The broader scale up programme requires approximately **?7.5 crore**.

The proposed deployment includes multiple interconnected components. Around **?5.05 crore** is allocated toward plant and process equipment, including the Oleum post processing system, a 100 kg/day highly instrumented engineering reactor and the first 5 TPD integrated commercial scale reactor system.

Approximately **?40 lakh** is allocated specifically toward Alkanalyze instrumentation, sensors, control hardware and associated process monitoring systems.

Approximately **?50 lakh** is planned for compliance, testing, certification, third party validation and customer trials.

Around **?1.05 crore** is planned for team, operations, feedstock procurement and working capital, with the remaining allocation maintained for contingency and implementation risks.

CarbonM expects the MIDC Grand Challenge support to act as catalytic funding toward this larger commercialization programme, while the balance can be supported through equity capital, corporate participation, strategic partnerships and other available innovation or climate funding.

The objective is not to remain dependent on grants. The grant supported pilot is intended to create the technical and commercial evidence needed for subsequent project finance and private investment.

### Partnerships Associated

The project is designed around collaboration between CarbonM, MIDC, industrial waste generators, customers and technology validation partners.

CarbonM is already in discussions with **Mercedes Benz in Chakan** regarding a potential automotive plastic waste pilot. This provides a relevant corporate pathway because automotive manufacturing generates multiple plastic streams that are difficult to recycle through conventional routes.

CarbonM has also been engaging with other large industrial companies across automotive, chemicals, cement, pharmaceuticals, engineering and carbon black regarding plastic waste sourcing, industrial fuel applications and hydrocarbon product testing. These engagements are intended to build a diversified ecosystem rather than depend on a single waste supplier or customer.

Within the MIDC ecosystem, the project can work with industrial units to establish structured waste collection and offtake arrangements. Waste generators can provide difficult plastic streams that are currently expensive or difficult to manage, while CarbonM converts them into usable products.

The project can also work with authorized waste aggregators and recyclers. CarbonM does not intend to compete with mechanical recycling for high quality recyclable plastics. Instead, the objective is to accept the residual mixed fraction that has limited mechanical recycling value.

Third party laboratories will be used for independent product validation and analytical testing. CarbonM also intends to pursue relevant sustainability and traceability certifications as operations scale.

At a later stage, Urban Local Bodies and other public waste management agencies could also become feedstock partners where suitable non recyclable plastic streams are available. However, the initial Chakan pilot will remain primarily industrial in nature because industrial waste provides better traceability, more controlled sourcing and faster validation.

### Expected Impact

The most immediate impact of the project will be the diversion of difficult plastic waste away from low value disposal pathways and toward productive industrial use.

At a 5 TPD scale, a fully utilized facility operating for approximately 300 days per year can process around **1,500 tonnes of plastic waste annually**. At CarbonM's targeted conversion levels, this can produce more than **1,000 tonnes per year of useful liquid hydrocarbon products**, depending on actual feedstock composition and operating performance.

The environmental impact extends beyond waste diversion. The project reduces demand for virgin fossil derived industrial hydrocarbons by replacing a portion of them with products derived from waste plastic. Where the product is eventually used as circular petrochemical feedstock, the material can also contribute toward closing the carbon loop by returning waste plastic carbon back into chemical manufacturing.

The project will generate detailed data on waste processed, product yield, energy use, operating conditions, product quality and destination of the final hydrocarbon. This will provide the basis for a measurable environmental impact framework rather than relying only on theoretical waste diversion estimates.

The project will also demonstrate an important technology innovation in **adaptive control of heterogeneous waste processing**. Conventional manufacturing plants generally operate with reasonably defined raw materials. Waste conversion plants face the opposite problem: the raw material changes continuously. Alkanalyze is designed to make this variability manageable by continuously linking the observed vapour condition with the operating state of the reactor.

If successful, this can improve liquid yield, reduce product variability, decrease off specification production and allow lower quality mixed plastic streams to be processed economically.

The economic impact is equally important. The facility creates value from waste that currently has limited commercial value while producing a product with an established industrial market. It creates direct employment for operators, process engineers, quality personnel, waste handling staff and technical personnel, while also creating indirect opportunities for aggregators, logistics providers and waste collection partners.

For participating corporations, the solution provides a potential pathway to improve waste diversion, circularity and sustainability performance without requiring them to develop their own recycling infrastructure.

Most importantly, the Chakan project is intended to become a **replicable industrial model**. After validating the process at pilot and 5 TPD scale, CarbonM plans to move toward a 50 TPD reference facility. Subsequent facilities can be deployed through a combination of CarbonM owned plants and strategic partnerships with industrial companies.

Chakan therefore represents more than a single pilot site. It can become the first demonstration of a decentralized circular hydrocarbon model where industrial plastic waste is collected locally, converted locally and returned to the industrial economy as a useful product.

Through MIDC support, CarbonM aims to demonstrate that difficult mixed plastic waste does not necessarily have to remain a disposal problem. With the right combination of conversion technology, adaptive process control, downstream upgrading and industrial partnerships, it can become a reliable raw material for the next generation of circular fuels and chemical feedstocks.

column36:
Urban drains and nallas across Maharashtra's ULBs carry a mix of raw sewage, industrial effluent, and stormwater into lakes, rivers, and eventually the coast. Most receive no treatment, or only partial treatment where STP capacity is inadequate or plants are poorly maintained. The result is chronic organic overload: depleted dissolved oxygen, foul odour, fish kills, and pathogen loads far above safe limits. This creates direct public health risk  mosquito-borne disease from stagnant, nutrient-rich water, and waterborne illness for communities living along drain edges, who are disproportionately lower-income households with the least ability to relocate or protect themselves. Choked, silted, biologically dead drains also worsen urban flooding by reducing effective carrying capacity, and degrade groundwater recharge quality downstream.
Conventional fixes  new STP construction, mechanical aeration, chemical dosing  are capital-intensive and slow to deploy, especially for the hundreds of smaller drains and secondary water bodies that never make it into formal infrastructure planning. Our innovation targets this underserved middle layer: drains, canals, and local water bodies too numerous and too small for big infrastructure investment but exactly where citizens experience pollution daily. We address the gap between "do nothing" and "build a new STP" with a low-capex, rapidly deployable, nature-based restoration approach  treated in-situ via periodic dosing stations on the banks, requiring no electricity and minimal manpower  that ULBs can apply at the neighborhood or ward level, including reaches fed by smaller sub-drains.
column37:
Our core technology is a nano-formulated nutrient dosing system that stimulates growth of naturally occurring diatoms throughout the water column and along the drain/lake bed. As diatoms photosynthesize, they release oxygen as nanobubbles consistently across the full water column and at the sediment interface  not only near the surface, as with conventional algae  directly reaching the anaerobic sludge layer where odour-causing bacteria live. This activates the water body's own indigenous aerobic bacteria, which multiply and release beneficial extracellular enzymes that further break down organic matter and sludge. Diatoms also take up nitrogen and phosphorus directly, and are grazed by zooplankton, eaten by fish, permanently exporting nutrients as fish are removed by birds, predation, or fishing  the same food-web growth that supports fishermen's livelihoods downstream.
The core mineral formulation contains no added bacteria, fungi, enzymes, or biocides  independent peer-reviewed research (IIT Roorkee) found this nutrient-based mechanism more effective than microbial/enzyme approaches. Our field protocol does, however, call for seeding with beneficial bacteria during the initial stage, layered on sustained Nualgi dosing  which stimulates continual diatom growth, rather than dosing diatoms themselves  as a deliberate accelerant for early sludge breakdown. Deployment is low-infrastructure: periodic dosing stations on the banks dispense product by gravity drip, in-situ, with no electricity and minimal manpower. Because oxygenation propagates along the sediment beyond the dosing point, rejuvenation extends into neighborhoods whose feeder sub-drains discharge into the treated drain, and remote monitoring plus a dosing-simulation model track results without new civil infrastructure.
column38:
The need is affordable, fast-to-deploy water quality restoration for the drains, canals, and lakes that fall outside formal STP infrastructure but directly affect public health, urban flooding resilience, and downstream river/coastal water quality. ULBs need a way to show measurable improvement  dissolved oxygen, BOD/COD reduction, coliform reduction  within months, not the years required for new treatment plant construction, and within budgets that rarely include large capital works for secondary drains.
Available alternatives each fall short in different ways. New or expanded STPs require significant capital, land, and multi-year timelines, and don't help drains outside the sewerage network. Mechanical aeration is energy-intensive and does little to remove underlying nutrient load. Chemical dosing  alum, chlorine, or other coagulant-based treatments  improves water quality short-term but, for coagulants specifically, generates large volumes of extra sludge that must be collected, dried, transported, and disposed of, an ongoing logistics and disposal burden for as long as treatment continues. Bacterial or enzyme-based bioremediation products are common, but independent peer-reviewed research (IIT Roorkee) found nutrient-based diatom stimulation more effective. Manual desilting offers only temporary relief and doesn't address the biological drivers of pollution. Our innovation sits between these options: no new civil works, no coagulant sludge to dispose of, lower ongoing cost, and evidence of stronger, more durable outcomes than comparable bio-based products.
column40:
Nualgi Nanobiotech holds patents on its core silica-based nanoparticle nutrient formulation in India, the United States, and Europe, protecting the proprietary blend of inorganic macro-minerals and trace elements  including silica, iron, manganese, cobalt, molybdenum, and other micronutrients  that selectively stimulates diatom growth over other algae. Beyond the patented formulation itself, our IP position includes trade-secret-protected dosing protocols, including the sequencing of sustained diatom-driven oxygenation with an initial period of beneficial-bacteria seeding, and site-specific calibration methods for different water body types (drains, lakes, rivers), developed and refined over more than a decade of field deployments across India. We hold the registered trademark for the Nualgi name and brand.

Alongside formal IP, we have built a substantial evidence base that functions as a practical barrier to imitation: independent peer-reviewed validation (IIT Roorkee, Journal of Environmental Chemical Engineering, 2021), third-party toxicity certification (Indian Institute of Toxicology Research, Lucknow), and over a decade of government empanelment relationships  Karnataka Fisheries Department since 2009, Tamil Nadu Water Resources Department since 2014  that would be difficult for a new entrant to replicate quickly.

Our CTO and VP, Dr. Arun Kumar Sridharan, separately holds five granted patents (two pending) from his prior technical career in solar energy, gas sensing, and photonics at Stanford, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, and GE  personal IP from his earlier work, distinct from Nualgi-held patents, but reflecting the depth of patent and product-development experience on Nualgi's leadership team.
column42:
Our current model is project- and service-based: we supply the dosing formulation, technical protocol, and lightweight dosing infrastructure, and are engaged directly by government bodies, NGOs, or CSR-funded partners on a per-project or per-MLD-treated basis, often starting with a free or low-cost pilot to demonstrate results before a paid O&M contract. We hold standing government empanelment in some states (e.g., Karnataka Fisheries Department since 2009, Tamil Nadu Water Resources Department since 2014) that converts pilots into recurring paid engagements, and have recently won a lake restoration tender based on our phycoremediation technology in Odisha, demonstrating our ability to convert competitive government tenders into active state projects.
For Maharashtra specifically, we have appointed seven liaison and implementation partners over the past year to develop ULB-partnered projects statewide, and are structuring a broader business-unit partnership with an established regional water/wastewater treatment company, combining our technology with local execution capacity. We are proposing project-specific exclusivity and revenue-sharing arrangements scoped to individual water bodies rather than a broad upfront territorial agreement. We are also piloting a CSR-funded model (tested in Coimbatore): a municipal corporation directs corporate CSR funds toward lake/drain rejuvenation, and the restored water is subsequently made available for industrial reuse, creating a secondary revenue stream. Overall revenue streams are: (a) per-MLD/day O&M service fees, (b) capital-light project setup fees, (c) government empanelment contracts, and (d) potential treated-water reuse revenue-share with industrial users.
column43:
The most significant risk is procurement and budget dependency: ULB tendering cycles are slow, and many projects depend on discretionary or CSR funding rather than committed municipal budgets. There is also incumbency risk  ULBs are more familiar with conventional STP and chemical-dosing vendors, and a biology-driven approach needs more upfront trust-building, against competitors (e.g., Bint Biotech, MIW Water Solutions, Apta Solvics) making similar claims with varying independent validation. Production capacity is not a constraint  the formulation scales with demand  but execution capacity is: multi-site rollout needs trained field teams and standardized monitoring, which is why we pair a regional execution partner with our own seven Maharashtra liaison partners.
A related financial risk: ULBs frequently expect a free pilot before any paid contract, so we bear cost upfront at each new ULB with no guaranteed conversion. A further risk is institutional: every drain differs in flow, inlet count, and sludge load, and some organic breakdown begun in a drain only completes once water reaches the receiving lake or river  a rigid success threshold ignoring this can misread genuine progress as underperformance and hold up payment on a contract that is working as expected. Many ULBs also lack staff able to fully evaluate a biological protocol's multi-dimensional benefits, favoring a familiar single-purpose incumbent. Training ULB counterparts to set drain-specific success criteria and view phycoremediation as a connected drain-to-lake/river system is a necessary part of our go-to-market work, not an afterthought.
column44: Quantitatively, we track catchment population, vector-borne disease indicators where available, and community engagement with restored sites. We also track livelihood impact: private fishermen across Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, and Andhra Pradesh have been repeat customers for 15 years, valuing the improvement to their fish yields  durable, revenue-backed proof our impact translates into real economic value. Qualitatively, we gather testimony from residents, fishermen, NGOs, and officials on livelihood, safety, and quality of life, and document institutional capacity built through our seven Maharashtra liaison partners and their DPR-stage work in Thane.
column46:
The primary beneficiaries are residents living along and downstream of urban drains, nallas, and neighborhood lakes in Maharashtra's ULBs  disproportionately lower- and middle-income households in informal settlements bordering these water bodies, with the highest exposure to odour, contaminated water, and mosquito-borne disease (dengue, malaria, chikungunya), and the least capacity to relocate. Women and children bear the greatest burden, from vector-borne illness and day-to-day water contact where formal supply is unreliable.

A second group is the broader city population using restored public lakes and talaos for recreation and community life, and benefiting from reduced flooding risk as drains regain carrying capacity. A third group is downstream users  farmers relying on drain/river water for irrigation and fisherfolk dependent on water quality, including the private fishermen in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, and Andhra Pradesh who have been regular Nualgi customers for 15 years. Municipal corporations and ULB staff are institutional beneficiaries, gaining a lower-cost route to compliance targets. Finally, industries piloting treated-water reuse stand to benefit from an alternative water source, reducing pressure on freshwater withdrawal in water-stressed parts of the state.
column47:
We do not yet have a completed water-quality outcome from a live Maharashtra ULB deployment, but this reflects an active, structured market-entry process already underway rather than a cold start into the state. Over the past year we have appointed seven liaison and implementation partners across Maharashtra to develop ULB-partnered restoration projects statewide. The most advanced of these is in Thane, where our engagement has progressed to the Detailed Project Report (DPR) stage for a lake rejuvenation project we expect the municipality to commission and pay for directly, independent of this accelerator. For the accelerator-funded pilot specifically, we propose to identify a separate drain or river stretch  in Thane, Mumbai, or possibly Pune, depending on where ULB receptivity proves strongest  as the site for this Waterway & Drain Protection pilot.
This pipeline sits alongside directly relevant recent evidence: we won a lake restoration tender based on our phycoremediation technology in Odisha within the past year, demonstrating our ability to convert a competitive government tender process into an active state project outside our founding markets of Karnataka and Tamil Nadu  the same conversion pathway (liaison partner engagement  DPR  tender/contract) we are now pursuing in Maharashtra
through Thane and our other six partners. Our closest related field evidence within the state itself is a 2017 trial (81 days) at the Old Navy Nagar STP in Colaba, Mumbai (0.45 MLD), a Military Engineer Services/Navy facility rather than a municipal one, which showed dissolved oxygen rising from 1.2 to 66.7 mg/l and COD/BOD dropping substantially, leading to a formal Navy recommendation for continued use. This kind of regulatory and institutional endorsement is not unique to Mumbai: the Karnataka State Pollution Control Board (KSPCB) has witnessed dissolved oxygen improvements at Nualgi-treated sites, the Karnataka Government's own planning document for the Suvarnamukhi Reservoir catchment rejuvenation documents and endorses our approach, and the National Green Tribunal  in proceedings concerning drains in Uttar Pradesh  has witnessed our results and recommended Nualgi's use, giving Maharashtra ULBs an established, multi-state pattern of regulatory validation to draw on.
Through this accelerator, we are seeking to establish our first formal Maharashtra ULB pilot on a drain or river stretch, with the specific site to be finalized among Thane, Mumbai, or Pune based on ULB receptivity. In Mumbai, we have already identified candidate river/drain reaches through screening of the city's waterways (drawing on BMC Climate Budget data), including the Mithi River reach, the Poisar reach, and the Dahisar/OshiwaraWalbhat reach, alongside lake/talao candidates (Kamal Talao, Bhujale Talao, Bandra Talao, the Powai lake inlet/zone) for our broader Maharashtra program  proposed in partnership with a Maharashtra-based water/wastewater treatment company with existing ULB relationships in the state.

Project Description
Nualgi Nanobiotech proposes to establish a dedicated Waterway & Drain Protection program in Maharashtra, built around
our proprietary nano-formulated nutrient dosing technology — a phycoremediation process that restores water quality in
polluted drains, canals, lakes, and river stretches without new civil infrastructure, added bacteria, enzymes, or chemicals.
The core mineral formulation stimulates growth of naturally occurring diatoms throughout the water column and along the
bed. As diatoms photosynthesize, they release dissolved oxygen as nanobubbles consistently across the full water depth and
at the sediment interface — not just at the surface, as with mechanical aerators — shifting the microbial community from
anaerobic to aerobic and activating indigenous bacteria, which multiply and release beneficial enzymes that break down
organic matter and sludge. Diatoms take up nitrogen and phosphorus directly; zooplankton graze on them, fish feed on the
zooplankton, and when fish are removed by birds, predation, or licensed fishing, the absorbed nutrients are permanently
exported — nature’s own nutrient-export mechanism, restored and accelerated. Our field protocol also calls for seeding
with beneficial bacteria in the initial stage, layered on sustained Nualgi dosing — which stimulates continual diatom growth,
rather than dosing diatoms themselves — as a deliberate accelerant for early sludge breakdown.
This mechanism is independently validated: an IIT Roorkee study (Simon & Joshi, 2021, Journal of Environmental Chemical
Engineering, Elsevier) identified our formulation as the most effective bio-preparation for surface water rehabilitation with
minimal inputs. Unlike coagulant-based treatments (e.g., alum), which precipitate pollutants as sludge requiring collection,
drying, transport, and disposal — an ongoing cost — our approach mineralises organic matter and exports nutrients through
the food web rather than creating a solid waste stream. Our MSDS confirms no added bacteria, fungi, enzymes, GMOs,
pesticides, herbicides, or biocides, and fish-toxicity testing (Indian Institute of Toxicology Research, Lucknow) established a
wide safety margin (LC50 >100 mg/L at 96 hours). Our benefits have also been directly witnessed and recommended by
regulatory and judicial bodies: the Karnataka State Pollution Control Board (KSPCB) has witnessed DO improvements at
Nualgi-treated sites, Karnataka’s own planning document for the Suvarnamukhi Reservoir catchment endorses our use, and
the National Green Tribunal, in proceedings concerning Uttar Pradesh drains, has similarly witnessed and recommended
Nualgi’s use.
Field evidence spans multiple states: a National Mission for Clean Ganga-commissioned drain remediation at Laksar,
Uttarakhand (193 MLD, feeding the Ganga), independently monitored by IIT Roorkee; an ongoing Coimbatore drain pilot
with the NGO Siruthuli and PSG Institute of Technology; standing empanelment with Tamil Nadu’s Water Resources
Department (since 2014) and Karnataka’s Fisheries Department (since 2009); an active Greater Bengaluru Authority lake
restoration; a certified municipal lake rejuvenation at Nandhivaram Thangal Lake near Chennai (BOD 78?2.0 mg/l, COD
380?20 mg/l, DO 3.2?7.2 mg/l over 12 months, certified by the Municipality Commissioner); and a competitively won lake
restoration tender in Odisha within the past year. Private fishermen across Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, and Andhra Pradesh have
been regular customers for 15 years — revenue-backed evidence of the livelihood value our technology delivers.
For Maharashtra, we propose a structured business-unit partnership with an established regional water/wastewater
treatment company, combining our technology with their existing ULB relationships and execution capacity. This builds on
ground already broken: over the past year we appointed seven liaison and implementation partners across Maharashtra,
with our Thane engagement the most advanced, currently at Detailed Project Report (DPR) stage for a lake rejuvenation
project we expect the municipality to commission and pay for directly. The project proposed for this accelerator is a
separate, phased pilot-to-scale program centred on a drain or river stretch: one demonstration site first, at whichever of
Thane, Mumbai, or Pune shows the strongest ULB receptivity, then expansion to a broader portfolio of lakes, drains, and
river stretches as the model proves itself.
A key advantage for drain and waterway protection is how little infrastructure this needs. Drains and rivers are treated via
periodic dosing stations on the banks — in-situ treatment, no pumping, diversion, or civil works, no electricity, and minimal
manpower, making it viable even for stretches ULBs would otherwise deprioritise. Because rejuvenation propagates along
the sediment beyond the exact dosing point, benefits extend to neighborhoods whose feeder sub-drains discharge into the
treated drain. Where a treated drain discharges into a downstream lake or river, this becomes an added benefit rather than
a burden: diatoms and oxygen flow onward and help seed the receiving water body’s food web, rather than depositing
unresolved load as bio-enzyme/microbial-only treatments tend to (see accompanying annexure, Section 6).
Geography
For this accelerator’s drain/river pilot, we intend to select the specific site from among three cities based on ULB receptivity:
Thane, where our liaison engagement is most advanced (albeit currently centred on a separate, directly-paid lake project);
Mumbai, where we have already screened candidate sites using BMC Climate Budget Reports (FY2024-25–FY2026-27),
including river/drain reaches on the Mithi, Poisar, and Dahisar/Oshiwara–Walbhat, alongside lake/talao candidates (Kamal
Talao, Bhujale Talao, Bandra Talao, Powai Lake inlet/zone) for our broader Maharashtra program; and Pune, an additional
city we are evaluating for receptivity through our liaison network. Beyond the pilot site itself, our seven statewide liaison
partners are developing further ULB opportunities across these and other Maharashtra cities that we intend to bring into the
pipeline over 18–24 months. Our execution partner’s regional presence may also extend the model into Southeast Asia,
though that sits outside this application’s immediate scope.
Timelines
Months 0–1: finalize the specific drain or river stretch — in Thane, Mumbai, or Pune, based on ULB receptivity — and secure
ULB agreement. Months 1–3: establish baseline testing (DO, BOD, COD, nitrogen, phosphorus, coliform) and install dosing
infrastructure. Months 3–6: active dosing with weekly independent testing, targeting 50–80% BOD/COD reduction,
dissolved oxygen above 6 mg/l, and reducing coliforms in the drain, with the receiving lake targeted at CPCB Class D —
realistic benchmarks, since no standardized water-quality targets currently exist for urban drains in India, a gap this pilot is
intended to help establish — while separately progressing the Thane lake engagement toward a directly-commissioned
contract. Months 6–12: formalize a longer-term O&M/empanelment agreement based on demonstrated results, scope the
next sites from our seven-partner pipeline, and document the pilot as a replicable case study. Year 1–3: scale to our target of
50 sites across Thane, Mumbai, Pune, and further Maharashtra ULBs, and pursue state-level empanelment as achieved in
Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, and Odisha. Beyond year 3: the Maharashtra business unit operates as a self-sustaining extension of
Nualgi, treated as a standard tool rather than a pilot program.
Funding Amount Required
We are seeking accelerator support of ?75 lakh to fund a single, well-resourced drain or river stretch pilot over 6 months, at
a site to be finalized in Thane, Mumbai, or Pune based on ULB receptivity (distinct from our separate, directly-paid Thane
lake engagement). A full 6-month window matters: it gives the diatom-driven food web time to establish and show sustained
water quality improvement, and gives us runway to build ULB confidence through visible, ongoing results, rather than a
thinner pilot risking loss of ULB interest before it proves itself. This covers dosing infrastructure and product supply for 6
months, independent third-party water testing, field team coordination across our liaison network, documentation for a
case study, and the ULB training/academic-collaboration component described below. This figure is calibrated to give the
pilot time and credibility to convert into a signed, paid O&M or empanelment agreement rather than lapsing once
accelerator funding ends. Business-development support to formalize our Maharashtra business unit would be scoped as an
additional, separately costed component.
Partnerships Associated
We are structuring a core business-unit partnership with an established, Maharashtra-focused water/wastewater
treatment company with existing ULB relationships (and potential Southeast Asian reach). This partner provides local
execution capacity and regulatory familiarity; Nualgi provides the phycoremediation technology, protocols, and validation.
We propose project-specific exclusivity and revenue-sharing scoped to individual water bodies rather than a broad
territorial agreement, expanding only as the partnership proves it can generate business — a deliberately cautious structure
for a new market entry.
This sits alongside a parallel track already built directly: our seven Maharashtra liaison and implementation partners, with
Thane most advanced at DPR stage for the directly-paid municipal lake project described above, giving us relationshipbuilding
capacity independent of any single execution partner and across multiple cities, including Mumbai and Pune, for the
accelerator-funded drain/river pilot. On the government side, we intend to adapt models proven elsewhere — for example,
our Coimbatore approach where the Municipal Commissioner directs corporate CSR funds toward rejuvenation, with
treated water then made available for industrial reuse, creating a secondary funding stream that eases the ULB’s own
budget burden. We also intend to engage NGO partners for community trust-building and co-funded monitoring (as with
Siruthuli, Gurujal, and MEGA Foundation elsewhere), and academic institutions for independent monitoring and
methodology standardization (as with PSG Institute of Technology in Coimbatore and IIT Roorkee on our Laksar Drain
project).
Value Across Multiple ULB Departments
A single treatment protocol delivers value across several ULB departments at once, rather than serving one narrow
mandate. The same program a water/sewerage department evaluates for BOD/COD and coliform compliance also delivers
public health value to a health department (reduced mosquito breeding and vector-borne disease risk), recreational and
biodiversity value to a parks/lakes department (restored fish, birds, usable water bodies), climate-resilience value to a
climate change mitigation/disaster management department (sludge mineralisation restores drain and lake water-holding
capacity, directly reducing urban flooding risk), and, where applicable, tourism and coastal-health value in beach-adjacent
contexts. Because many ULBs lack staff positioned to weigh all these benefits at once, a proposal evaluated through only one
department’s lens can be undervalued. Our go-to-market approach therefore presents this multi-departmental case
explicitly and seeks endorsement or budget participation from more than one department where possible.
ULB Training and Success-Criteria Alignment
Every drain we treat differs in flow rate, pollutant concentration, inlet count, sludge load, and seasonal rainfall/runoff.
Nualgi significantly improves water quality across this range, but combined with the fact that organic breakdown begun in a
drain sometimes only completes once the water reaches the receiving lake or river, a rigid, uniform success threshold can
misread genuine progress as underperformance and hold up payment on a contract that is in fact succeeding. Structured
ULB training — helping staff set drain-specific success criteria and understand phycoremediation as a connected drain-tolake/
river system rather than judging a drain in isolation — is therefore a necessary part of scaling this program. We see this
accelerator, through academic collaboration and independently validated pilot data, as a valuable vehicle for giving
Maharashtra ULBs credible evidence to adopt appropriate success criteria from the first project, rather than learning this
through a disputed early contract.
Expected Impact Description
At pilot scale, we expect our selected drain/river site — Thane, Mumbai, or Pune — and the separately-progressing Thane
lake project to show measurable DO increase, BOD/COD reduction, and coliform reduction within 8–12 weeks, with visible
qualitative change (reduced odour, clearer water, less floating algae/hyacinth) consistent with our Karnataka, Tamil Nadu,
Uttarakhand, and Odisha outcomes. As the program scales toward our target of 50 sites over 1–3 years, we expect
cumulative restoration of dissolved oxygen and reduced pollution load across a meaningful portion of Maharashtra’s
degraded lakes and drains, reduced pollutant discharge reaching rivers and the coast, reduced methane generation as
ecosystems shift from anaerobic to aerobic, and improved air quality from reduced hydrogen sulphide near treated sites.
Because aerobic bacterial activity mineralises legacy sludge rather than relocating it, treated beds also see a durable
reduction in sludge depth — restoring water-holding capacity and reducing urban flooding risk, a climate-resilience outcome
relevant to any ULB department focused on climate mitigation, not only water quality.
A further expected benefit, evidenced by our 15-year fishermen relationships in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, and Andhra
Pradesh, is improved fisheries and agricultural productivity: as diatoms grow in a treated drain, the resulting food-web
growth supports fish stocks and fishermen’s livelihoods in the lake, river, or coastal waters the drain feeds — even where
fish offtake does not happen in the drain itself, offtake points located downstream in the receiving lake or river still benefit
directly from the upstream drain having been treated. Water with fewer pollutants and higher dissolved oxygen also
supports healthier soils and higher yields where used for irrigation.
Socially, the communities most affected are lower- and middle-income households in informal settlements bordering
Maharashtra’s nallas and drains, who bear the highest exposure to odour, contaminated water, and mosquito-borne
disease, plus the broader city population benefiting from restored public lakes and talaos. Because rejuvenation propagates
along the sediment beyond the exact dosing point, this benefit extends to neighborhoods whose feeder sub-drains
discharge into the treated drain. We expect measurable reduction in mosquito breeding within roughly two months,
restored public access to water bodies, and over the medium term, reduced vector-borne disease burden. Downstream
agricultural and fishing communities benefit as treated reaches carry less pollutant load into irrigation and fishing waters.
Institutionally, this project gives Maharashtra ULBs a lower-cost tool for water quality compliance on drains and secondary
water bodies outside the scope of large STP investment, and establishes Nualgi, our execution partner, and our liaison
network as a credible, locally embedded resource — with the ambition of achieving the standing government empanelment
we have built in Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, and Odisha, making this a repeatable model for other water-stressed states.
Scenario-Specific Benefits
The specific benefits of this project vary by water body type and by what a treated drain or river flows into, so we set these
out explicitly by scenario.
Lakes and talaos treated directly: as diatom-driven oxygenation establishes, zooplankton grow on the diatom bloom and fish
grow in turn — a visible, measurable increase in fish population and biomass, supporting local fishermen’s livelihoods where
the lake is fished. This fish growth has a self-reinforcing effect: ducks, herons, kingfishers, and other birds that feed on fish
and aquatic life increase in number, restoring visible biodiversity. Because diatoms outcompete cyanobacteria and green
algae, harmful algal bloom incidence decreases, reducing surface scum, discoloration, and cyanotoxin risk, and improving
the lake’s safety and usability.
Drains or rivers discharging into a downstream lake or slower reach: diatoms and oxygen generated in the treated drain flow
onward and help seed the receiving water body’s food web, extending the fish-growth and bird-return benefits described
above, and supporting fishermen’s livelihoods at the lake or river even where fish offtake happens only downstream, not in
the drain itself — having treated the upstream drain still leaves that downstream fishery better off, while reducing the
organic and nutrient load that would otherwise fuel harmful algal blooms.
Rivers discharging into the sea: reducing the nutrient and organic load carried downstream reduces the risk of harmful algal blooms along the adjoining coastline, translating into cleaner coastal water and improved beach conditions, with direct benefit to coastal tourism, coastal fisheries and fishermen’s livelihoods, and the health of residents and visitors who swim, fish, or otherwise use those beaches.

column48: The deployment of technologically enabled Reverse Vending Machines (RVMs) across high-density transit nodes in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region (MMR)specifically Mumbai, Thane, and Kalyan represents a critical intervention in urban waste management. By transitioning away from traditional, centralized waste sorting toward decentralized, point-of-disposal recovery, this initiative drives measurable outcomes across environmental, economic, and civic vectors.  The anticipated impact is structured across a three-phase maturation cycle, moving from immediate behavioral shifts to systemic circular economy integration.  Phase 1: Short-Term Impact (012 Months) Focus: Operational Activation and Behavioral Economics  In the foundational year, the primary objective is establishing the infrastructure and driving user adoption through instant gratification and accessibility.  Behavioral Modification via Micro-Incentives: By leveraging digital reward systems (e-wallet cashback, retail discount vouchers), the RVM network effectively monetizes waste for the consumer. This behavioral economics approach transforms casual commuters into active participants, establishing a habitual return culture.  Immediate Municipal Relief: Transit hubs in the MMR experience immense foot traffic, leading to high volumes of surface litter. RVMs provide immediate relief to railway sanitation operations by capturing plastic before it enters the generalized waste stream or becomes public litter.  Source Segregation and Purity: Traditional municipal recycling suffers from high contamination rates. RVMs isolate PET (Polyethylene Terephthalate) bottles at the source, crushing them instantly. This prevents cross-contamination with organic waste, resulting in premium, high-yield feedstock for recyclers.  Phase 2: Medium-Term Impact (13 Years) Focus: Supply Chain Optimization and Corporate Synergies  As the network reaches critical mass and user habits solidify, the impact shifts toward commercial scalability and data generation.  Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) Enablement: Fast-Moving Consumer Goods (FMCG) and beverage corporations face strict regulatory mandates to recover the plastic they introduce into the market. The RVM network provides these corporations with a transparent, auditable mechanism to meet their EPR targets, fostering lucrative B2B partnerships.  IoT and Consumer Data Analytics: Modern RVMs are equipped with smart sensors and connected back-ends. The data harvestedsuch as peak disposal times, volume density per station, and brand-specific return ratesallows municipal bodies and corporate partners to optimize logistics and understand micro-market consumption patterns.  Geographic and Sectoral Expansion: Proven success and high utilization rates at railway stations will attract private investment, facilitating the expansion of RVM infrastructure into commercial real estate, including IT parks in Thane, shopping multiplexes in Kalyan, and large-scale residential complexes.  Phase 3: Long-Term Impact (3 Years) Focus: Urban Resilience and Macro-Circular Economy  In the mature phase, the RVM infrastructure acts as a catalyst for systemic environmental change and public policy evolution.  Urban Flood Mitigation: Mumbai's monsoon vulnerability is severely exacerbated by plastic waste clogging its storm-water drainage networks. By successfully diverting millions of non-biodegradable units annually, the RVM network directly enhances urban resilience and reduces the severity of localized flooding.  Marine Ecosystem Protection: A significant reduction in unmanaged plastic waste in the MMR directly correlates to lower plastic leakage into the Arabian Sea, protecting coastal ecosystems around Juhu, Versova, and the wider Konkan

Title : LACTIC ACID FERMENTATION COMPOSITION DERIVED FROM CITRUS PEEL DISTILLATION RESIDUE FOR CLEANING APPLICATIONS AND ANIMAL FEED BY-PRODUCT
Abstract : The present invention relates to an integrated bioprocess for the valorization of citrus peel distillation residue through lactic acid fermentation. After the extraction of essential oils, the residual citrus biomass is fermented using selected microbial cultures to produce a bio-based composition enriched with organic acids, enzymes, and microbial metabolites suitable for cleaning applications. The process also enables the recovery and utilization of the residual fermented biomass as a value-added poultry feed component, ensuring near-complete utilization of citrus processing waste. The invention provides a sustainable, circular biomanufacturing approach that reduces agricultural waste, creates multiple value-added products from a single feedstock, and offers an environmentally responsible alternative to conventional manufacturing processes.

PuroFarms addresses the interconnected challenges of agricultural waste management, soil degradation, farmer income, and climate change by converting cotton stalksone of Indias major underutilized agricultural residuesinto biochar and permanent carbon removal.

In cotton-growing regions such as Vidarbha, large quantities of cotton stalks are generated after harvest. Farmers often have limited economical options for managing this biomass, leading to open burning, which contributes to air pollution and greenhouse-gas emissions while wasting a valuable carbon resource. At the same time, agricultural soils are increasingly affected by declining organic matter, excessive dependence on synthetic inputs, poor water retention, and reduced soil health and productivity.

PuroFarms provides a circular solution by collecting cotton stalks from farms and converting them into stable biochar through decentralized and industrial pyrolysis systems. Our innovation combines biochar production with an advanced digital Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (dMRV) platform that tracks feedstock origin, farmer details, biomass quantity, processing parameters, biochar production, quality, application, and carbon-removal data.

This approach prevents open burning, converts agricultural waste into a durable carbon sink, and enables high-integrity carbon removal credits. The resulting biochar can also be returned to agricultural soils to improve soil structure, water retention, nutrient-use efficiency, and long-term soil health.

By integrating waste management, carbon removal, digital MRV, and regenerative agriculture, PuroFarms aims to create a scalable model that delivers measurable climate benefits while creating additional economic opportunities for farmers, rural communities, and local enterprises.
column37: Technology is central to PuroFarms innovation, enabling us to transform agricultural waste into measurable, scalable, and high-integrity carbon removal while improving soil health and creating value for farmers.  Our core technology combines advanced biomass conversion, digital Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (dMRV), data analytics, and carbon accounting. We use decentralized Kon-Tiki systems and industrial pyrolysis technology to convert cotton stalks into stable biochar while minimizing open burning and capturing carbon in a durable form.  A key innovation is our in-house dMRV platform, designed specifically for biochar and carbon-removal projects. The platform digitally records the complete project lifecyclefrom the source and quantity of biomass collected from individual farms to processing conditions, including moisture, weight, temperature, batch information, and biochar production. It also tracks biochar quality, sampling, laboratory testing, transportation, distribution, and final application.  Digital data collection reduces manual errors, improves traceability, and creates an auditable chain of evidence for carbon-credit verification. GPS-enabled records, photographs, timestamps, batch IDs, and standardized data fields help establish transparency and prevent double counting or inaccurate reporting.  Technology also enables PuroFarms to aggregate data from multiple decentralized production units into a centralized system, allowing us to monitor large numbers of farmers and production sites efficiently. In the future, we aim to integrate IoT sensors, automated data capture, remote monitoring, AI-based anomaly detection, and predictive analytics to further improve process efficiency and data quality.
column38:
PuroFarms addresses the urgent need for a scalable, economically viable, and traceable solution for agricultural biomass management and carbon removal. India generates large quantities of cotton stalks after harvesting, much of which has limited economic value and may be openly burned or left unmanaged. At the same time, many agricultural soils are experiencing declining organic matter, poor water retention, nutrient inefficiency, and reduced long-term productivity.

PuroFarms converts cotton stalks into biochar and permanent carbon removal, creating value from an underutilized agricultural residue. Our model simultaneously reduces open-field burning, stores carbon in a stable form, supports regenerative agriculture, and creates new opportunities for farmers and rural communities. Our digital dMRV platform further addresses the need for transparent, verifiable, and traceable carbon-removal data.

Current alternatives include open burning, incorporation of residues into soil, composting, biomass collection for fuel, and conventional industrial disposal. Open burning is inexpensive but causes air pollution and releases carbon back into the atmosphere. Leaving or incorporating large quantities of residues can be challenging because of slow decomposition and field-management constraints. Composting can produce valuable soil amendments but requires additional infrastructure, time, and management. Biomass can also be used for combustion or energy generation, but this generally returns most of the carbon to the atmosphere rather than creating durable carbon storage.

PuroFarms provides an alternative that combines waste management, durable carbon storage, soil-health benefits, digital traceability, and carbon-credit generation in one integrated and scalable system.

PuroFarms operates a circular bioeconomy and carbon-removal business focused on converting cotton agricultural residue into biochar and generating high-integrity carbon removal credits.

Our business model has three integrated revenue streams. First, we collect and process cotton stalks through decentralized and industrial pyrolysis systems to produce biochar. The biochar can be supplied for agricultural applications, soil restoration, water filtration, construction, and other industrial uses.

Second, our primary revenue stream is carbon removal credits generated from the durable carbon stored in biochar. We use our proprietary digital Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (dMRV) platform to track biomass sourcing, processing, biochar production, quality, application, and carbon-removal data. Verified credits are sold to corporates, climate-focused organizations, ESG funds, and international carbon-removal buyers.

Third, PuroFarms generates revenue through technology and services, including the sale of Kon-Tiki kilns, pyrolysis equipment, moisture and temperature sensors, dMRV solutions, EPC services, project development, carbon-credit consultancy, and carbon-project management.

We follow a scalable model combining owned production facilities, decentralized farmer-level units, and partnerships/franchise-based expansion. This allows us to increase biomass processing capacity without relying solely on capital-intensive centralized plants.

Our long-term objective is to build a vertically integrated cotton-waste-to-carbon-removal platform that creates value from agricultural residues while delivering measurable climate and soil-health benefits.

PuroFarms has identified several key challenges and risks associated with scaling a cotton-waste-to-biochar and carbon-removal business.

Feedstock availability and logistics: Cotton stalks are dispersed across large farming areas, making collection, transportation, aggregation, and seasonal storage challenging. We address this through partnerships with farmers and FPOs, decentralized collection models, and planned biomass storage.

Technology and operational risk: Maintaining consistent pyrolysis conditions, biochar quality, and production efficiency across decentralized and industrial units requires robust equipment, skilled operators, process monitoring, and preventive maintenance.

Carbon-credit market and regulatory risk: Carbon-credit prices, methodologies, verification requirements, and market demand can change over time. Changes in carbon standards or government regulations may affect project economics and credit issuance timelines. PuroFarms mitigates this through strong documentation, transparent dMRV, diversified buyers, and alignment with recognized carbon-removal standards.

Data and MRV risk: Incomplete or inaccurate field data can affect carbon-credit verification. Our dMRV platform addresses this by capturing standardized, time-stamped, location-linked data, photographs, batch records, production parameters, and biochar application information.

Market adoption: Farmers and industrial customers may require awareness, demonstrations, and evidence of biochar benefits before adoption. We address this through field trials, farmer engagement, and performance monitoring.

Financial and scaling risk: Expansion requires significant capital for equipment, infrastructure, working capital, and project development. We plan to mitigate this through phased expansion, strategic partnerships, equipment sales, and diversified revenue streams.

Previously Conducted Pilots within ULBs in Maharashtra

PuroFarms has been developing and implementing decentralized biochar production and carbon-removal solutions in Maharashtra, with a particular focus on cotton-growing regions of Vidarbha. Our work has primarily involved converting agricultural biomass, especially cotton stalks, into biochar through decentralized Kon-Tiki systems and establishing the associated digital Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (dMRV) processes.

Our pilot activities have focused on demonstrating that agricultural residues generated within and around rural and semi-urban communities can be systematically collected, processed, converted into biochar, and tracked for carbon-removal purposes.

 1. Decentralized Biochar Production Pilot  Vidarbha, Maharashtra

PuroFarms has worked with farmers and local agricultural networks in the Vidarbha region to establish a decentralized biomass collection and biochar production model. The pilot involved the collection of cotton stalks after harvesting and their conversion into biochar using Kon-Tiki-based pyrolysis systems.

Through this model, we have connected with 3,000 farmers and 10 FPOs and developed a biomass aggregation network covering approximately 20,000 tonnes of agricultural residue. The decentralized approach reduces the transportation burden associated with dispersed biomass and enables local communities to participate in biomass processing.

 2. Biochar Production and Field Application

As part of our field operations, PuroFarms has supported the production of 5,000 tonnes of biochar from agricultural biomass and contributed to the generation of 10,000 carbon-removal credits through project activities in Vidarbha.

The produced biochar has been used as a soil amendment, including blending with vermicompost before application to agricultural fields. Field-level observations and demonstrations have indicated improvements in soil conditions and crop productivity. In selected demonstrations, crop yields increased from approximately 30 quintals/hectare to 55 quintals/hectare, although results vary depending on soil type, crop management, weather, and application practices.

 3. Digital MRV Pilot

A major component of the PuroFarms pilot model has been the development and field testing of an in-house digital Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (dMRV) platform specifically designed for biochar carbon-removal projects.

The system captures information throughout the project lifecycle, including:

 Farmer and farm details
 Biomass source and collection records
 Batch ID and Kon-Tiki identification
 Biomass weight and moisture
 Production photographs
 Pyrolysis/processing parameters
 Biochar quantity produced
 Biochar sampling and laboratory testing
 Quality parameters
 Transportation and distribution
 Biochar application records
 Farmer acknowledgement and supporting evidence

This pilot demonstrated the importance of digital traceability in decentralized biochar projects, where conventional paper-based systems can result in missing or inconsistent data.

 4. Community and Rural Participation

The decentralized model was designed to involve farmers, rural youth, local operators, and FPOs in the biomass value chain. Instead of treating cotton stalks as waste, the pilot demonstrates how agricultural residues can become a source of additional economic and environmental value.

The model also reduces the need for farmers to burn residues in the field, while creating opportunities for local employment in biomass collection, transportation, processing, equipment operation, and field application.

 5. Relevance to Urban Local Bodies (ULBs)

While the initial pilots have primarily been implemented through agricultural and rural networks rather than as municipal solid-waste projects directly operated by ULBs, the underlying technology and operating model are highly relevant to Urban Local Bodies in Maharashtra, particularly ULBs located in cotton-growing districts.

ULBs can potentially use this model to facilitate the aggregation and decentralized processing of agricultural and horticultural biomass generated within their surrounding service areas. Instead of open burning or uncontrolled disposal, biomass can be directed toward controlled biochar production, with the resulting carbon removal and environmental benefits digitally documented.

 6. Learning from the Pilots

The pilot activities have provided PuroFarms with practical experience in:

1. Biomass aggregation: Building farmer/FPO networks for reliable feedstock supply.
2. Decentralized processing: Operating biochar production systems close to biomass sources.
3. Quality control: Monitoring feedstock and biochar characteristics.
4. Digital MRV: Capturing project data from biomass collection through final biochar application.
5. Carbon accounting: Developing traceable datasets required for carbon-removal projects.
6. Farmer engagement: Demonstrating the agricultural value of biochar.
7. Scalability: Understanding the operational requirements for expanding from individual decentralized units to larger networks.

 7. Proposed Next Phase with ULBs

Based on these experiences, PuroFarms aims to collaborate with Maharashtra ULBs to develop integrated decentralized biomass-to-biochar pilots. The proposed model would identify suitable biomass streams, establish collection and aggregation systems, deploy appropriate biochar technologies, and monitor the entire process through the PuroFarms dMRV platform.

The objective is to demonstrate a replicable model that can help ULBs reduce biomass burning and unmanaged residue disposal while generating biochar, creating local employment, improving soil health, and potentially generating verified carbon-removal credits.

Overall, PuroFarms previous field pilots have established the technical, operational, community, and digital-MRV foundation required to scale decentralized biochar and carbon-removal projects in Maharashtra. The next opportunity is to adapt and deploy this proven model in partnership with ULBs at a larger municipal and regional scale.

# Project / Scaling Opportunity – PuroFarms

## 1. Project Description

PuroFarms proposes to scale a **decentralized agricultural biomass-to-biochar and carbon-removal model** that converts cotton stalks and other underutilized agricultural residues into stable biochar, while preventing open-field burning and creating measurable environmental, social, and economic benefits.

India is one of the world's major cotton-producing countries and generates substantial quantities of cotton stalk residue every year. In cotton-growing regions, farmers often have limited economically viable options for managing this biomass, resulting in open burning, uncontrolled decomposition, or low-value disposal. At the same time, agricultural soils are facing declining organic matter, reduced water-retention capacity, increasing input dependence, and declining soil health.

PuroFarms addresses these challenges through an integrated **waste-to-value and carbon-removal platform**. Agricultural residues are collected through farmer and FPO networks, processed through decentralized Kon-Tiki systems and industrial pyrolysis units, and converted into biochar. A portion of the biochar can be applied to agricultural soils, while other applications include construction materials, water filtration, and other industrial uses.

A critical component of the project is our **in-house digital Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (dMRV) platform**. The system digitally tracks the complete carbon-removal lifecycle, including farmer and farm details, biomass source, collection quantity, moisture, batch identification, processing parameters, biochar production, quality testing, transportation, distribution, and final application. This creates a transparent and auditable data trail for carbon accounting and verification.

The scaling project will establish a network of decentralized and industrial biochar production units connected through a centralized digital MRV system. The model will enable PuroFarms to process substantially larger quantities of agricultural residues while maintaining traceability and quality control.

## 2. Geography

The initial scaling geography is **Maharashtra**, with a primary focus on the **Vidarbha region**, one of India's important cotton-growing areas.

PuroFarms has already developed field-level relationships with **3,000+ farmers and 10 FPOs** in the region and has experience in cotton-stalk collection, decentralized biochar production, farmer engagement, and carbon-removal data collection.

The project will initially focus on cotton-producing districts of Vidarbha and subsequently expand to other cotton-growing regions of Maharashtra and India.

Potential expansion geographies include:

* Maharashtra
* Gujarat
* Telangana
* Madhya Pradesh
* Karnataka
* Other major cotton-producing states of India

The decentralized nature of the model allows production units to be located close to biomass sources, reducing transportation distances and enabling local employment.

## 3. Project Timeline

### Phase 1 – Preparation and Pilot Scaling: 0–6 Months

* Identify priority ULBs, FPOs, farmer clusters, and biomass sources.
* Strengthen biomass aggregation and storage infrastructure.
* Deploy and optimize decentralized biochar production systems.
* Establish baseline environmental and social indicators.
* Improve and field-test the dMRV platform.
* Develop partnerships with ULBs, government agencies, corporates, and carbon-removal buyers.

### Phase 2 – Demonstration and Operational Scaling: 6–18 Months

* Deploy additional decentralized and/or industrial pyrolysis units.
* Expand farmer and FPO participation.
* Increase biomass collection and processing capacity.
* Implement standardized quality-control procedures.
* Digitize project-level MRV across all operational sites.
* Conduct field demonstrations of biochar application.
* Begin/expand third-party validation and carbon-credit certification processes.

### Phase 3 – Regional Scale-Up: 18–36 Months

* Expand across multiple districts of Maharashtra.
* Establish additional production hubs through partnerships and franchise/decentralized models.
* Integrate ULB biomass streams where technically and legally suitable.
* Scale carbon-credit generation and sales.
* Establish long-term corporate and international carbon-removal buyer relationships.

### Phase 4 – National Replication: 3–5+ Years

Replicate the model across major cotton-producing states of India and expand the dMRV platform to support a large network of decentralized biochar projects.

## 4. Funding Required

PuroFarms is seeking approximately **INR 3–5 crore** in funding for the proposed scaling phase, depending on the final project configuration and number of production units deployed.

The funding will primarily support:

* Biochar production and pyrolysis equipment
* Decentralized biomass-processing infrastructure
* Biomass collection, aggregation, and storage
* Site development and utilities
* dMRV platform development and IoT integration
* Sensors and field-monitoring equipment
* Biochar quality testing and laboratory analysis
* Carbon-project development, validation, and verification
* Personnel and technical expertise
* Farmer and community engagement
* Pilot demonstrations and field trials
* Project management and working capital

PuroFarms will also explore blended financing through strategic investors, corporate partnerships, carbon-removal offtake agreements, equipment partnerships, government schemes, and ULB collaborations.

## 5. Partnerships Associated

The scaling project will be implemented through a multi-stakeholder ecosystem.

### Farmers and FPOs

Farmers and FPOs will be the primary biomass suppliers and beneficiaries. They will participate in residue collection, aggregation, biochar application, and field demonstrations.

### Urban Local Bodies

PuroFarms proposes to work with relevant ULBs in Maharashtra to identify suitable agricultural, horticultural, and other biomass streams and develop decentralized biomass-to-biochar solutions. ULB partnerships can provide access to biomass, local infrastructure, community networks, and municipal support.

### Government and Public Institutions

We will explore partnerships with relevant departments and institutions of the Government of Maharashtra and Government of India, agricultural universities, research institutions, and local authorities for technology validation, field trials, farmer outreach, training, and project implementation.

PuroFarms is also incubated at **PDKV Akola**, providing an important institutional connection within the agricultural ecosystem of Vidarbha.

### Corporate Partners

Corporate partners can participate through:

* Carbon-removal credit purchase/offtake
* CSR-supported biomass and farmer programs
* Technology partnerships
* Biochar application and research
* Sustainable supply-chain initiatives

### Carbon Registries and Verification Partners

PuroFarms intends to work with recognized carbon-removal standards, registries, validation/verification bodies, laboratories, and technical partners to ensure that carbon-removal claims meet appropriate scientific and methodological requirements.

### Technology Partners

Equipment manufacturers, IoT companies, software developers, laboratories, and engineering partners will support the deployment of reliable pyrolysis technology, sensors, data systems, and quality-control infrastructure.

## 6. Expected Environmental Impact

The project will create measurable environmental benefits by:

* Diverting large quantities of cotton stalks from open burning and unmanaged disposal.
* Converting agricultural residues into stable biochar.
* Permanently storing a portion of biomass-derived carbon in biochar.
* Generating verified carbon-removal credits.
* Reducing air pollution associated with crop-residue burning.
* Supporting improved soil organic matter and soil-health practices through biochar application.
* Promoting circular use of agricultural resources.
* Reducing dependence on linear waste-disposal practices.

PuroFarms will quantify impact through its dMRV system using biomass weight, moisture, source, production parameters, biochar yield, carbon content, application records, and other relevant data.

## 7. Expected Social Impact

The project is designed to ensure that carbon removal creates value at the rural community level.

Expected outcomes include:

* Engagement of thousands of farmers and FPO members.
* Creation of employment for rural youth and women.
* New economic opportunities in biomass collection, transportation, processing, equipment operation, and field services.
* Improved awareness of sustainable residue management.
* Reduced dependence on open burning.
* Increased access to biochar-based soil-management practices.
* Strengthening of local agricultural value chains.

PuroFarms will monitor the number of farmers engaged, jobs created, women and youth participating, biomass collected, communities reached, and farmer feedback.

## 8. Expected Economic and Climate Impact

The project creates a new economic pathway for agricultural residues by transforming a low-value waste stream into **biochar, carbon-removal credits, and technology-enabled services**.

PuroFarms will generate revenue through carbon-removal credit sales, biochar and equipment sales, EPC and consultancy services, dMRV solutions, and carbon-project development.

Our long-term objective is to build a scalable network capable of generating approximately **500,000 carbon-removal credits annually by 2030**, subject to project performance, applicable methodologies, and third-party verification.

## 9. Scalability Opportunity

The major scaling opportunity lies in the combination of **abundant agricultural biomass, decentralized production, digital MRV, carbon markets, and farmer networks**.

Rather than building only large centralized plants, PuroFarms will use a hub-and-spoke approach in which decentralized production units are located near biomass sources and connected to a centralized digital platform. This reduces logistics challenges and allows the model to scale district by district.

The dMRV platform is designed to standardize data collection across multiple production sites, enabling PuroFarms to manage a geographically distributed carbon-removal portfolio while maintaining traceability.

The model can initially focus on cotton stalks and subsequently expand to other eligible agricultural residues where technically and environmentally appropriate.

## 10. Overall Expected Impact

The proposed project will demonstrate that agricultural residue can be transformed from an environmental liability into a **climate, agricultural, and economic asset**.

By combining biomass management, biochar production, permanent carbon removal, digital MRV, soil-health applications, and rural employment, PuroFarms aims to develop a replicable model for Maharashtra and eventually for other agricultural regions of India.

The project will contribute to three interconnected outcomes:

**Climate:** Permanent carbon storage and reduction of emissions associated with residue burning.

**Environment:** Improved biomass management, reduced open burning, circular resource utilization, and improved soil-health practices.

**People:** New rural employment and economic opportunities, stronger farmer/FPO participation, and greater value creation from agricultural residues.

PuroFarms seeks to use this scaling opportunity to establish Maharashtra as a strong demonstration region for **decentralized, digitally monitored biochar carbon removal**, creating a pathway that can be replicated nationally and contribute to India's broader climate and circular-economy goals.

column36: PadCare tackles the menstrual waste crisis that India's sanitation system was never built to handle. Roughly 12 billion sanitary pads get thrown away every year, and because they're made of plastic and super-absorbent polymers, each one sits in a landfill for 500 to 800 years before it breaks down. That's the environmental side. The human side is just as stark355 million women and girls menstruate in India, many without any safe or private way to dispose of pads at school, at work, or at home, and over 4 million sanitation workers end up sorting this waste by hand with little to no protective gear. So really, we're addressing a problem that sits at the intersection of environment, public health, and dignity, not just a waste-management gap.
