Technology is implemented across multiple stages to implement a circular economy for sanitary pad waste.
1. Collection: At the point of use, our PadCare Bins run on patented PadCare Vap vapour-phase technology, which lets a single bin safely hold up to 75 used pads (about 1.5 kg) for 30 days without odour or hygiene risk  that's what makes low-frequency pickup viable.
2. Recycling: Once collected, all the waste goes to PadCareX, our recycling facility, where patented 5D technology separates it into clean cellulose pulp and plastic that can actually be reused. This replaces the existing options of landfilling, which causes the pads to break down into microplastics or incineration, which releases harmful gases (such as dioxins and furans) into the atmosphere.
With our technology serving as the core of the menstrual hygiene ecosystem that we provide, we're currently hitting a 98 material recovery rate and over 90 plastic purity.
3. Monitoring, Analysis and Reporting: Apart from the hardware, we run a digital dashboard that tracks important metrics of the intervention being deployed. This includes collection volumes, emissions avoided, and landfill space saved, so the impact side isn't guesswork  it's measured and reportable to every partner and CSR funder we work with.

Implementing Sanitary Pad Waste Management for Adolescent Girls in Schools of BMC

PROJECT DESCRIPTION:
Many schools in India do not have the plan or infrastructure for what happens after the girls use sanitary pads. Since there is no dedicated safe space for disposal, so it either ends up mixed in with dry waste — which means a sanitation worker somewhere handles it by hand, unprotected-or it's incinerated or landfilled, which just hides the problem instead of solving it. India throws away around 12 billion pads a year, and each pad takes 500 to 800 years to break down. More than 4 million sanitation workers handle this waste daily, without gloves, training, or choice. Inside a school specifically, this gap shows up as something much more personal: girls skipping school, feeling embarrassed, or just quietly managing a bad situation because there's no better option.

This proposal helps solve the problem for schools under the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC). PadCare has already run this model in over 300 schools across India, where it visibly helped with attendance and hygiene habits and diverted real, measurable tonnage away from landfill. The projects have consequently retained more than 55% of the schools to continue the service thus ensuring long-term sustainability.

The approach has 4 main parts:
1. Awareness-We run structured MHM sessions with students and staff, in the local language, because that's what's consistently made the difference in our past projects.
2. Infrastructure - PadCare Bins, which use our own PadCare Vap™ technology, get installed on-site. These can hold used pads safely for weeks without odour or hygiene issues, which is exactly what makes a low-frequency, low-cost pickup schedule realistic.
3. Service-Timely periodic service for pickup of pads 
4. Technology-Every sanitary pad collected goes to our PadCareX facility, where a patented 5D process (disintegration, decolorization, deodorization, disinfection, and deactivation of the super-absorbent polymer) actually breaks the material down into usable cellulose and plastic. We're recovering over 98% of the material. 

This project will cover the capex and opex for both the equipment and the running costs in year one, schools keep using the system long after the official project wraps up. Once the bins are already paid for, continuing the service is just a small, easy decision.

-

GEOGRAPHY:
The project covers schools under BMC-Mumbai's municipal school network. It's a natural fit for a few reasons. These schools serve large numbers of adolescent girls from lower-income households, exactly the group least likely to have access to sanitary products or facilities anywhere else. BMC also runs everything under one civic authority, which makes coordination, approvals, and future scale-up far more manageable than working across dozens of independent institutions. And BMC already has waste-management and public-health mandates this project fits neatly into. We'll work with BMC's education and health departments to shortlist schools-prioritising ones with higher enrolment of adolescent girls, weaker existing sanitation setups, and practical collection-route logistics, since that keeps costs efficient.

-

TIMELINES
The rollout runs over 12 months, in five phases:

Months 1–2, Identification & School Onboarding — we design the survey and IEC material, pull enrolment and infrastructure data on BMC schools, and run outreach visits to shortlist schools that are actually interested and ready. We start formal sign-off from BMC and individual school administrations for bin installation, plus finalising the O&M arrangements and committee approvals at each school.

Months 2–3-First Awareness Round and Installation Initiation-The first MHM session runs as a common assembly-style talk across onboarded schools, and bin installation starts in parallel.

Months 4–6-Monitoring and Operations

Months 5–9-Monitoring,Operations and Second Awareness Round — all bins are in place by month 9, and a second, more focused awareness round — smaller group or classroom-level sessions — runs between months 7 and 9 to reinforce what was covered earlier and answer more specific questions.

Months 10–12, Post-Installation Outreach & Reporting — a third common-session awareness push keeps engagement going, while service delivery and monitoring run continuously in the background from the moment the first bins go in. By month 12, we pull together a full impact report — usage data, waste recycled, and shifts in attendance and awareness, measured through pre- and post-programme surveys.
-
FUNDING:
We've structured this in three slabs — 25, 50, or 100 schools — because bulk deployment genuinely brings our costs down. Each slab covers full year-one capex (bins, vending infrastructure where needed) and full year-one opex (fortnightly collection, recycling, three rounds of awareness workshops, and impact reporting).
-
PARTNERSHIPS:
This is a three-way effort. BMC, as the Urban Local Body, gives us the institutional access and mandate — approvals to install bins in municipal schools, coordination with principals and school staff, and alignment with existing sanitation and Swachh Bharat Mission goals. The corporate or CSR funder (whoever takes this proposal forward) provides the year-one funding across whichever slab they choose, and in return gets clean, reportable impact data — CO2eq avoided, landfill space saved, material recycled, attendance shifts — the kind of numbers that hold up in ESG reporting. PadCare brings the actual delivery — the patented bins, trained collection teams, the PadCareX recycling facility, and the awareness content and facilitators, all pulled from the same playbook we've already run across 300+ schools. Where it makes sense, we'd also loop in local NGO partners for the awareness sessions specifically, since that's consistently strengthened adoption in past projects.

-

EXPECTED IMPACT:
In the short term, within year one, every onboarded school gets Safeboxes installed and running, three awareness sessions delivered, a fortnightly collection cycle in place, and a proper baseline established — so later progress is measured against something real, not a guess.

Environmentally, our own life-cycle assessment (done to ISO 14040/14044 standards) shows this process produces about 84% lower emissions than landfilling and 88% lower than incineration. Even at the smallest slab of 25 schools, we'd expect several thousand pads a month diverted away from landfill, which we'll report out as concrete litres of landfill space saved and kilograms of CO2 avoided — school by school and in total.

Socially, every adolescent girl and every female staff member at each school benefits directly — and based on what we saw in multiple schools, that tends to show up as steadier attendance during menstruation and a school environment that's simply easier for girls to be in. Sanitation staff benefit too, moving from handling loose, unsealed waste by hand to a sealed, safe collection system.

Over the medium to long term, once schools take on the smaller year-two costs themselves, we'd expect to see the same pattern we've already seen elsewhere — steady, habitual use of the system rather than something that fades out once the funding period ends.

-

LONG TERM SUSTAINABILITY
The whole sustainability argument here comes down to one design choice: the funder pays for capex and opex only in year one. That single decision removes the biggest barrier we consistently run into — schools can rarely absorb the upfront cost of new infrastructure on their own, but once it's already paid for, keeping the service running is a small, easy call rather than a new line item they have to fight for in a budget meeting.

After year one, this is a genuinely low-maintenance system. The bins don't need constant servicing — PadCare Vap™ technology means they can hold waste safely for extended periods without odour or hygiene concerns, so there's no specialist upkeep required. The only ongoing cost is fortnightly collection and recycling, and at the volume one school generates, that's a small, predictable expense — nowhere close to what year one costs. This is exactly the pattern we've already seen across the 300+ schools we've worked with: once a school gets full capex-and-opex support in year one, it tends to keep the programme going at its own pace and its own budget, long after our formal involvement ends, simply because the hard part — the upfront cost — is already behind them.

This project will also make a strong retention case for BMC. Once bins are in place and awareness has taken hold across however many schools the funder chooses to cover, BMC ends up with a low-cost, highly visible public-health initiative it can either continue running as-is or expand to more schools on its own — reinforcing its Swachh Bharat Mission commitments without needing anywhere close to the year-one investment. This project will act as a one-time push that turns a real infrastructure gap into a small, manageable running cost the schools and BMC can carry on their own, indefinitely.

column36:
Anantagni addresses the challenge of efficiently managing and recovering value from heterogeneous, contaminated and difficult-to-recycle waste streams. Conventional waste management systems are largely fragmented: segregation, recycling, disposal and energy recovery operate as separate processes, while many thermal conversion systems are designed for relatively uniform feedstocks.

As a result, mixed waste is difficult to characterise, inconsistent to process and often ends up in landfills, open disposal or low-value recovery pathways. This creates environmental burdens while valuable carbon and energy resources remain underutilised.

Anantagni is developing an integrated waste-to-resource platform that first identifies and engineers heterogeneous feedstock, then converts suitable waste into useful resources such as fuel-range liquids, char and syngas. The approach is designed to improve feedstock flexibility, resource recovery and process consistency while enabling measurable waste diversion and emissions impact.

Our objective is to build scalable, modular systems that can be deployed closer to waste-generation points and adapted to different waste streams, creating a circular alternative to disposal-led waste management.
column37:
Technology is the core enabler of Anantagnis solution. Our innovation integrates multiple technology layers rather than relying on a standalone pyrolysis reactor.

The first layer is AI-assisted waste identification, which helps detect and classify heterogeneous feedstock and generate digital waste intelligence. This is followed by engineered preprocessing to prepare suitable feedstock for conversion.

The core conversion system uses proprietary thermal upcycling/co-pyrolysis, supported by catalytic upgrading and multi-stage condensation to improve resource recovery and product consistency. Controlled emission systems and process monitoring are incorporated into the architecture.

The resulting platform is designed for multi-feedstock operation, allowing suitable combinations of plastic, biomass and other difficult waste streams to be processed according to their characteristics.

We have progressed the technology to TRL 5 through prototype and semi-pilot validation, with more than 100,000 data points used for AI model development and over 80-82 classification accuracy reported in our current development stage. The next objective is larger-scale continuous demonstration and validation before commercial deployment.
column38:
The primary need is for a scalable and economically viable way to manage waste that is too heterogeneous, contaminated or difficult to recycle through conventional systems, while recovering useful material and energy value from it.

Current alternatives include conventional recycling, manual/mechanical segregation, landfill disposal, RDF-based energy recovery, incineration and feedstock-specific pyrolysis or other thermal conversion systems. Each has limitations depending on waste composition, contamination, economics and required preprocessing. Conventional recycling, for example, works best with relatively clean and segregated streams, while many existing thermal systems are designed around specific feedstocks.

Anantagni addresses this gap by integrating waste identification, feedstock engineering, thermal conversion, upgrading and resource recovery into a single technology architecture. Instead of treating heterogeneous waste simply as a disposal problem, the system aims to understand the feedstock first and then determine an appropriate recovery pathway.

This enables a more flexible, modular and data-driven approach to waste-to-resource conversion, particularly for difficult-to-recycle mixed streams.

Anantagni is developing a multi-channel waste-to-resource business model combining project deployment, resource recovery and technology-led services.

In the initial phase, we will focus on pilot and demonstration deployments with industries, municipalities, waste aggregators and other waste-generating or managing organisations. Revenue can be generated through waste processing/tipping arrangements, sale of recovered products such as fuel-range liquids, char and syngas, and engineering or technology deployment services.

As the technology is validated and standardised, the business will expand through modular plant deployment, long-term operations & maintenance contracts and technology licensing. Additional revenue opportunities include EPR-related services, technical consulting and carbon/MRV-linked services where applicable.

Our long-term model combines company-operated/deployed modular systems with partnerships, licensing and decentralised installations at suitable waste-generation sites. This creates multiple revenue streams rather than dependence on a single product or customer segment.

The immediate commercial objective is to validate technical performance, economics and customer adoption through demonstration-scale deployment and then replicate the model across multiple sites.

The key risks are technology scale-up, feedstock variability, regulatory compliance, capital requirements, output quality and commercial adoption.

Technology scale-up: Moving from pilot validation to continuous commercial operation requires controlled engineering, commissioning and staged validation.

Feedstock variability: Mixed waste composition can affect process performance. We are addressing this through AI-assisted identification, feedstock characterisation and engineered preprocessing.

Regulatory compliance: Waste processing and thermal conversion require appropriate environmental approvals, testing and monitoring. Compliance is being incorporated into the deployment pathway before commercial operations.

CAPEX and execution: Scaling physical infrastructure requires disciplined capital deployment and experienced engineering/EPC partners. We plan to follow a phased deployment strategy.

Output quality and offtake: Recovered products must meet defined specifications and customer requirements. Structured testing and qualification with potential offtake partners will be used to validate product quality.

Commercial adoption: Customers may require technical demonstrations before committing to long-term deployments. We therefore plan to use controlled pilots, performance validation and early partnerships to reduce adoption risk.

Anantagni Industries is developing an end-to-end Waste-to-Resource recovery platform for difficult and heterogeneous waste streams that are not efficiently addressed by conventional recycling, biological treatment or existing disposal pathways.

The proposed project will establish a 1 TPD integrated waste-to-resource demonstration plant in Maharashtra, designed to validate the complete process chain from waste characterisation and feedstock preparation to thermal resource recovery, product separation, emission control and process monitoring.

The platform combines:
Waste Characterisation ? Feedstock Engineering ? Continuous Resource Recovery ? Product Recovery ? Process Intelligence & MRV

Our technology is designed to work with selected difficult-to-process carbon-rich waste streams, including suitable combinations of biomass, plastics and mixed/residual waste. The objective is not to replace recycling or other established waste-management systems, but to address the fraction that remains difficult to recover economically through conventional pathways.

The project is the next step in Anantagni's technology development. We have already demonstrated co-pyrolysis on a 50 kg/day semi-batch rotary-kiln system, processing groundnut shell biomass with LDPE, HDPE and PP at multiple blending ratios. We have also developed, with Shree Balaji Engineering Works, a 30 kg/hr continuous rotary-kiln engineering platform that has validated continuous solids feeding, heat transfer, vapour recovery and process-control functions using biomass.

Our patented 10–20 kg/hr feedstock-flexible demonstration reactor is currently under fabrication. The 1 TPD system will build on these validated components and integrate them into a complete operating system.

The project will generate real-world data on feedstock variability, process stability, product quality, resource recovery, emissions, operating costs and revenue potential. This data will be used to standardise the technology and create a repeatable modular deployment model.

#Geography:
Primary geography: Maharashtra, India.

Maharashtra is strategically important for the project because of its large urban population, industrial activity, agro-industrial clusters and diverse waste streams. The initial deployment will focus on identifying a suitable location in Maharashtra with:

Reliable access to difficult-to-process waste;
Suitable land and utilities;
Proximity to waste generators/aggregators or a ULB;
Potential offtake for recovered products; and
A suitable regulatory and operating environment.

We intend to work with Maharashtra ULBs, waste-management companies, industrial waste generators and other relevant local stakeholders to identify the most suitable feedstock and deployment location.

The project is intended to become a Maharashtra-based demonstration that can subsequently be replicated across other Indian cities and industrial/agro-industrial clusters.

#Project Timeline:
The project will follow a staged approach:

0–3 months — Demonstration reactor & engineering
Complete fabrication and commissioning of the 10–20 kg/hr demonstration reactor.
Validate feedstock flexibility and operating conditions.
Finalise engineering of the 1 TPD integrated system.
Identify site, feedstock partners and potential offtake partners.

3–6 months — Site preparation & integration
Finalise deployment location.
Complete detailed engineering and procurement.
Establish feedstock preparation/pre-processing infrastructure.
Integrate conversion, condensation/recovery, emission-control and monitoring systems.

6–12 months — 1 TPD demonstration
Commission the integrated 1 TPD plant.
Conduct sustained operational trials with selected real-world waste streams.
Measure resource recovery, product quality, emissions, energy consumption and operating costs.
Generate the technical and economic data required for commercial deployment.

12–18 months — Commercial validation
Optimise operating parameters and feedstock combinations.
Validate unit economics and product offtake.
Secure the first paid deployment/commercial contract.
Standardise the modular design for replication.

This staged roadmap is consistent with our current commercialisation plan: demonstrate one integrated system, prove its economics, standardise it and then replicate it through deployment partnerships.

#Funding Required:
The estimated total capital requirement for the proposed 1 TPD project is approximately ?4 crore.

The funding will primarily be utilised for:
Integrated plant CAPEX;
Pre-processing and feedstock preparation;
Reactor and thermal conversion system;
Condensation and product recovery;
Emission-control systems;
Instrumentation, automation and process monitoring;
Engineering and fabrication;
Testing, compliance and validation;
AI-based waste characterisation/feedstock intelligence;
Initial operating and working capital; and
Site development and commissioning.

We intend to use TVARAN/T-MAP support as catalytic funding for the project, while leveraging the programme to mobilise complementary equity, grants and strategic/industry participation where appropriate.

The objective is to ensure that the funding directly translates into a measurable technology and deployment milestone rather than simply supporting R&D. The primary outcome will be a working 1 TPD end-to-end demonstration system with independently measurable technical, environmental and economic performance.

#Partnerships and Institutional Engagement:
Anantagni has already developed an ecosystem of technical, academic, government and industry relationships.

Government / institutional engagement:
We received a prototype grant and were selected among the Top 18 finalists in the Rajasthan Green Innovation Challenge, organised by Rajasthan State Pollution Control Board and MNIT Jaipur.
We showcased the technology before senior government stakeholders during the RGIC programme.
We have participated in government/startup platforms including Startup Marathon and other technology challenges.
We are currently seeking to establish appropriate Maharashtra ULB and municipal partnerships for the proposed demonstration.

Technology / corporate partnership:
Shree Balaji Engineering Works has collaborated with us in developing the 30 kg/hr continuous rotary-kiln engineering platform, providing an important engineering base for continuous operation.

Academic / incubation ecosystem:
Anantagni is incubated at Atal Incubation Centre – Manipal University Jaipur (AIC-MUJ).
We have academic collaboration/MoU relationships with institutions including IIT Dhanbad, UPL University and JNTUA, as documented in our existing institutional material.

For the Maharashtra deployment, the key partnership structure we intend to build is:

ULB / waste generator ? Anantagni ? technology/engineering partners ? offtake partners

This will allow the project to address the complete deployment chain rather than demonstrating only the reactor in isolation.

#Expected Impact:

The project is expected to create impact across environmental, economic and social dimensions.

Environmental Impact
The immediate objective is to divert difficult-to-process waste from low-value disposal pathways and recover useful resources from it.

We will quantitatively measure:
Tonnes of waste received and processed;
Tonnes diverted from landfill/disposal;
Resource/product recovery per tonne;
Energy/resource substitution;
Emissions generated and avoided;
Process efficiency and material balance.

The project will establish a baseline for each feedstock and compare the Anantagni pathway with the relevant existing disposal/recovery route.

Economic Impact
The project will demonstrate whether difficult waste streams can be converted into commercially valuable resources while reducing disposal dependence.

The key metrics will include:
Processing cost per tonne;
Recovery yield;
Product realisation;
Disposal cost avoided;
Revenue per tonne;
Plant utilisation;
Operating margin potential; and
Payback economics for future modular deployments.

The most important commercial outcome will be proving a repeatable unit of infrastructure, rather than simply demonstrating a laboratory process.

Social Impact
The project can create local employment in plant operations, maintenance, feedstock handling, logistics and supporting services. It can also reduce dependence on unsafe and highly manual handling of difficult waste streams by improving the organisation and automation of waste identification and processing.

Where informal waste workers are part of the local ecosystem, our approach will seek to complement existing livelihoods through safer working conditions, training and integration rather than simply displacing them.

#Scaling Opportunity:

The 1 TPD system is deliberately positioned as a commercial demonstration bridge—large enough to generate meaningful operational and economic data, while remaining manageable in terms of capital and deployment risk.

Once the system is validated, Anantagni's strategy is to standardise the architecture and replicate it through modular deployments.

The planned scale pathway is:

1 TPD demonstration ? standardised modular systems ? 5–10 TPD deployments ? multiple regional deployments ? EPC/JV/licensing model

The longer-term opportunity is to deploy these systems across Maharashtra and subsequently other Indian markets where suitable difficult waste streams, waste generators and offtake opportunities exist.

Our objective is therefore not to build a single waste-processing plant. The 1 TPD project is intended to establish the technical, operational and economic blueprint for a repeatable Waste-to-Resource infrastructure platform.

#Overall Project Outcome:
At the end of the project, Anantagni aims to have:

A commissioned 1 TPD end-to-end waste-to-resource demonstration plant in Maharashtra;
Demonstrated operation on selected real-world difficult waste streams;
Validated feedstock preparation, conversion, recovery and emission-control performance;
Measured environmental impact and waste diversion;
Established validated unit economics;
Secured waste supply and product offtake relationships;
Generated the operational data required for standardisation; and
Established a clear pathway to the first repeatable commercial deployments.

The core objective is simple: prove one complete system in Maharashtra, measure everything that matters, standardise what works, and replicate it across India.

India's urban water systems face three interconnected challenges that most existing solutions don't fully address.
The first is wastewater treatment. Conventional aeration in STPs and ETPs typically achieves only 5-10 gas dissolution, which leaves BOD, COD, and pathogen levels higher than they should be even after treatment. The usual response is to add more chemicals or expand plant capacity, both of which are costly and slow to implement.
The second challenge involves smaller, decentralized waste streams -aquaculture ponds, swimming pools, and irrigation systems for agriculture or sports facilities. These don't fit well within standard STP or ETP frameworks. Most available technology is either too large-scale, too capital-intensive, or too dependent on chemicals to be practical at this scale.
The third issue is the state of urban lakes, ponds, and drains. Untreated inflow and poor circulation lead to stagnation, algal blooms, and declining oxygen levels. Common remedies like dredging or chemical treatment are expensive, disruptive, and often only provide temporary relief before the problem resurfaces.
column37:
Our innovation is built entirely around nanobubble technology, and how it treats water and waste. Nanobubbles are gas bubbles smaller than 100 nanometers, far tinier than the bubbles used in standard aeration or flotation systems. Their small size and negative surface charge give them exceptional stability, allowing them to remain suspended in water for hours or even days, rather than rising and bursting within seconds like conventional bubbles.
This stability translates directly into performance. Because nanobubbles have a much higher surface area relative to their volume, they transfer gas into water far more efficiently than coarse bubbles, significantly increasing dissolved oxygen levels without a proportional rise in energy use. Higher dissolved oxygen accelerates the biological breakdown of organic matter, which drives down BOD and COD more effectively than conventional aeration.
Nanobubbles also generate reactive oxygen species, such as hydroxyl radicals, when they collapse. These radicals oxidize organic pollutants and inactivate a broad range of bacteria and viruses, enabling disinfection without added chemicals. This same mechanism supports odor control and helps suppress algal blooms in stagnant waterbodies.
In practice, the technology functions as a retrofit layer: it enhances gas transfer, oxidation, and disinfection within existing treatment infrastructure, rather than requiring new civil construction. This is what allows the same underlying nanobubble platform to be adapted across different treatment contexts, from wastewater to waterway remediation, without redesigning the core system each time.
column38:
India generates roughly 72,368 MLD of urban sewage daily, but only about 28 is treated, and even installed treatment capacity is overpowered by heavy flow due to weak sewer networks, poor operation and maintenance. Conventional aeration, the core process in most treatment plants, transfers gas inefficiently, which limits pollutant removal and forces heavier reliance on chemical dosing to meet discharge norms. use.
The alternatives available today do not fully address this gap. Mechanical and diffused aeration remain the industry standard but achieve low oxygen transfer efficiency, often below 5, and consume significant energy. Chemical disinfection methods, such as chlorination, are inexpensive but generate residues and are less effective against certain pathogens and organic pollutants. Advanced oxidation processes break down complex pollutants effectively but are costly and complex to operate at scale. Reverse osmosis and UV systems improve effluent quality but carry high energy costs and, for RO, produce concentrated reject streams requiring separate disposal. 
Nanobubble-based aeration is an emerging alternative that has demonstrated gas transfer efficiency above 8590, compared to roughly 35 for conventional aeration, while also enabling chemical-free disinfection through the generation of reactive oxygen species. It functions by intensifying existing processes rather than replacing infrastructure, but adoption in India remains limited relative to its demonstrated performance elsewhere.

Our business model combines equipment sales with recurring service revenue, structured to serve both institutional and government clients.
The primary revenue stream comes from direct sales of nanobubble generators, ranging from smaller submersible units to industrial-scale systems designed for high-volume treatment. Pricing is tiered by capacity and application, allowing us to serve decentralized users as well as large municipal or industrial buyers from a single product platform.
The second stream is after-sales servicing and maintenance contracts, which provide recurring revenue beyond the initial equipment sale and ensure long-term system performance for clients who require continuous water quality management.
The third stream is turnkey project contracts for waterbody rejuvenation and treatment deployments, where we manage design, installation, and commissioning end-to-end. These projects typically involve higher contract values and longer engagement periods, often with municipal bodies or large institutional clients.
To access the public sector specifically, we develop project proposals aligned with government schemes such as Jal Jeevan Mission, Swachh Bharat Abhiyan, and Namami Gange, AMRUT 2.0 positioning our technology for municipal procurement and grant-supported pilot programs. This channel also builds credibility that supports enterprise and institutional sales.
Going forward, we are exploring a Nanobubbles-as-a-Service model, where clients pay based on usage or treatment outcomes rather than upfront equipment cost, lowering the barrier to adoption for smaller municipal and industrial users. Grant support through this program would help expand manufacturing capacity and accelerate deployment of this model across additional sites.

Capital cost acceptance: Nanobubble generators involve higher upfront capital investment than conventional aerators, which can make procurement decisions slower, particularly with municipal bodies operating under tight budgets. Overcoming this requires demonstrating lifecycle cost savings clearly through pilot data and phased deployment.
Regulatory and procurement cycles: Government and municipal projects often involve long approval timelines and multi-stage tendering processes. This creates unpredictable sales cycles and can delay revenue realization even after a successful pilot.
Awareness and adoption gap: Nanobubble technology remains less familiar to Indian municipal and industrial buyers compared to conventional treatment methods, requiring sustained education and demonstration efforts to shift procurement preferences toward a still-emerging technology category.

Sewage Treatment Plant for Non-Potable Water Reuse
This project involves setting up a Sewage Treatment Plant (STP) that converts wastewater into non-potable, reuse-grade water. Untreated or partially treated sewage creates problem in urban India, contributing to declining water quality, strain on freshwater supplies, and pollution of drains and waterbodies. This project addresses that gap directly by treating wastewater to a standard suitable for reuse in applications like garden and landscape irrigation, toilet flushing, floor washing, and general municipal cleaning, reducing dependence on freshwater for these non-drinking needs.

The treatment train is built around our nanobubble generators, which handle primary and secondary-stage aeration far more efficiently than conventional aeration systems, improving oxygen transfer and accelerating the biological breakdown of organic matter . This is supported by targeted probiotic dosing to further reduce sludge load, and manual skimming to remove floating debris. Following biological treatment, the water passes through a tertiary filtration and disinfection stage, using nanobubble-based ozone disinfection to bring down pathogen levels without heavy reliance on chemical treatment.

Since the intended output is non-potable reuse water rather than drinking water, the plant is designed to meet reuse-grade standards, such as BOD below 10 mg/L, COD below 50 mg/L, and near-complete removal of faecal coliforms, rather than the significantly stricter thresholds required for potable water. This makes the plant considerably more affordable to build and operate than a drinking-water-grade facility, while still fully complying with CPCB norms, which now mandate reuse of STP-treated water for flushing, irrigation, and similar non-potable applications. This approach directly supports our modular wastewater treatment and reuse focus area, converting a waste stream into a locally usable resource instead of letting it degrade the surrounding environment untreated.

For a treatment plant of 25 KLD. We need a budget of INR 55 lacs

The key risk is whether we can build sufficiently predictable, repeatable economics while scaling capital-intensive city and industrial deployments. 

Our plants need three conditions to work together: reliable waste supply, committed offtake for recycled composite products, and timely project payments. In practice, municipal procurement cycles are long, approval and commissioning timelines can shift, and government-payment delays can create working-capital pressure. On the market side, developers and contractors remain accustomed to conventional cement and concrete, so even technically validated recycled products can take longer to secure repeat orders and standard-specification acceptance. 

This risk is amplified by the shift from selling products to executing turnkey plants, PPPs, and licensed facilities. These models create greater long-term value, but require upfront capex, strong project management, quality control, and patient capital. Inconsistent mixed-waste feedstock is an additional operational risk because variable input quality can affect plant utilisation and product consistency. 

We are reducing this risk through long-term municipal concessions, industrial waste partnerships, modular plant design, product testing and certification, diversified revenue streams, and a mix of COCO and FOFO deployment. However, our success depends on turning early pilots into repeatable multi-year contracts, not simply accumulating demonstrations.

Public urinals across Indian cities generate large volumes of urine-rich wastewater that is typically flushed untreated into sewers or open drains, contributing to nitrogen and phosphorus pollution, groundwater contamination, and eutrophication of local water bodies. Centralized sewage treatment plants are poorly suited to this waste stream  dilution with mixed sewage destroys the nutrient concentration that makes urine valuable for recovery, and conveying it to distant treatment plants adds infrastructure cost with no resource benefit.

EnvironHeal addresses this gap through our MFC Brick Technology  a modular, wall-integrated bioelectrochemical reactor system that treats urine at the point of generation, directly at public urinals. The system uses gravity-driven flow (no pumps or external energy input) to pass urine through a stack of microbial fuel cell units, where electroactive bacteria break down organic and nitrogenous compounds.

This decentralized approach solves three problems simultaneously: it prevents nutrient-rich, pathogen-bearing waste from reaching drains and water bodies untreated it recovers clean, reusable water on-site (for flushing, gardening, or non-potable reuse) and it captures the embedded value in urine  nitrogen and phosphorus  as usable fertilizer, rather than letting it become a pollutant. The technology has been validated with support from the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs under the India Water Pitch pilot-scale startup challenge (AMRUT 2.0), which is helping us move from lab validation to real-world pilot deployment at public sanitation infrastructure.
column37:
Technology is central to EnvironHeal's value proposition. Our MFC Brick Technology combines microbial electrochemical treatment with a modular, brick-format architecture that can be physically integrated into the walls of public urinal/toilet blocks  turning existing sanitation infrastructure into a treatment and resource-recovery system without requiring separate land or civil works.

Electroactive microorganisms colonize the anode, oxidizing organic and nitrogenous compounds in urine while generating electrons that are captured through an external circuit as usable electricity.

The gravity-driven, modular design means units can be scaled up or down by adding or removing brick modules according to urinal usage volume, without pumps, aeration, or grid power  making the system viable even in low-infrastructure public sanitation settings. Our ongoing technical work focuses on improving treatment rate, electrode durability, and nutrient-recovery efficiency, and on standardizing the module for manufacturability at scale.

In short, the technology converts what is normally a purely disposal-oriented process (urine going to drain/sewer) into a distributed platform that simultaneously treats waste, generates electricity, and recovers water and fertilizer  with government-backed pilot validation already underway through AMRUT 2.0
column38:
The need is for a low-cost, energy-independent way to treat urine and prevent it from becoming a pollution source at public urinals  a category of infrastructure that is widespread but almost never connected to functional treatment. India has millions of public urinals, most discharging directly into open drains or unlined pits.

Available alternatives include: connecting urinals to centralized sewage treatment plants (expensive, requires sewer network coverage that's often unavailable, and destroys nutrient value through dilution) septic tanks and soak pits (inadequate treatment, groundwater contamination risk, require periodic desludging) and source-separation urine-diversion systems, which are gaining research interest but typically require external energy or chemical dosing (e.g., struvite precipitation) to recover nutrients, adding operating cost and complexity.

EnvironHeal's MFC Brick Technology differs by being self-powered (net energy-positive rather than energy-consuming), modular enough to retrofit into existing urinal structures rather than requiring new civil infrastructure, and designed to recover three outputs  water, electricity, and fertilizer  from a single passive, gravity-driven process. This makes it viable in exactly the settings where conventional alternatives fail: decentralized, low-infrastructure, high-footfall public sanitation sites where connecting to centralized treatment is impractical.

column43:
A key technical risk is variability in urine composition and dilution across sites (mixed with flush water, cleaning agents, or ambient moisture), which affects treatment consistency and resource-recovery yield. We are addressing this through pilot deployments across multiple site types to characterize real-world variability rather than relying solely on lab-scale, standardized urine.

A second risk is long-term electrode durability under continuous public-use conditions  fouling, mineral scaling (struvite formation), and mechanical wear can degrade performance over time. Our ongoing R&D is focused on electrode material stability and periodic-maintenance protocols to manage this.

On the market side, public sanitation infrastructure procurement is typically slow-moving and government-dependent, with municipal budget cycles and approval processes that can delay adoption. There is also limited existing awareness of decentralized urine treatment as a category, requiring investment in stakeholder education and demonstration.

Fertilizer off-take is an emerging risk: recovered nitrogen/phosphorus products need clear regulatory pathways and buyer channels (agricultural or horticultural use) that are still developing in India for recovered/recycled fertilizers.

Finally, as a pre-revenue company, we face funding and cash-flow risk during the transition from grant-funded pilots (such as our AMRUT 2.0 support) to paid commercial deployments.

We are mitigating these through phased pilot validation, government and institutional partnerships, modular design that allows incremental scale-up, and active engagement with municipal bodies to build a procurement pipeline ahead of full commercialization.

Project Description

Environ_Heal is scaling MFC Brick Technology, a modular, wall-integrated bioelectrochemical reactor system designed to treat urine from public urinals at the point of generation, rather than routing it through conventional sewer or septic infrastructure. The system is built around a stack of microbial fuel cell (MFC) modules in a compact, brick-like form factor that can be physically embedded into the wall structure of a urinal block. Flow through the system is entirely gravity-driven — no pumps, aeration blowers, or external electrical input are required — making it viable in low-infrastructure public sanitation settings where reliable power or plumbing upgrades cannot be assumed.

Inside each module, electroactive microorganisms colonize the anode and oxidize organic and nitrogenous compounds in urine, releasing electrons that are captured as usable electricity while simultaneously reducing organic load and pathogen content. The treated effluent is suitable for non-potable reuse after polishing, and the nitrogen- and phosphorus-rich residual fraction can be recovered as fertilizer — turning a waste stream into three distinct recoverable resources: water, electricity, and fertilizer.

This technology is backed by a portfolio of three patents. Two are already granted: "Flexible Electrode for Microbial Fuel Cell" (Indian Patent No. 473839, granted, published 21 January 2022), covering the high-performance flexible electrode material (conducting polymer- and nanomaterial-coated substrates) at the heart of the system; and "Multi-Anode Assembly Microbial Fuel Cell" (Indian Application No. 202211022174, granted, patent number pending issuance, published 29 August 2022), covering the multi-anode architecture that enables modular scaling of treatment capacity. A third, newly filed application — "Modular Wall-Integrated Bioelectrochemical Reactor System for Gravity-Driven Wastewater Treatment and Energy Generation" (Indian Application No. 202611085151) — covers the wall-integrated system architecture itself. Together, these three patents protect the technology at the material, component, and system level, giving Environ_Heal a defensible, multi-layered IP position rather than a single point of protection.

Our first real-world validation step was a pilot supported by a ?20 lakh grant from the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, awarded under the India Water Pitch pilot-scale startup challenge as part of the AMRUT 2.0 program. That grant funded fabrication of a 600-litre-capacity reactor and validated the core treatment mechanism and modular construction approach outside the lab. Having established this technical and IP foundation, Environ_Heal is now seeking to move from single-unit validation to a small, real-world deployment cluster in Mumbai, generating the operational performance data, durability evidence, and municipal relationships needed to build a repeatable, scalable deployment model for Indian cities more broadly.

Geography

The proposed scaling opportunity is centered on Mumbai, Maharashtra. Mumbai has an extremely high density of public urinals relative to most Indian cities, driven by population density and heavy reliance on public transit and street-level commercial activity, meaning individual sites see high daily footfall — maximizing both the volume of urine available for treatment and the pace at which we can gather meaningful performance data. Its coastal geography also means untreated nutrient-rich discharge has a direct pathway to marine and estuarine ecosystems, strengthening the environmental case for source-level treatment. As India's largest municipal economy, a successful demonstration in Mumbai — ideally in partnership with the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) or another relevant urban local body — carries outsized credibility for subsequent expansion into other Maharashtra cities and beyond.

Timelines

We propose a 12-month program:

Months 1–3: Engagement with Mumbai-based urban local bodies to identify suitable public urinal sites based on footfall, structural feasibility, and willingness to participate. In parallel, fabrication of additional reactor units, applying learnings from the AMRUT 2.0 pilot to refine module design for faster, more consistent assembly.

Months 4–6: Installation and commissioning of units at selected Mumbai sites, with baseline monitoring protocols established from day one — influent/effluent water quality, electricity output, and flow rates.

Months 7–9: Continuous operation across real-world conditions, including Mumbai's monsoon season, which will stress-test the gravity-driven design under high ambient moisture. Iterative troubleshooting of any fouling, wear, or performance drift, alongside initial outreach to potential offtake partners for the recovered fertilizer output.

Months 10–12: Consolidation of operational data into a standardized performance and deployment package, underpinning formal discussions with Mumbai ULB partners about expanded deployment and serving as the evidence base for follow-on funding conversations.

Funding amount required

We are requesting a grant of ?25 lakh. Having already validated the core technology through a ?20 lakh AMRUT 2.0-funded pilot and secured a three-patent IP position, this tranche is calibrated for real-world municipal deployment rather than further lab-stage R&D: fabrication and installation of additional reactor units in Mumbai, the instrumentation and monitoring needed to generate credible performance data, ULB stakeholder engagement, and initial groundwork toward the certifications municipal procurement will eventually require. This is a bridge tranche, sized to take us from a single validated pilot unit to a small but real operating cluster — the evidence base needed to unlock larger, non-grant funding in the next phase.

Partnerships associated

Government: Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, through the India Water Pitch pilot-scale startup challenge under AMRUT 2.0, which funded our first pilot.

Urban Local Body: No formal partnership yet; securing one with the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) or another Mumbai-area municipal/transit authority is an explicit goal of this 12-month program.

Corporate: None currently established; open to corporate CSR partnerships (water, sanitation, or urban sustainability focus) as co-funders or hosts for installations, and would welcome introductions from Villgro.

Expected impact description

The immediate impact is environmental: preventing nutrient-rich, pathogen-bearing urine from Mumbai's public urinals from reaching drains and coastal waters untreated, while recovering water, electricity, and fertilizer at the source — at exactly the dispersed, low-infrastructure sites where centralized treatment will never be practical. Beyond individual sites, the strategic impact is the operational evidence and municipal relationships this deployment generates: proof, under real conditions of weather, footfall, and maintenance demand, that a patent-protected, three-layer-defensible technology can move from validated pilot to procurable municipal product. This evidence base, and the ULB engagement model built alongside it, will directly inform expansion across Mumbai, into other Maharashtra cities, and eventually other Indian urban centers facing similar decentralized sanitation and wastewater challenges.

Buffindia addresses the largely unmanaged problem of cigarette waste, particularly discarded cigarette butts, which are generated in large quantities across urban commercial and public environments but are rarely handled through a dedicated waste-management system.
Cigarette waste is difficult to manage through conventional waste streams because cigarette filters contain cellulose acetate and retained tobacco and chemical residues. Discarded butts are commonly mixed with general waste or littered, creating environmental pollution and making responsible recovery difficult.
Our innovation addresses this gap by creating a specialized end-to-end cigarette waste management system covering dedicated disposal infrastructure, collection, transportation, recycling and resource recovery. Buffindia enables businesses to segregate cigarette waste at source and ensures that collected material is processed through a dedicated circular pathway rather than entering conventional waste streams.
The recovered material is further utilized to create sustainable products, while organizations receive measurable impact and ESG reporting. Through this model, Buffindia converts a difficult, overlooked waste stream into a managed resource while creating opportunities for circular manufacturing and green livelihoods.
column37:
Technology enables Buffindia to make cigarette waste management measurable, traceable and scalable. Our technology supports the operational layer of the ecosystem by connecting customer data, disposal infrastructure, collection activities, recycling records and environmental impact reporting.
Buffindia is developing a customer platform that enables organizations to access their service information, ESG impact data, reports and product-claim information through a centralized digital interface. This creates transparency between the physical waste-management process and the measurable impact delivered to each customer.
Technology also helps us standardize operations across multiple cities by maintaining structured customer and collection data, enabling better monitoring, reporting and decision-making. As the network expands, this digital layer will help Buffindia manage a distributed operational network more efficiently while building a growing database of cigarette waste collection and recovery.
The technology is therefore not a standalone product it is an enabling layer that strengthens Buffindia's specialized waste-management infrastructure, improves operational efficiency and creates the data foundation required to scale cigarette waste circularity across India.
column38:
The key need addressed by Buffindia is the absence of a dedicated, scalable system for managing cigarette waste. Businesses that have smoking areas often rely on housekeeping teams, general waste contractors, conventional bins or standalone ashtrays, which do not provide specialized segregation, collection, recycling or measurable environmental impact.
The available alternatives are primarily conventional disposal methods: cigarette waste is mixed with general waste, discarded in regular bins, handled manually by facility teams, or collected by general waste-management providers. These approaches focus on disposal rather than recovery and typically do not provide dedicated traceability or impact reporting for cigarette waste.
Buffindia provides a specialized alternative by combining dedicated cigarette-waste disposal infrastructure, scheduled collection, recycling and resource recovery into one managed service. The model enables organizations to segregate cigarette waste at source and divert it into a dedicated circular pathway, while providing measurable ESG impact reporting.
This addresses both the environmental need for responsible cigarette-waste management and the operational need for organizations to manage this specialized waste stream efficiently.

column42:
Buffindia operates a B2B subscription-based cigarette waste management model. We provide organizations with dedicated cigarette-waste disposal infrastructure, scheduled collection, transportation, recycling and ESG impact reporting. Customers pay an annual service fee based on their requirements, including the number of smoking areas, disposal units and collection frequency.
Our current customers include corporates, hotels, commercial establishments and hospitality businesses. The recurring subscription model creates predictable revenue while allowing us to build long-term customer relationships.
The recovered cigarette waste is processed through our circular economy system and converted into sustainable products under our KraftReborn initiative. These products are currently used primarily for customer engagement and retention, with future potential for commercial sales.
As the network expands, Buffindia is also developing additional revenue opportunities through a retail and hospitality advertising network across pan vendors, bars, cafs, restaurants and other smoking-point businesses. This will create a complementary recurring advertising revenue stream while expanding the reach of our cigarette-waste infrastructure.
Our model therefore combines recurring waste-management revenue with future advertising opportunities, supported by recycling, circular resource recovery and technology-enabled impact measurement.

Project Description
Buffindia proposes to establish a city-scale cigarette-waste management and circularity network through the deployment of 300 dedicated cigarette-waste disposal kiosks across selected high-footfall locations. The project will demonstrate a scalable model for managing cigarette waste at source and creating a dedicated pathway from disposal and collection to recycling, resource recovery and measurable environmental impact.
Cigarette waste is a highly overlooked waste stream. Conventional waste-management systems generally do not provide dedicated infrastructure for its segregation and recovery, resulting in cigarette butts being mixed with general waste or littered in public and commercial environments.
Buffindia's proposed intervention will create dedicated infrastructure that allows cigarette waste to be segregated at source. The collected waste will then be transported through a structured collection network to recycling and resource-recovery operations. Recovered material can subsequently be utilized in circular products through Buffindia's KraftReborn initiative.
The project will also create a measurable data layer covering locations deployed, waste collected, waste processed and recycled, and environmental impact generated. This will enable participating organizations and stakeholders to understand the measurable outcomes of the intervention.
The project is designed not only to deploy infrastructure but to establish a replicable city-level model for specialized cigarette-waste management that can subsequently be expanded to other cities across India.
Geography
The initial project will be implemented in one selected city in Maharashtra, with the final city and deployment locations to be identified in consultation with the relevant Urban Local Body (ULB), government stakeholders and participating corporate or commercial partners.
The proposed network will cover approximately 300 locations, prioritizing high-footfall areas and locations where cigarette consumption is significant, such as commercial establishments, hospitality venues, corporate premises and other suitable smoking-point locations.
Buffindia already has experience operating its cigarette-waste management model across multiple Indian cities. This project will use that operational experience to establish a structured city-level model in Maharashtra and create a framework that can subsequently be replicated across additional cities.
Timelines
The proposed implementation timeline is approximately 12–18 months.
Phase 1 – Partner Identification & Project Planning (Months 1–2)
Buffindia will identify and engage with the relevant ULB, government stakeholders, corporate partners and participating locations. Baseline data will be established and deployment locations finalized.
Phase 2 – Infrastructure Deployment (Months 2–6)
Approximately 300 cigarette-waste disposal kiosks will be deployed at selected locations. The deployment will include installation, commissioning, stakeholder orientation and establishment of collection schedules.
Phase 3 – Collection & Recycling Operations (Months 3–12)
Regular collection of cigarette waste will begin as kiosks are commissioned. Collected waste will be transported through Buffindia's operational network for processing, recycling and resource recovery.
Phase 4 – Impact Measurement & Reporting (Throughout the Project)
Buffindia will measure waste collected, quantities processed and recycled, locations covered, environmental impact and circular products generated. Participating stakeholders will receive structured impact reporting.
Phase 5 – Evaluation & Replication (Months 12–18)
The project outcomes will be evaluated against predefined environmental, operational and social indicators. The resulting city-level model will be documented for replication across other cities and ULBs.
Funding Amount Required
Buffindia is seeking ?1.20 crore in project funding.
The proposed infrastructure requirement is based on:
300 cigarette-waste kiosks × ?40,000 per kiosk = ?1,20,00,000 (?1.20 crore).
The funding will enable deployment of the 300-kiosk city-scale network and establish the infrastructure required to demonstrate the model at meaningful scale.
Partnerships
The project is designed as a collaborative model involving multiple stakeholders.
Buffindia will provide its existing expertise in cigarette-waste management, disposal infrastructure, collection operations, recycling, circular resource recovery and impact measurement.
The project will seek collaboration with the relevant Urban Local Body and government stakeholders for suitable deployment locations, local coordination, awareness and integration with the city's broader waste-management ecosystem.
Buffindia will also engage corporates, hotels, hospitality establishments, commercial properties and other suitable organizations to participate as deployment locations and help establish cigarette-waste segregation at source.
Where appropriate, facility-management and collection partners can support on-ground operations, while recycling and circular-product partners can contribute to resource recovery and downstream utilization.
At the time of application, Buffindia has not yet conducted a formal Maharashtra ULB pilot, and therefore no existing ULB partnership is being represented as confirmed. The proposed project is intended to establish such collaboration and demonstrate the model in partnership with the relevant stakeholders.
Expected Environmental Impact
The primary environmental objective is to create a dedicated pathway for cigarette waste that prevents it from being mixed with conventional waste streams or littered into the environment.
The project will create 300 dedicated cigarette-waste collection points, enabling source-level segregation across the selected city. The quantity of cigarette waste collected, processed and recycled will be measured throughout the project.
Environmental impact indicators will include:
Number of kiosks deployed
Number of locations covered
Quantity of cigarette waste collected
Quantity of waste processed and recycled
Quantity of material recovered
Circular products created from recovered material
Number of participating organizations and locations
Environmental impact generated and reported
Expected Social Impact
The project will also contribute to green livelihood creation through collection, processing, recycling and circular-product manufacturing activities. As the network scales, it can create additional opportunities for people involved in the circular value chain, including women artisans engaged in sustainable product manufacturing.
The project will also increase awareness among participating organizations, employees, visitors and communities regarding responsible cigarette-waste disposal and source segregation.
Expected Long-Term Impact
The ultimate objective is to use the Maharashtra deployment as a city-scale demonstration and replication model for cigarette-waste infrastructure across India.
A successful implementation will demonstrate that a difficult and overlooked waste stream can be managed through dedicated infrastructure, structured collection, recycling, resource recovery, impact measurement and circular manufacturing.
Buffindia aims to use the project to establish a replicable framework that can be adopted by additional ULBs, corporates and commercial ecosystems across India, creating a nationwide cigarette-waste infrastructure network and generating measurable environmental and social impact at scale.

Construction & Demolition (C&D) waste is one of the most difficult urban waste streams for ULBs to govern because generation is dispersed across thousands of construction sites, while collection, transportation, processing and disposal involve multiple independent stakeholders. Large volumes remain untracked or are illegally dumped, contributing to road dust, air pollution, flooding, land degradation and loss of recoverable construction materials.
While regulations place increasing responsibility on ULBs to monitor C&D waste, most cities still rely on fragmented, manual processes, spreadsheets, permits and point solutions. This limits visibility into how much waste is generated, where it moves, whether it reaches an authorized facility, and how much is actually recycled.
Trace Resource addresses this municipal operational gap through a specialized digital system that enables ULBs to monitor the complete C&D waste lifecycle, improve compliance, identify leakages and build a data-driven circular waste management system.
The solution is envisaged go beyond operational management build a holistic ecosystem entailing mobile application(ease of use & wider adoption), integration to the ICCC of City Police/Traffic systems (curb illegal transportation and dumping), Custom interface for allied major Infra project entities like Metro/ UDA (catering larger projects where even regulations are not firm), air pollution monitoring systems (cause & effect monitoring), environmental protocols audit module, etc.  Thus creating a global-first all-rounded platform catering the hard to abate Built environment form urban governance perpsective.
column37:
Technology is the core enabler of Trace Resource. We convert a fragmented, largely offline C&D waste ecosystem into a digitally traceable, multi-stakeholder network connecting ULBs, waste generators, transporters, recyclers and material buyers.
The platform digitizes workflows such as project registration, waste estimation, waste management plans, approvals, collection requests, transportation and final channelization. GIS, GPS/vehicle tracking, digital transaction records, dashboards and analytics provide visibility into waste movement and enable ULBs to identify exceptions and monitor compliance.
The architecture is modular and configurable, allowing the same core platform to be adapted to different municipal workflows and regulatory requirements without rebuilding the system for every city. API-based integrations can connect with existing municipal systems and construction-permit databases.
Technology also extends beyond waste tracking: our integrated marketplace connects recycled C&D materials with potential buyers, enabling the transition from waste management to material circularity.
Thus, technology is not merely digitizing paperwork it creates the operational intelligence and traceability layer required for a ULB to manage C&D waste as a measurable city-level system.
The next phase of development will enhance the techonology quotient by introducing dedicated mobile application, advanced AI features, and external system integrations for holistic monitoring and governance.
column38:
The primary need is for ULBs to have a single, reliable digital system through which they can operationally manage and monitor C&D waste rather than relying on fragmented records and manual enforcement.
The need is not simply another waste-management application, but a dedicated digital operating layer for a material stream that is large, decentralized, increasingly regulated, and high on pollution and GHG emissions. 
For ULBs, this can improve operational efficiency and evidence-based monitoring for developers and contractors, it simplifies compliance and for recyclers, it improves visibility of material flows and potential demand.
With additional modules, the innovation goes beyond waste governance from municipal viewpoint, but addresses urban region wide strategic governance and oversight entailing diverse insitutional establishments

Following deployment, the platform's ongoing operational and maintenance costs can be recovered through user charges already collected by the ULB from relevant C&D waste generators, transporters, developers and other ecosystem participants. This approach keeps the recurring financial burden on the ULB minimal while creating a sustainable mechanism for continued platform operation, support and improvement.
The model therefore combines one-time deployment support with a recurring, user-charge-backed operating model. Once the initial design and customization are completed, the core technology can be replicated across cities with limited additional development effort, while city-specific workflows and integrations can be configured as required.

Municipal adoption/procurement: ULB decision-making and procurement can have long cycles. We mitigate this by demonstrating working deployments, engaging multiple ULBs
simultaneously and designing the platform to accommodate existing municipal workflows rather than requiring complete process replacement.
Stakeholder adoption: Generators, transporters and recyclers may initially resist digital processes. Assisted onboarding, simple workflows, training and phased implementation are therefore
built into deployments.
Integration and data quality: Municipal systems and data formats vary across cities. Our configurable architecture and API-based approach reduce dependence on a single technology
environment, while validation and reconciliation mechanisms improve data integrity.

Revenue timing/working capital: Government contracts can have longer payment cycles. We are diversifying through B2B subscriptions and marketplace revenues while maintaining a lean
operating model.
Market development: C&D digital governance is an emerging category. However, increasing regulatory requirements and demonstrated ULB demand provide a strong structural driver for
adoption.

Dostbin Solutions addresses critical urban waste management challenges by providing compact, source-level processing systems specifically designed for organic wet waste in residential and commercial spaces.

Key problems resolved include:

High Logistics Costs & Landfill Burden: Traditional waste models depend on municipal daily collection and long-distance transport, generating high carbon emissions. On-site compact units eliminate transport dependency and significantly divert organic mass away from overflowing landfills.

Environmental & Health Risks: When food waste decomposes anaerobically in open dumps, it produces potent methane gas and toxic leachate that contaminates groundwater. Dostbins aerobic processing prevents anaerobic breakdown, mitigating greenhouse gas emissions and chemical run-off.

Urban Space & Odor Constraints: Urban apartments and commercial kitchens lack space for traditional outdoor compost pits. Dostbins small footprint fits into utility areas and balconies while utilizing sealed designs, controlled aeration, and pest-proof housing to prevent foul odors and flies.

Labor-Intensive Composting: Traditional composting requires tedious manual mixing. Dostbin simplifies the process through integrated shredding, optimized mixing mechanisms, and user-friendly automated or manual options that require minimal effort.

Resource Waste: Rather than treating food scraps as expensive waste, the compact processing converts daily organic refuse into nutrient-rich compost and liquid fertilizer directly at the source.
column37:
Role of Technology in Dostbin Composters

Technology in Dostbin composters transforms conventional, labor-intensive composting into an automated, hygienic, and space-efficient process designed for urban environments.

Key technological elements include:

 Mechanical Engineering & Shredding: High-durability stainless steel blades crush incoming organic food scraps. This volume reduction maximizes surface area for microbial activity, significantly accelerating decomposition.
 Patented Multi-Chamber Separation: Designed with a two-stage batch system, the inner geometry keeps fresh daily waste strictly separated from older digesting material. This layout prevents cross-contamination and maintains a continuous, uninterrupted composting cycle.
 Automated Aeration & Processing: Microcontroller-driven Electronic Control Units (ECUs) govern motorized mixing rotors. By periodically cycling internal agitation, the system maintains consistent aerobic digestion, which completely eliminates foul odors, methane production, and pest breeding.
 Smart Leachate Collection: Built-in moisture routing channels automatically drain excess liquid into a separate collection reservoir. This keeps solid waste at optimal moisture levels while producing a ready-to-use liquid organic fertilizer.
 IoT & App Integration: Modern variants feature Wi-Fi/Bluetooth connectivity for real-time status monitoring, maintenance alerts, and seamless ordering of microbial starter mixes through a mobile application.
 Energy-Efficient Operation: Optimized low-power motor drivers consume minimal electricity (under 510 kWh per month), making automated home waste processing practical and economical.

By merging mechanical automation, electronic control, and optimized biotechnology, Dostbin turns everyday organic kitchen waste into nutrient-rich compost without the mess, smell, or manual effort.
column38:
Dostbin Solutions addresses critical urban challenges surrounding decentralized organic wet waste management:

 Logistical & Environmental Costs: Municipal reliance on long-distance wet waste transportation generates high carbon emissions and overloads landfills. On-site processing eliminates transit dependency.
 Pollution & Odors: Anaerobic decomposition in dumpsites releases methane gas and toxic groundwater leachate. Dostbins aerobic processing prevents methane, isolates leachate for liquid fertilizer, and uses sealed, aerated designs to eliminate odors and pests.
 Urban & Labor Friction: Urban homes lack space for traditional compost pits. Dostbin provides a compact footprint with integrated shredders and automated mixing, removing labor-intensive manual turning.

---

Available Alternatives

1. Traditional/Tumbler Bins (e.g., Daily Dump Kambha, Terracotta Stackers): Rely on natural aerobic breakdown or worms without electricity. Drawbacks: Requires manual turning, takes weeks, and risks odors if unbalanced.
2. Electric Countertop Dehydrators (e.g., Lomi, FoodCycler): Rapidly heat, dry, and crush food scraps in 424 hours. Drawbacks: High electricity consumption, small capacity, and produces dried biomass rather than fully cured compost.
3. Commercial Organic Waste Convertors (e.g., ECOMAN, Reddonatura): Large, heavy-duty machines for bulk waste processing in apartments or commercial sites. Drawbacks: High capital cost, large footprint, and substantial power usage.
4. Municipal Off-Site Collection: Reliance on city waste transport to centralized facilities. Drawbacks: High transportation emissions, frequent schedule disruptions, and risk of mixed-waste contamination.

Business Challenges & Risks for Dostbin Solutions

Dostbin Solutions faces operational, market, financial, and competitive risks inherent to hardware-driven green technologies:

 Inconsistent Waste Segregation & Consumer Habits: Decentralized processing depends entirely on households separating organic kitchen waste from recyclables. Unsegregated garbage causes mechanical jams in shredding blades and disrupts bacterial digestion.
 Perception of Garbage as a Free Service: Many consumers view waste management as a municipal responsibility rather than a private product investment, making upfront hardware adoption challenging in cost-sensitive segments.
 Fear of Odor and Pests: Misbalancing moisture or carbon-to-nitrogen ratios can cause foul smells or flies indoors, leading to customer dissatisfaction and negative word-of-mouth.
 Logistics & Regional Support Overhead: Shipping heavy, non-standard composter units incurs high surface freight costs. Providing timely on-site technician support for motorized rotors, sensors, and Electronic Control Units (ECUs) across multiple regions threatens profit margins.
 Consumable Dependency: The system relies on customers continuously repurchasing bio-culture starters and cocopeat. Interrupted supply chains or failure to replenish starters degrades bin performance.
 Competition & Municipal Shifts: Dostbin competes against low-tech terracotta stackers on one end and electric countertop dehydrators on the other. Subsidized municipal composting initiatives could also reduce individual household demand.
 Working Capital Intensity: Sourcing high-grade stainless steel blades, electronic controllers, and assembling units requires substantial upfront inventory financing.

SECTION 1: PROJECT DESCRIPTION
1.1 Executive Summary & Core Innovation
Dostbin Solutions Private Limited is submitting this application to Villgro’s TVARAN 3.0 – Maharashtra Tech Accelerator Project (T-MAP) to scale its proprietary, decentralized green technology hardware and circular waste management system.
Urban India faces a severe solid waste management crisis driven by rapid urbanization, inadequate landfill capacities, and inefficient centralized collection systems. Over 60% of municipal solid waste generated in Indian urban centers consists of biodegradable organic kitchen scraps. When this wet waste is mixed with dry recyclables and transported to open landfills, it undergoes anaerobic decomposition, releasing potent methane gases (CH4), creating hazardous toxic leachate that contaminates groundwater tables, and generating public health vectors such as flies, mosquitoes, and rodents.
Dostbin Solutions solves this systemic failure directly at the point of origin. We manufacture engineered, multi-chamber, zero-odor aerobic composting units that process organic food and kitchen waste right where it is generated. Our technology stack spans manual household units, semi-automatic residential complex systems, and fully automated, Internet-of-Things (IoT)-enabled commercial processing units.
By integrating multi-stage mechanical shredding, dynamic airflow aeration, and specialized microbial bio-culture starters, Dostbin units convert organic food waste into high-grade, nutrient-dense organic fertilizer within 10 to 15 days without foul odors, flies, or liquid leakage.
1.2 The Circular "Waste-to-Wealth" Business Model
Hardware deployment represents only the initial touchpoint of Dostbin’s comprehensive circular ecosystem. Our operational framework connects urban consumption directly with rural and suburban agricultural replenishment:
At-Source Capture: Wet waste is intercepted at the kitchen counter, residential building, or commercial kitchen before it enters the municipal collection stream.
On-Site Aerobic Processing: Waste is shredded and aerated within Dostbin units, eliminating methane generation and preventing leachate formation.
Nutrient Recovery & Aggregation: The harvested organic compost and liquid bio-fertilizer are collected through an integrated buy-back network.
Agricultural Redistribution: Bulk organic fertilizer is tested, packaged, and distributed to Farmer Producer Organizations (FPOs), commercial agricultural networks, local plant nurseries, and urban gardeners, directly replacing synthetic chemical fertilizers and restoring depleted soil organic carbon.
