column36:
MRFs in India today run almost entirely on manual, bulk waste processing. Material comes in, gets sorted by hand into broad categories, and moves out, with no quality control, no traceability, and no digitization anywhere in the process. Sorting, weighing, quality checks, output logging: none of it is tracked in any structured way. Operators have no real time visibility into throughput, purity, or contamination levels, and no digital record of what actually happened to a given batch of material.

This creates two problems that feed into each other. First, operational blindness: operators can't diagnose inefficiencies or quality issues because there's no data to look at, so decisions end up being guesswork rather than evidence based. Second, compliance risk: brands and recyclers relying on these MRFs for their EPR obligations have no auditable proof of material quality or origin, which puts their own compliance on shaky ground even when the underlying work is being done.

At its core, this is a problem of an entire link in the recycling value chain operating with no data layer at all. Every downstream decision, whether it's a recycler judging material quality, a brand reporting EPR numbers, or an operator trying to improve their own facility, is being made without any reliable information about what's actually happening on the sorting floor. That gap is what our innovation is built to close.

At Wastefull Insights, we've built three products that work together. VisionBox is a camera and computer system that identifies waste types on the sorting line in real time. A robotic arm attached to it physically picks and separates the identified material, at 3,500 to 3,600 picks per hour. KUDA.AI is the dashboard that records everything sorted, so anyone can see what came through, in what quantity, and at what quality.

Today, MRFs in India process waste in bulk. Workers sort by hand, and once material leaves the facility there's no record of how it was sorted, how clean it is, or whether it meets any quality standard. It's a purely manual process with no digital trail, and manual pick rates can't match what a machine sustains hour after hour.

Our system solves this at scale directly. It's completely modular and retrofittable onto existing manual sorting lines, so a facility doesn't need to rebuild its plant to adopt it, keeping setup capex low. Once installed, the camera and robot run up to 16 hours a day at that pick rate, sorting continuously while logging every unit. The machine doesn't tire or make inconsistent calls the way people do, so quality stays consistent regardless of volume, and it simply outperforms a manual line.

On the economics, run at an average of 16 hours a day, a facility recovers the full cost of the unit within about 15 months, purely from labor savings and higher recovery rates.
column38:
The core need is getting real quality control and digital traceability into a part of the recycling and waste value chain that currently has neither. Ask an MRF operator how much of their output meets a given purity standard, and they can't tell you, because nobody's tracking it. If a brand or recycler wants proof of where material came from or how clean it is, that proof doesn't exist.

Our three products fill that gap together. VisionBox identifies the material, the robotic sorter handles the physical work, and KUDA.AI keeps the record. Facilities finally know what they're producing, and can prove it to whoever needs that proof, whether it's a buyer, recycler, or regulator further along the chain.

The current alternatives fall short in different ways. Manual labor is the norm, but can't guarantee consistency and generates no data. Air sorters are the best automated technology available today, but need clean, pre-sorted infeed, so facilities spend heavily on preprocessing just to use them, carry a high capex of their own, and even then only sort one material type at a time. Global robotic players like AMP Robotics or ZenRobotics are priced for large Western facilities with uniform waste, and come as standalone lines, not retrofits. EPR platforms like Recykal track transactions after material leaves the facility, never at the sorting stage itself.

Our model uses hardware as the way into a facility, and recurring revenue as the real engine after that.

We install VisionBox units and robotic sorters at MRFs, either sold outright or offered as leased equipment, so operators aren't forced into a large upfront cost just to get started. Once a system is running, we monetize it through a few ongoing streams: SaaS access to the KUDA.AI dashboard for tracking and reporting, AMC contracts for maintaining the hardware, RaaS or robotics as a service for facilities that prefer a pay-per-use or leased arrangement over ownership, and EPR data services, where we sell verified traceability data to brands and producers who need proof of compliance.

The hardware sale or lease gets the system into a facility and funds the initial deployment. From there, the SaaS, AMC, RaaS, and data services layers build a recurring revenue base that grows with us as we add more facilities. Over time, this shifts us from being a hardware company selling equipment to being more of a platform company, where the ongoing data and service relationship with each facility matters more than the one time hardware sale.

A few real risks we keep an eye on.

The biggest one is hardware reliability out in the field. MRFs are dusty, high vibration, high contamination environments, and mechanical parts take a beating there. We actually ran into this early on, which is part of why we brought in igus as a manufacturing partner, since their components handle those conditions better.

Sales cycles are another challenge. Most MRF operators in India are small to mid sized businesses with limited capital, so getting them to adopt hardware, even retrofittable hardware, takes time and often needs financing options like leasing rather than upfront purchase.

We also depend on outsourced manufacturing for a lot of the mechanical and electrical components, things like control panels and pneumatics, which come from external vendors. That creates some supply chain and quality control dependency that we have to manage closely.

On the policy side, a chunk of our future revenue, particularly the EPR data services piece, depends on how consistently EPR regulations get enforced in India. If enforcement stays patchy, that demand grows more slowly than we'd like.

There's also competitive risk. Global players like AMP Robotics, ZenRobotics, and Greyparrot are well funded and could eventually turn their attention to India, so we need to keep our cost and localization advantage sharp.

**Project Description**

The system combines VisionBox for real-time material identification, a robotic gantry sorter operating at 3,500–3,600 picks per hour, and KUDA.AI for traceability and quality data logging. It retrofits onto existing manual sorting lines, so facilities don't need to rebuild their plant to adopt it, keeping capex low.

Our scaling model runs on two parallel tracks. First, partnering with Urban Local Bodies and government-run MRF infrastructure under state solid waste management programs, where we deploy our sorting and traceability layer within facilities the ULB provides, and report back verified data on how much waste is actually diverted from landfill against their Swachh Bharat and SWM targets. Second, a leasing route for privately operated MRFs, run through a financing partner, so operators can adopt the system without the upfront capex barrier that has kept automation out of reach for smaller players.

**Geography and rollout approach (Maharashtra as the lead example)**

We anchor our Maharashtra rollout at Lucro Plastecycle's existing facility in Baramati, Pune district, an already-live client relationship with an operational conveyor-based sorting line. This becomes our state reference site.

From there, we expand in tight geographic clusters rather than scattering units across the state. The first cluster is the Pune–Baramati–Solapur MIDC belt, targeting 8–10 units concentrated in this corridor, using the anchor site as proof and expanding through the operator's own network and comparable nearby facilities. Once that cluster is stable, we replicate the model across Maharashtra's other established MIDC industrial and recycling belts: Nashik, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (Aurangabad), Nagpur, Kolhapur, and the Mumbai–Thane–Bhiwandi belt. Each becomes its own 8–10 unit cluster following the same site-selection criteria: an existing conveyor line, comparable processing volume (around 15 TPD per facility), and some baseline operational maturity to retrofit onto.

At roughly 10 units per cluster and 15 TPD per unit (about 150 TPD per cluster), 6–7 such clusters across Maharashtra bring us to approximately 900–1,050 TPD of processing capacity within the state alone, putting us at or above 1,000 TPD. Realistically, Pune–Baramati plus one or two additional clusters (Nashik, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar) are achievable in year one, with the remaining clusters following as the model and financing structure prove out.

The same cluster-based approach is applied in parallel across Gujarat, Telangana, and Karnataka.

Project Description

Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) across Maharashtra send large volumes of dry recyclable waste, particularly plastics, e waste and cloth, to landfills due to informal, unsegregated collection and limited links to organised processing. This increases landfill pressure and municipal transportation and disposal costs, while waste pickers continue to recover valuable recyclables from dumpsites.

SORT IT addresses this through decentralised Reduce, Reuse, Recycle (RRR) Centres, managed by trained women from Self Help Groups (SHGs). The centres intercept recyclable waste at source, segregate it and channel it to local users or recyclers for reuse and further processing.

The model integrates waste management with womens economic empowerment through three pillars:

 Livelihood Generation: Formalising women SHGs as specialised waste management service providers.

 Circularity and Traceability: Converting recyclables into valuable commodities while digitally tracking quantities and recycling outcomes.

 Landfill Diversion: Promoting decentralised collection and segregation to reduce recyclable waste sent to landfills and long haul transportation.

A digital intelligence layer will enable operational transparency, impact aggregation and institutional trust, creating a replicable model for ULBs.

Through our partner organisation, Kushaagra Innovations Foundation (KIF), four centres operate in Rajgurunagar, Alandi, Dehu and Saswad, with a fifth being initiated in Satara. The project proposes five additional centres in Thane, Vasai Virar, Khopoli, Umred, and Hinganghat, creating a 10-centre network. This scale will enable a revenue generating, self sustaining waste to wealth model.
column37:
Digital transparency acts as the trust layer that enables SORT IT to scale within the complex waste management value chain. For ULBs and companies meeting Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) obligations, verified data is essential for accountability and impact measurement.

The SORT IT central platform is designed as a Software as a Service (SaaS) solution with two revenue generating verticals:

A1: Certification and Placement: The platform trains and certifies individuals for employment in the waste sector, connects them with placement opportunities, and certifies waste management teams to improve operational efficiency. This creates a skilled workforce network mapped to RRR units.

A2: SaaS Management Tool: A comprehensive digital tool for RRR centres covering waste traceability, accounting, inventory, HR, receipt management and reporting. It provides ULBs with live, auditable data on waste diverted from landfills and enables SORT IT and SHG partners to monitor performance and improve operations.

Both verticals operate on a common technology platform, reducing development and operating costs while creating independent revenue streams.

Importantly, A2 generates verified data that can support access to EPR and carbon credit opportunities. Aggregated tonnage data across centres provides evidence of environmental impact, while A1s certification network strengthens market access for skilled labour and recycled products.
column38: Traditional municipal waste management is defined by economic leakage, where crores are spent annually on haulage rather than value recovery. SORTT IT offers decentralized alternative that prioritizes source recycling through the RRR centres. Specifically, it addresses five issues in the current system  high waste transportation cost, high dependency on landfills for waste, loss of valuable resources and income-generating opportunities, and significant carbon footprint. The SWM Rules 2026 advocate circularity in waste management, and the Swachh Sarvekshan and Garbage Free Cities frameworks have been promoting the setting up of RRR centres by ULBs. The reality is that ULBs have set up RRR centres mainly for scoring purposes, and barring a few examples, these are not designed as financially sustainable revenue models. SORTT IT has piloted its first four centres to build them into revenue-generating models that can attain self-sufficiency through scale. The market alternatives are informal waste systems such as scrap shops and a few dying traditional bartering systems where women collected old clothes for steel vessels. These informal systems exploit  wastepickers who sell mixed dry waste to scrap dealers with no quality control, price transparency, or safety net. SORTT IT's digital platform, which aggregates the decentralised RRR-centre model, fills this gap. The centres are closer to the source, run by trained women SHGs, and produce saleable, quality-checked material for recyclers. This directly meets the ULB's need to demonstrably divert waste from landfill and generates a stable, skilled, income-generating occupation.
column42: SORTT IT utilizes a hybrid social enterprise framework focused on long-term financial self-reliance. Following this project's restructuring, the model is organised into three distinct pillars, each with its own cost base and revenue stream:  A1  Certification & Placement (SaaS platform vertical): Revenue from certification and placement fees charged to individuals seeking waste-sector work, and to waste-management entities seeking to certify their own teams. This sits under the SaaS platform umbrella but is tracked as its own separate vertical from A2.  A2  SaaS Management Tool (SaaS platform vertical): Revenue from    (a) Membership & Training Fees  nominal registration fees from RRR units to ensure commitment and completion of onboarding, (b) O&M Module Service Fee  for professional management, financial recordkeeping, operational guidance and market linkages, and (c) Impact Credits  future monetisation of Carbon and EPR credits enabled by the platform's digital traceability.  A3  RRR Centre Operations: A fully separate cost-and-revenue unit, generating (a) Recycled Product Sales  revenue from processed and upcycled material sold to local buyers, recyclers or industrial users, and (b) Retail sale of reusable goods  repaired clothes, books and other goods sold directly at the centre. A1 and A2 share one development cost base  the SORTT IT portal  reflecting that both verticals run on the same underlying technology A3 carries its own capital and operating cost, with no cross-subsidy between the platform and the centres.
column43:
Based on our experience operating four RRR centres, the major challenges we have encountered are:
Turnover of women operating the RRR centres  Personal or financial reasons can pull women away before they accrue the benefits of higher income. Training at least 20 women per ULB builds a substitute pool and fosters healthy competition. 
Variation in recyclable waste quantities and quality  The size and socio-economic nature of the ULB determines the quality and quantity of recyclable waste from each town. Integration of several centres under one portal provides an opportunity to cross-subsidise across towns.
Market risk  Price fluctuations of recyclables if localised. We propose secure offtake agreements or MoUs with buyers and diversifying the buyer base across multiple ULBs. Scale and supporting data will help mitigate this risk.
Dependency on ULB for space  Administrative approvals for ULB-provided space take time. Once a centre becomes financially stable, it can independently rent space instead. 
Membership to the IT Portal  Centres that turn profitable quickly may be tempted to exit the platform. We will make continued portal membership a contractual condition in the founding MoU for each centre.

Quantitatively: Number of SHG women and wastepickers onboarded and trained, number with stable monthly income from RRR-centre work, average monthly earnings per member, and number of centres reaching operational milestones.

Qualitatively: SHG member feedback on income stability, confidence and social standing within the household and community improvements in group governance (attendance, participation in decision-making, meeting minutes/voting records) and ULB/community perception of SHGs as credible, formal waste-management partners rather than informal wastepickers.
column46:
The primary beneficiaries are women members of Self-Help Groups (SHGs) and independent waste pickers working in various ULBs in Maharashtra  largely women from low-income families who have been SHG members for a few years under the city's National Urban Livelihood Mission. They are currently engaged in informal or domestic work, or in income-generating activities such as tailoring, food service or beautician work, and are looking for opportunities offering increased income, flexibility and stable work. A structured, skilled role at an RRR centre offers a significant improvement in income stability, safety and social standing. Beneficiaries are onboarded through the SHG federation structure and awareness sessions on business opportunities, and trained progressively so that over time a core group of women can take on supervisory or entrepreneurial roles within each centre.

A secondary beneficiary group is the ULB itself, which gains a measurable reduction in landfill-bound waste and a formal, accountable partner for its recyclable dry-waste stream.

A third group is companies that must comply with EPR regulations the digital platform provides them a single, reliable data source to meet their requirements.
column47:
SORTT IT's pilot approach builds directly on Kushaagra Innovations Foundation's (KIF) prior work in this sector  a study on business models for integrating wastepickers and women SHGs into waste management across ULBs in Maharashtra, and a 2025 state-level SHG training programme implemented across 382 ULBs to build awareness of livelihood opportunities in waste.
Under KIF, RRR centres are running in Rajgurunagar, Dehu, Alandi and Saswad, where SHG women conduct surveys, IEC and handle the entire RRR centre together. These four centres have become operational within the last six months. Each centre has been collecting an average of 700 kg to 3,000 kg of material each month.
At each site, the pilot follows the same staged approach:
ULB shows interest and provides space to set up a RRR centre.
Women SHG members are identified and ready to operate the RRR centre.
Hands-on operator training for SHG women, including quality control and basic maintenance.
RRR centre is set up and inaugurated.
Awareness and IEC activities are conducted in identified neighbourhoods for recyclable waste collection.
Collection drives are conducted and schedules created.
Sale linkages are established for the material.
Site-level performance  waste collected, waste processed, output, and SHG livelihoods generated  is recorded in registers. Early learnings, particularly around feedstock quality and buyer-side price fluctuation, are captured in the register.
In addition to the RRR centres, KIF is also promoting other waste-to-value business models such as Flower waste to Agarbatti and Dry waste to pellets.

column50:
SORTT IT is seeking support to develop a SaaS digital platform for the coordination of training on Waste-to-Wealth models for interested participants across Maharashtra (and beyond), and to provide the operational, monitoring and aggregation support to the units established. The platform is structured as two revenue-bearing verticals sharing one technology backbone — A1 (Certification & Placement) and A2 (SaaS Management Tool) — alongside a third, physically separate pillar, A3 (RRR Centre Operations).
India's urban waste management sector faces a structural gap: while thousands of women's Self-Help Groups (SHGs) and informal waste workers possess the willingness and latent capacity to participate in waste-based livelihoods, there has historically been no standardised, trusted mechanism to train, certify, and connect them to real economic opportunity nor a systematic way for Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) to monitor, verify, and aggregate the environmental impact of the decentralised units that do exist. SORTT IT's platform is designed to close both gaps simultaneously. 
To provide the scale for a proof of concept, the project seeks support to establish five decentralised RRR (Reduce–Reuse–Recycle) centres (A3). The model currently spans four operational centres and one soon to be established, across Maharashtra, and is at the proof-of-concept stage.

Geography: 
The current footprint covers Rajgurunagar, Alandi, Dehu and Saswad in Maharashtra, with one more in the process of initiation at Satara. We propose to expand to five more ULBs — Thane, Vasai Virar and Khopoli in the Mumbai region, and Umred and Hinganghat in the Nagpur region. Scaling is planned within the state over the next three years. There are close to 400 ULBs in Maharashtra, and per Swachh Sarvekshan norms each is expected to establish an RRR centre in every ward — so the scope for expansion is substantial.

Timelines: 
The SORTT IT digital platform (A1 + A2) can be developed within the first four months of the project, with pilots and testing over the following three months before go-live in month 8. In parallel, the five new RRR centres (A3) will be set up within four months of the project (ULB MoUs, space, training of women, etc.) and made operational within the following three months, reaching full functionality by month 6 hence the six months of operational cost support proposed.
The slightly offset timelines centres reaching functionality by month 6, platform going live by month 8 are deliberate, allowing the newly established centres to generate real operational data that can be used to test and refine the A2 management tool as it nears launch.

Funding amount required: 
Funding is estimated for two areas, aligned to the three internal pillars:
The required funding totals 143.5 Lakhs across two main implementation areas aligned with the three internal pillars. A total of 70 Lakhs is allocated to the SORTT IT SaaS platform development and deployment (combining pillars A1 and A2), which covers portal development by a third-party vendor and a three-person program management team for one year—divided roughly equally between A1 and A2, with each maintaining its own distinct revenue line. The remaining 73.5 Lakhs covers the establishment and operation of 5 RRR centres under pillar A3 as a fully separate cost-and-revenue unit; this accounts for capital expenditures, six months of operational expenses, an eight-person program management team, and other programmatic costs. Additionally, there is a potential Year-2 viability-gap-funding requirement of ?20 Lakhs anticipated for ongoing platform operations.
Partnerships associated: 
SORTT IT operates the digital platform. Kushaagra Innovations Foundation, whose SAKSHAM programme provides the broader capacity-building, financial-guidance and knowledge-partner ecosystem, incubates and mentors SORTT IT's RRR centres. The centres will be established under KIF in collaboration with the host ULBs, with MoUs signed with each ULB. ULBs will also provide logistics support and are the primary counterpart for waste-sourcing surveys and collection-drive coordination.
Expected impact description: 
The one-year project is expected to deliver:
-A SaaS digital platform with two verticals (A1 Certification & Placement, A2 SaaS Management Tool) that registers participants and creates the foundation of verified, tonnage-linked impact data — positioning SORTT IT (and its ULB partners) to access future carbon-credit and EPR-linked revenue streams.
-Twenty women SHG members provided livelihood in structured, trained, income-generating roles at the five new RRR centres, in addition to those already engaged at existing centres.
-Approximately 300 MT of recyclable waste diverted annually from ULB landfills, contributing toward Maharashtra's circular-economy and waste-diversion goals.
Over three years:
-Creation of an integrated portal to provide training, support operations, and deliver aggregation benefits for over 300 units across the state — recycling close to 3,000 MT of recyclable waste.
-Creation of a replicable, self-financing unit-economics model for RRR centres, moving toward product-revenue-funded operations that can be handed over to ULBs and SHG federations for long-term ownership.
Other waste-related business models can also be integrated into the SaaS platform in future, providing wider scale and a broader base for the A1 certification and placement vertical.

Swastha 2.0 is an Intelligent Collaborative System that orchestrates material-to-energy flows using real-time, verifiable data. We integrate GPS across multiple OEM fleet systems to track vehicles in real time, and generate a unique QR code for every trip along with a digital trip sheet  validating routes taken and creating an auditable record at each handoff. Routes are managed dynamically and optimised via APIs to open-market routing models, allowing live rerouting based on traffic, load, and proximity to the next collection or drop-off point.

This layer of real-time coordination connects waste generators, logistics providers, MRFs, certified plastic recyclers, and energy recovery systems  closing the circularity loop end-to-end within a single platform, and replacing manual, siloed tracking with dynamic, verifiable orchestration.
column38:
Waste collectors, contractors, and recyclers currently lack digital systems for real-time visibility into their operations, and ULBs lack tools to hold waste generators or contractors accountable. This gap puts timely compliance with the SWM 2026 rules at risk.

Some waste-collecting organisations have built digital systems to monitor their own internal operations, but these are siloed  built for a single stakeholder's use and not designed for interoperability across generators, transporters, recyclers, and ULBs. As a result, no unified, cross-stakeholder accountability layer exists today. Swastha 2.0 fills this gap by connecting all parties on one platform, rather than digitising each in isolation.
column42:

Commission-based revenue  We charge fleet operators 4 of the order value for every trip we assign to them.
Pay-per-use  We charge waste collectors INR 40 per trip for generating trip sheets to meet compliance requirements.
Performance-based billing  We charge ULBs and waste contractors 30 of the OPEX savings achieved through migration to our system.( YET TO COMMERCIALISE)

column50:
Project Description
Swastha 2.0 is an Intelligent Collaborative System built to solve one of the most persistent gaps in India's waste management ecosystem: the absence of real-time, verifiable coordination between the many actors who together determine whether waste is properly collected, transported, processed, and recovered. Waste generators, collection contractors, logistics providers, Material Recovery Facilities (MRFs), certified recyclers, and energy recovery systems today operate largely in isolation from one another, relying on manual paperwork, informal trust relationships, and static, non-optimized routes. This fragmentation leads directly to energy-blind operations - inefficient transportation, avoidable emissions, processing losses, and, most critically, landfill leakage where waste never reaches its highest-value recovery pathway at all.

Our current system already addresses a meaningful part of this problem. We have built and deployed a GPS-integrated, multi-OEM fleet-tracking layer that gives us real-time visibility into vehicle movement, combined with a QR-code-based trip validation system that generates a unique, auditable digital trip sheet for every single movement of waste - from the point of collection through every intermediate handoff to its final destination, whether that is a recycler, a processing plant, a Waste-to-Energy (WTE) facility, or a cement kiln for co-processing. Route management is handled dynamically, with live optimization delivered through APIs to open-market routing models, allowing us to reroute vehicles in response to real-time traffic, load conditions, and proximity to the next collection point. This is not a static, one-time-mapped system - it continuously adapts to ground conditions, which is precisely what makes it possible to guarantee traceability at scale.

What we are proposing to build under this program is the next, necessary layer on top of this foundation: three new modules that convert Swastha 2.0 from an operational efficiency tool into a full ULB-facing governance platform.

The first is a ULB Monitoring Dashboard. Presently, Urban Local Bodies have no unified, real-time way to see how the multiple waste contractors operating within their jurisdiction are actually performing - how much waste is being collected, whether it is reaching sanctioned processing destinations, whether contractors are meeting their service-level commitments, and where breakdowns or diversions are occurring. This dashboard will give ULB officials a single pane of visibility across every contractor in their jurisdiction, converting our existing trip-level and vehicle-level data into contractor-level and jurisdiction-level accountability - the exact tool ULBs need to enforce SWM 2026 compliance, but currently lack.

The second is a Payments Module, designed to manage and track payments made for waste collection from waste generators. Today, this financial layer of the waste value chain is almost entirely informal and undocumented, which creates leakage, delay, and disputes between generators, contractors, and collection agents. By embedding payment tracking directly into the same platform that already validates every trip, we close the loop between physical movement of waste and the financial transactions associated with it - giving both ULBs and contractors a single, reconciled source of truth.

The third is an HR Module, built to manage people operations - onboarding, attendance, and performance tracking - across the drivers, operations managers, and plant operators who form the human backbone of this entire system. A large share of the waste collection workforce in India operates informally, without structured records of their work history, attendance, or performance. Formalizing this layer does two things simultaneously: it gives operators and ULBs a reliable, auditable record of who is doing the work and how well, and it gives the workers themselves a foothold into a more structured, recognized employment relationship.

Together, these three modules extend our current GPS- and QR-based trip validation system into a genuinely end-to-end orchestration layer - connecting waste generators, contractors, transporters, and ULBs on a single platform, with visibility, accountability, and traceability built in at every stage, not bolted on afterward. This is directly aligned with T-MAP's Digital Operational Intelligence focus area, and reflects the exact kind of embedded, municipally-integrated digital solution the program is designed to support.

Geography

This project will be implemented across two geographies, representing both our existing operational base and the new scaling opportunity this program enables.

Kerala is where Swastha 2.0 is already live and operational, not a pilot or proof of concept. We currently operate across all 14 districts of Kerala and in Pune, orchestrating roughly 6,000 MT of waste per month from source to end-of-life. This is not a theoretical claim - it is backed by a live network of over 3,000 mapped collection points, 35 processing plants, 1 Waste-to-Energy plant, and 8 cement kiln partners for co-processing, operating through a fleet of 402 vehicles and more than 5,000 tracked trips. We are empanelled by the Suchitwa Mission, Government of Kerala, specifically to implement transparency and accountability for waste generation and processing across ULBs in all 14 districts of the state, and we have successfully implemented full system tracking across the entire district of Kozhikode - monitoring material movement from ULB to processing plant, as well as its interstate movement to cement kilns. We have also been selected under FC 2.0, an initiative of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA). This gives us both the operational maturity and the government-recognized credibility to now extend the model into a second state.

The second geography is a new pilot with an Urban Local Body in Maharashtra, specifically within the T-MAP program's eligible cities of Mumbai, Thane, or Mira Bhayandar. Within this ULB, we will map waste collection from 5,000 households, along with the drivers, vehicles, and processing infrastructure associated with that collection network. This scope was chosen deliberately to be large enough to generate statistically meaningful operational data - on efficiency, contractor accountability, and payment traceability - while remaining small enough to execute rigorously within a defined 12-month program window, and to serve as a genuine, well-validated template rather than a rushed or superficial rollout.

We see these two geographies as complementary, not parallel. Kerala demonstrates that our model works at genuine multi-district, multi-stakeholder scale, under formal government empanelment. Maharashtra is where we prove that the model - including the three new governance modules - is replicable outside the state where it was originally built, which is exactly the kind of validation T-MAP is designed to support before wider civic adoption.

Timelines

We are proposing a 12-month program, structured into three sequential four-month phases, each with clearly defined outcomes.

Enable (Months 1–4): In this phase, our core deliverable is to build and deploy the ULB Monitoring Dashboard, Payments Module, and HR Module - the three governance layers described above - aligned with T-MAP's Digital Operational Intelligence focus area. In parallel, we will formalize our ULB partnership or MoU with the target Maharashtra civic body, which is a prerequisite for any ground deployment. We will also prepare the underlying system architecture and complete GPS/QR integration work specific to the target city's contractor and fleet network, since every city has its own configuration of vehicles, OEM systems, and existing infrastructure that our platform needs to integrate with before any household-level mapping can begin.

Pilot Deployment & Efficiency Optimization (Months 5–8): With the modules built and the ULB partnership formalized, we move into live deployment. We will pilot Swastha 2.0 in the allotted ULB, mapping waste collection from the target households in 1 ULB , along with their associated drivers, vehicles, and processing infrastructure - mirroring the approach we have already validated with our Loople pilot in Pune, where we mapped 231 collection points using QR codes, deployed a trained fleet, and onboarded dedicated operations and plant staff. Throughout this phase, we will actively monitor contractor accountability, payment traceability, and workforce management KPIs through the new modules, and - critically -we will iterate module workflows based on real pilot data and direct ULB feedback, rather than treating this as a one-way deployment.

Scale-Up & Replication Readiness (Months 9–12): In the final phase, we move from pilot to a scale-up posture. We will use pilot learnings to move toward full city-wide deployment within the target ULB, with a specific focus on demonstrating SWM 2026 compliance and measurable, quantified operational efficiency gains - following the same efficiency-improvement approach that delivered a 7% collection efficiency gain in our Loople pilot. By the end of this phase, our goal is to have packaged the ULB dashboard, payments, and HR modules into a documented, replicable model - one that is ready for adoption not just in the initial pilot city, but across other Maharashtra ULBs under the broader T-MAP program.

Funding Amount Required

We are requesting INR 40,00,000 (Forty Lakhs) to execute this 12-month program. We have broken this down into four heads, reflecting both the technology build and the on-ground deployment costs required to run a credible, fully operational ULB pilot rather than a limited proof-of-concept.

Module Development - INR 18,00,000. This covers the build, testing, and deployment of the ULB Dashboard, Payments Module, and HR Module. This is justified by a dedicated pod of 3 full-stack engineers working for 4 months - the core Enable phase of our timeline - to ensure these modules are production-ready, not prototypes, by the time we begin pilot deployment.

Technology Infrastructure - INR 4,00,000. This covers GPS/OEM API integration and the collection-point mapping and validation system specific to the pilot city. This is justified by the need for a single mid-level technical staff member dedicated to system management across the full 8-month deployment window (Enable through Pilot Deployment), ensuring continuity of technical support as the system moves from build to live operation.

City Operations and Deployment Team - INR 15,00,000. This is our largest single line item, reflecting the reality that a genuinely accountable waste-tracking pilot depends on strong on-ground operational presence, not just software. It covers a local operations manager and field operator for the full pilot duration, along with fleet onboarding, driver and operator training, and plant/MCF staff onboarding for the single ULB pilot. This is justified by a team of 3 managing operations across an 8-month period, mirroring the operations-manager-plus-plant-operator structure we already use successfully in our Loople pilot.

Contingency - INR 3,00,000. A standard contingency allocation to absorb unforeseen costs in on-ground deployment, particularly given that this is our first Maharashtra-based rollout and some ground realities - contractor structures, vehicle types, existing municipal systems - may differ from what we've encountered in Kerala.

We see this funding ask as proportionate and specific: it is not a request for the full T-MAP cohort pool, but a clearly justified slice of it, tied line-by-line to a 12-month, four-person-plus-team execution plan.

Partnerships Associated

Our partnership base spans government, ULB, and corporate stakeholders, reflecting the multi-actor coordination that Swastha 2.0 is built to enable.

Government (Stateof  Kerala): We are empanelled by the Suchitwa Mission, Government of Kerala, to implement transparency and accountability for waste generation and processing across ULBs in all 14 districts of the state.

Government (National): We have been selected under GFC 2.0, an initiative of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA), reflecting national-level recognition of our platform's approach to waste governance.

Program Partnership (Maharashtra): Through this application, we are seeking to formalize a new partnership under T-MAP - the Maharashtra Tech Accelerator Project run by Villgro, as part of Cisco's 40 Communities initiative - which will directly support our pilot deployment in Mumbai, Thane, or Mira Bhayandar.

Urban Local Body (Maharashtra): Our target ULB will serve as our pilot partner for household-level waste mapping and contractor monitoring, and we anticipate formalizing this relationship through an MoU during the Enable phase of the program.

Corporate/Industry: We have an existing operational partnership with Loople, an organisation focused on the collection, segregation, and recycling of glass waste in Pune, where we have fully digitised operations across 231 mapped collection points. We also work with 8 cement kiln partners in Kerala for co-processing of waste sourced from Material Collection Facilities (MCFs).

Contractors and Fleet Operators: These are onboarded onto our platform through our commission-based and pay-per-use revenue models, and form the operational backbone of last-mile collection and transport across all our active geographies -currently including 302 vehicle operators across Kerala and Pune.

Expected Impact Description

This project will formalise waste management operations across two states, bringing an estimated 5,000 households under transparent, traceable digital monitoring through the Maharashtra pilot, in addition to sustaining and building on our existing Kerala footprint of roughly 6,000 MT of waste orchestrated per month across all 14 districts.

The most immediate and structural impact will be governance-level: by giving ULBs real-time dashboard visibility into contractor performance, this project directly addresses the accountability gap that currently prevents consistent SWM 2026 compliance. ULB officials today have no reliable, real-time way to know whether contractors under their jurisdiction are meeting collection and processing obligations — our dashboard converts this from an opaque, manually-audited process into a continuously visible one.

Financially, the Payments Module will reduce leakage and delay in the generator-to-collector payment chain - a part of the waste value chain that is currently undocumented and prone to dispute, and which becomes far more resistant to fraud once it is tied to the same trip-validated, GPS- and QR-verified records already used for physical waste movement.

On the social impact side, the HR Module formalises employment for a workforce that is largely informal today - building directly on our existing base of 302 vehicle operators already onboarded in Kerala, and extending that same model of structured, tracked, and recognized employment into the Maharashtra pilot. This has a compounding effect: it improves the reliability of the people the ULB is depending on, while giving those workers a documented employment history and more predictable, tracked work.

Environmentally, the underlying trip-validation and route-optimization system that powers all three new modules continues to do what it already does in Kerala — ensuring that waste is diverted away from landfill and toward its correct recovery pathway, whether that is a recycler, a WTE plant, or a cement kiln, with GPS tracking, QR-coded checkpoints, and digital trip sheets providing a verified, auditable diversion trail rather than self-reported data.

Taken together, these modules position Swastha 2.0 to scale from a single-state, operationally proven system into a replicable, multi-state ULB governance model. The Maharashtra pilot is not intended to be a one-off deployment - it is designed, from the outset, to serve as the validated template for adoption across other Maharashtra ULBs under T-MAP, moving both this project and the broader circular economy ecosystem it serves closer to the ultimate goal of 100% traceable waste collection and disposal, from source to end-of-life.

column36: RNisarg Foundation is a doctor-led, women-led public charitable trust based in Thane, Mumbai, working at the intersection of public health and environmental sustainability. Since our founding, we have built and scaled community-rooted health interventions in partnership with government health systems, urban local bodies, and corporate donors.  Through this application, we bring forward two interlinked initiatives tackling one of urban India's most overlooked public health and sanitation gaps: the safe management of menstrual and special-care biomedical waste generated within households.  Project Sakhi, our flagship menstrual health programme, addresses this at the source  building awareness, driving adoption of sustainable menstrual products, and shifting behaviour among women and adolescent girls across urban and semi-urban communities, in active partnership with the public health department.  Complementing this, our Sanitary & Special-Care Waste Management programme, run in direct partnership with the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC), tackles the downstream challenge: how sanitary waste and special-care waste from home-based patient care (diapers, catheters, dressings, and similar items) are segregated, collected, and disposed of safely at the household and ward level. This includes a dual-QR service model for waste audits and doorstep collection requests, piloted across BMC wards with promising early registration and service-uptake data.  Together, these programmes represent a full-cycle model  from behaviour change and product adoption to last-mile collection infrastructure  for a waste stream that is high-volume, high-risk, and largely invisible in India's sanitation and public health planning.
column37: Technology is central to how we make an otherwise invisible waste stream visible, trackable, and actionable at scale.  At the core of our BMC partnership is a dual-QR digital model: a Waste Audit QR that allows ward-level sanitation staff and citizens to log and classify sanitary and special-care waste generation at the household level, and a Service Request QR that lets residents request doorstep collection on demand. This converts a manual, ad-hoc collection process into a data-driven, on-demand service  giving BMC real-time visibility into waste volumes, hotspots, and service gaps across wards, and giving us a live registration funnel to track adoption and identify where uptake is breaking down.  On the Project Sakhi side, we use lightweight digital tools  including WhatsApp-based communication flows  to reach women and adolescent girls with menstrual health information and product adoption support in local language, without requiring smartphone literacy or app downloads. This mirrors the low-friction, high-reach digital engagement models we've deployed in other public health programmes, including a Hindi-language health tracker used by community health workers.  Underlying both workstreams is a simple design principle: technology should reduce friction for the citizen, generate structured data for the civic body, and remain lightweight enough to work in low-resource, low-connectivity urban settings. This lets us move from awareness to service delivery to verifiable outcomes  conversion rates, collection volumes, response times  using data we can defend to donors, government partners, and evaluators alike.
column38: The Need  Menstrual and special-care biomedical waste  sanitary pads, diapers, catheters, dressings, and other home-based patient-care waste  is generated in nearly every household, yet remains one of the most poorly managed waste streams in urban India. It is routinely mixed with dry/wet household waste, exposing sanitation workers, waste handlers, and community members to infection risk, while overwhelming municipal systems that have no dedicated collection or audit mechanism for it. Simultaneously, awareness and access gaps mean many women and girls still lack the knowledge or means to manage menstrual health safely and with dignity  a need distinct from, but directly upstream of, the waste problem itself. Together, these create a full-cycle gap: from safe product use and behaviour change, to safe segregation, to safe civic collection and disposal.  Available Alternatives  Today, most cities  including Mumbai  rely on generic dry/wet waste segregation drives that do not specifically address sanitary or special-care waste as a distinct category. Where interventions exist, they tend to be one-off awareness campaigns (largely NGO-led, without civic system integration) or municipal solid-waste initiatives that treat all waste uniformly, without a dedicated audit, collection-on-demand, or tracking mechanism. There is no existing model we are aware of that combines menstrual health behaviour-change at the household level with a structured, ward-level, technology-enabled collection and audit system run in direct partnership with a municipal corporation  which is the specific gap our combined Sakhi BMC  model is designed to close.
column40:
Intellectual Property

Project Sakhi's brand identity is protected through a formal trademark application filed before the Registrar of Trade Marks, Mumbai, under the Trade Marks Act, 1999, supported by a sworn affidavit under Rule 25(2) of the Trade Mark Rules, 2017 (filed August 2025). The "SAKHI" label has been filed across three classes reflecting our actual scope of work: Class 41 (educational content, training modules, Training-of-Trainers and community trainer models, impact metrics and communication tools), Class 42 (cup donation documentation, user support structures, and training processes), and Class 45 (social services for women's empowerment).

This application is backed by an already-registered parent trademark  RNisarg Foundation, registered under No. 3496425 (Class 41), Certificate No. 1647912, dated 11/09/2017  giving Sakhi's filing the legal standing of an established, registered house mark.

The affidavit affirms continuous, open use of the "SAKHI" mark since its adoption on 21/05/2019, with documented third-party funding as evidence of market recognition and goodwill  donor support has grown from 51,000 (FY2019-20) to over 90 lakh (FY2024-25), backed by corporates .

Status: Trademark application filed and pending registration (not yet granted). No patents have been filed, as our innovation is a service delivery and behaviour-change model rather than a patentable product or process.
column42:
Current Model

RNisarg Foundation currently operates on a grant and CSR-funded model. Project Sakhi is funded through corporate CSR partners (e.g., PwC, HDFC Bank, TruHome Finance) on a per-ward or per-beneficiary-cohort basis, with costs structured around product distribution, awareness sessions, and outcome tracking (adoption/conversion rates). The Sanitary & Special-Care Waste programme operates through a formal partnership with BMC, where implementation budgets are proposed and approved ward-wise (e.g., 10.72 lakh for a 10-ward Phase 5 rollout), with BMC providing civic infrastructure access, sanctions, and eventual absorption of the operating model into its own systems.

Proposed Revenue Model for Scale

We are working toward a cost-per-ward, outcome-linked service model that can be adopted by any ULB: municipal corporations pay a structured implementation fee (covering the QR-based audit/collection system, waste handler training, and monitoring) benchmarked against verified outcomes  registration rates, service response times, safe disposal volumes  making the model budget-defensible and replicable across cities, not just Mumbai.

On the Sakhi side, we are exploring a hybrid model: continued CSR-funded rollouts for underserved geographies, combined with a modest per-adopter product/logistics cost recoverable from institutional partners (hospitals, corporates, PHCs) who sponsor cohorts directly, rather than one-time grants.

Longer-term, we see potential to license our replication playbook and technology stack (QR audit system, WhatsApp engagement flows) to other NGOs or municipal bodies for a fee, converting our operational learnings into a repeatable, revenue-generating asset rather than a one-off intervention.
column43:
Challenges & Risks
Funding dependency: Both Sakhi and the BMC waste programme currently rely on CSR grants and civic budget cycles rather than a self-sustaining revenue stream. CSR priorities shift year-on-year, and municipal budget approvals (e.g., ward-wise waste management sanctions) can be delayed by administrative or political cycles, creating funding gaps between phases.

Behaviour change is slow and non-linear: Menstrual product adoption and household waste segregation both require sustained community trust-building. Conversion rates vary significantly by geography (8695 in our pilots), and replicating this in new, unfamiliar wards or districts carries execution risk if local trust networks aren't rebuilt from scratch.

Government partnership dependency: Our BMC and public health department partnerships are foundational but non-contractual in the traditional commercial sense  continuity depends on institutional relationships, ward-level officer turnover, and civic priorities, which can shift with administrative changes.

Data and last-mile tracking: The dual-QR system depends on consistent citizen and field-staff usage low digital literacy or connectivity gaps in some wards can cause registration funnel drop-off, requiring ongoing field-level troubleshooting.

Regulatory/compliance risk: Special-care and biomedical waste handling is subject to evolving state and municipal waste management regulations any regulatory change could require us to re-adapt collection protocols.

Scale-versus-quality tension: Rapid replication across wards/cities risks diluting the on-ground trust-building and data-verification rigor that has driven our credibility with donors and civic partners to date.
column44: Quantitatively, we track beneficiary conversion and retention rates, service request volumes (Service Request QR usage), and training reach among ASHA workers and sanitation staff. Qualitatively, we assess dignity and stigma reduction through structured beneficiary feedback on comfort discussing menstrual health and comfort requesting waste collection services, plus civic-side feedback from ward officers on reduced informal/unsafe disposal incidents. Verified case narratives from pilot wards  supplement quantitative data, capturing shifts in household practice, community trust in civic systems, and reduced health-risk exposure for sanitation workers.
column46: Our beneficiary base spans two interconnected groups. Under Project Sakhi, primary beneficiaries are women and adolescent girls  across urban and semi-urban ,rural and tribal areas of Maharashtra, including low-income and lower-middle-income households in municipal wards and peri-urban clusters such as Amravati and Sonapur  communities with limited prior access to menstrual health education or sustainable products. Under the BMC Sanitary & Special-Care Waste programme, beneficiaries include general ward residents across Mumbai (particularly households managing home-based patient care  elderly, chronically ill, or bedridden family members generating diapers, catheters, and dressing waste), community toilets,educational institutions,beauty parlour as well as municipal sanitation workers and waste handlers who benefit indirectly through reduced infection exposure. Both groups are largely  service recipients for these specific interventions, with moderate digital literacy, necessitating low-friction engagement tools (WhatsApp, QR codes) rather than app-based systems. Secondary beneficiaries include ASHA workers, community health volunteers, and ward-level civic staff who receive training and capacity-building support as programme intermediaries, extending impact beyond direct beneficiaries into the local health and sanitation workforce.
column47:
Previously Conducted Pilots within Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) in Maharashtra
RNisarg Foundation's pilot work with Maharashtra's urban local bodies spans two interlinked programme areas  the Sanitary & Special-Care Waste Management initiative with the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC), and the Sakhi programme, also anchored in partnership with BMC health department across Mumbai's ward system. Both have generated ground-level data, civic buy-in, and operational learnings that directly inform the innovation being proposed for scale-up.

1. Sanitary & Special-Care Waste Management Pilot  BMC, across 26 Ward, Mumbai

Our flagship ULB pilot was conducted in all Wards, Mumbai, in direct partnership with BMC, targeting the safe segregation, collection, and disposal of sanitary and special-care biomedical waste generated within households  a waste stream that had no dedicated civic collection mechanism prior to this intervention.

The pilot introduced a dual-QR digital model:

A Waste Audit QR, enabling household-level classification and logging of sanitary/special-care waste generation, giving BMC granular visibility into volumes and waste types at the ward level for the first time.
A Service Request QR, allowing residents to request doorstep collection on demand, converting an informal, inconsistent collection process into a trackable, on-demand civic service.

The pilot generated a structured registration funnel, tracking citizen sign-up, activation, and repeat usage  giving us and BMC real data on where adoption succeeds and where it drops off (e.g., digital literacy gaps, awareness gaps, or service response delays). 

2. Project Sakhi  Community-Level Pilots in Maharashtra 

While Project Sakhi's ULB engagement is  formally structured through ASHA workers and PHC route. We have generated some of our most rigorously tracked outcome data, and are directly relevant to demonstrating our ability to convert awareness into measurable behaviour change at community scale:
With over one lakh women educated and 24000 women provided Menstrual cups. Conversion to using menstrual cups is close to 80 percentage.



These pilots demonstrate that our community engagement and behaviour-change methodology performs consistently even across different geographies and beneficiary base sizes, which is central to our replication playbook's credibility.

Cross-Cutting Learnings from ULB Pilot Work

Across both the BMC waste management and Sakhi, a few consistent operational learnings have emerged, which we believe strengthen the case for incubation support:

Digital tools must be low-friction for civic-side adoption to succeed. The dual-QR model's success depends on simplicity for both citizens and ward-level sanitation staff  any added complexity directly reduces registration funnel conversion.
Formal review touchpoints (e.g., DMC-level meetings) are critical checkpoints  not just for approval, but for surfacing civic-side operational blockers (staffing, infrastructure, training gaps) early.
Data verification builds institutional trust. Our practice of independently verifying conversion and adoption figures before external use has been a key factor in sustaining both donor confidence and BMC's willingness to continue phased partnership.

These pilots collectively represent proof points across the two core dimensions of our proposed innovation  behaviour change at the household/community level (Sakhi) and civic-system-integrated waste collection infrastructure (BMC Sanitary & Special-Care Waste)  and form the operational and evidentiary basis for the phased, technology-enabled scale-up we are proposing through this application.

column48: Short Term (0-12 months)  Our immediate focus is on consolidating our existing 26-ward BMC rollout and initiating outreach to other ULBs within the Mumbai Metropolitan Region (MMR). For the Sanitary & Special-Care Waste programme, this means strengthening the dual-QR system's registration funnel and service delivery consistency across all 26 BMC wards, formalising the operational support requests already tabled at DMC level, and using this proven, city-wide dataset as a proof-of-concept package to approach other MMR municipal corporations (e.g., Thane, Navi Mumbai, Kalyan-Dombivli) for pilot adoption of the model. For Project Sakhi, short-term impact means formally mapping and onboarding ASHA workers across Primary Health Centres (PHCs) as our core delivery network, training them as community-level Sakhi facilitators, and establishing baseline outreach protocols through which they can reach women in their assigned communities. We expect to finalise standard training modules, data-collection formats, and impact-tracking tools during this phase, alongside early indicative conversion data from the first PHC clusters onboarded.  Medium Term (1-3 years)  Over this horizon, we aim to convert our proven 26-ward BMC model into a replicable, multi-ULB framework across MMR. On the waste management side, this means having fully embedded, data-mature systems across all 26 BMC wards  with waste audit data feeding directly into BMC's own solid-waste planning  while extending the dual-QR model to at least 34 additional municipal corporations beyond BMC, each running phased, ward-wise rollouts modelled on our proven structure. For Sakhi, medium-term impact means full integration with the ASHA network across all PHCs within our target districts, using ASHA workers as the primary channel to reach community women at scale  moving from initial onboarding to sustained, PHC-anchored delivery with measurable, consistent conversion rates across catchment areas. We expect to demonstrate that our model produces comparable outcomes regardless of ULB, ward, or PHC catchment, giving us the evidence base to formalise our cost-per-ward and cost-per-PHC-cluster models with donors and civic partners, reducing dependency on one-off CSR grants through more predictable, outcome-linked funding structures.  Long Term (3-5 years and beyond)  Our long-term ambition is systemic adoption across the MMR region and beyond: for the Sanitary & Special-Care Waste model  already operational across 26 BMC wards  to become the standard municipal protocol across all ULBs in MMR, with special-care and sanitary waste formally recognised as a distinct category in urban sanitation planning, supported by policy-level advocacy building on our existing research framework on home-generated medical waste. For Sakhi, we envision near-universal ASHA-network coverage across MMR's PHCs, making menstrual health education and sustainable product access a standard extension of existing public health infrastructure rather than a parallel NGO-run initiative  ensuring every community woman within the ASHA network's reach has access to Sakhi's support. Longer-term, we aim to license or hand over our technology stack (QR-based audit tools, WhatsApp engagement flows, training modules) to civic bodies and public health systems directly, embedding both interventions into government-owned infrastructure  with measurable, sustained reductions in landfill-bound special-care waste, infection risk for sanitation workers.

**Project Description**

We propose to scale two complementary, government-partnered interventions addressing an overlooked public health and sanitation gap: menstrual health and special-care biomedical waste management. **Project Sakhi** drives menstrual health awareness and sustainable product adoption among women and adolescent girls, delivered through the ASHA worker network across Primary Health Centres (PHCs), in partnership with the public health department. The **Sanitary & Special-Care Waste Management programme**, run with the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) and currently active across 26 Mumbai wards, uses a dual-QR digital model — a Waste Audit QR for household-level waste classification and a Service Request QR for on-demand doorstep collection — to formalise safe segregation and civic collection of sanitary and special-care waste (diapers, catheters, dressings). Together, these form a full-cycle model: behaviour change at the household level, feeding into safe, trackable civic collection infrastructure.

**Geography**

Current operations span 26 wards under BMC (Mumbai) and PHC-linked community outreach in parts of Maharashtra. Through this incubation, we propose scaling the BMC waste model to additional Urban Local Bodies across the Mumbai Metropolitan Region (MMR) — including Thane, Navi Mumbai, and Kalyan-Dombivli — and expanding Sakhi's ASHA-led delivery to cover all PHCs within our target MMR districts.

**Timelines**

- *Short term (0–12 months):* Consolidate the 26-ward BMC model; onboard ASHA workers across target PHCs; initiate outreach to 2–3 additional MMR ULBs.
- *Medium term (1–3 years):* Full ASHA-PHC integration for Sakhi; dual-QR adoption by 3–4 additional MMR municipal corporations; formalise outcome-linked funding models.
- *Long term (3–5+ years):* Sanitary waste model as standard protocol across MMR ULBs; near-universal ASHA-network coverage for Sakhi; technology stack licensed/handed to civic and public health systems.

**Funding Amount Required**

Based on our BMC Phase 5 budget benchmark (?10.72 lakh per 10-ward cohort) and the 26-ward GHP budget (?49.76 lakh), we estimate **?1.5–2 crore over 18–24 months** to fund expansion into 2–3 new ULBs (ward-wise phased rollout), ASHA network onboarding and training across target PHCs, technology stack adaptation (QR systems, WhatsApp flows) for new geographies, and outcome measurement infrastructure. *[Please confirm/adjust this figure based on your actual budget model before submission.]*

**Partnerships Associated**

- **Government:** Maharashtra Public Health Department, National Health Mission (NHM) Maharashtra — for ASHA network access and Sakhi delivery.
- **Urban Local Body:** BMC (existing, 26-ward operational partner); target ULBs for expansion (Thane, Navi Mumbai, Kalyan-Dombivli Municipal Corporations).
- **Corporate CSR:** Existing donor relationships (PwC, HDFC Bank, TruHome Finance, L&T, RCF, Toyo, Shriram, UNS) for Sakhi and GHP funding continuity.
- **Technical/Programme Partners:** PATH, GSK (AMR and training collaborations).

**Expected Impact Description**

At scale, we expect measurable reduction in landfill-bound special-care waste through ward-wise segregation and collection data, reduced infection risk for sanitation workers, and formal recognition of special-care waste as a distinct municipal waste category. For Sakhi, we expect sustained menstrual product adoption (targeting 85%+ conversion, consistent with existing pilot performance) across all PHC catchments reached, translating into quantified reduction in disposable product waste and improved menstrual health outcomes and dignity for community women. Structurally, we aim to shift both interventions from donor-funded pilots into standard, budgeted civic and public health services — embedding our technology and training systems into government-owned infrastructure for long-term sustainability beyond our direct involvement.

Gatisheel addresses the lack of integrated digital operational intelligence in water infrastructure managed by Urban Local Bodies (ULBs), irrigation departments, government utilities, and industries. Many water assets such as pumping stations, WTPs, STPs, distribution networks, valves, and flow systems are still operated through manual processes or fragmented monitoring solutions. This results in delayed fault detection, reactive maintenance, inefficient water distribution, excessive energy consumption, water losses, and limited visibility into asset performance.

Gatisheel’s AI-powered IoT and SCADA platform connects distributed assets and converts real-time operational data into actionable intelligence. It enables centralized monitoring, remote control, automated alerts, anomaly detection, predictive maintenance, and water-energy analytics. This helps ULBs and other infrastructure operators move from reactive to proactive management, improving service reliability, resource efficiency, transparency, and operational decision-making.
column37:
Technology is the core enabler of Gatisheels innovation. Our AI-powered Industrial IoT and SCADA platform connects field-level assets such as pumps, motors, valves, flow meters, sensors, PLCs, cloud-based platform. This enables real-time data collection, remote monitoring and control, automated alerts, and operational analytics.

AI and machine-learning models analyze equipment and process data to identify abnormal patterns, support predictive maintenance, and provide actionable operational insights. The platform also integrates water-flow and energy-consumption data to identify inefficiencies and optimize operations.

Our hardware-agnostic architecture allows integration with existing infrastructure, enabling organizations to digitize legacy systems without replacing their entire setup. This transforms fragmented and manual operations into connected, intelligent, and data-driven infrastructure management.
column38:
Gatisheel addresses the need for reliable, efficient, and data-driven management of distributed water infrastructure. ULBs, irrigation departments, government utilities, industries, and agri-enterprises need real-time visibility of pumps, valves, flow, water levels, energy consumption, and asset health to reduce water losses, downtime, energy costs, and manual intervention.

Current alternatives include manual inspection and logbooks, standalone sensors, conventional PLC/SCADA systems, and fragmented IoT monitoring solutions. These approaches often provide limited integration, reactive fault management, or data without actionable intelligence.

Gatisheel differentiates itself by combining IoT, AI, SCADA, remote automation, anomaly detection, predictive insights, and water-energy analytics in a unified, hardware-agnostic platform. It can integrate with existing infrastructure, enabling organisations to progressively digitise operations without replacing their entire systems.
column42:
Gatisheel Agritech operates a hybrid B2B/B2G business model, serving ULBs, government utilities, irrigation departments, agri-enterprises, industries, Water User Associations, and EPC partners. We provide end-to-end digitalization and automation of water infrastructure through our AI-powered IoT and SCADA platform.

Revenue is generated through (1) sale and installation of IoT devices, sensors, controllers, and automation systems (2) project-based system integration and commissioning (3) recurring SaaS subscriptions for the Gatisheel SCADA platform (4) Annual Maintenance Contracts (AMCs) and remote monitoring services and (5) customized analytics, upgrades, and ESG/water-management reporting for industrial customers.

This hybrid model combines upfront project revenue with recurring software and service income, enabling long-term customer engagement and scalable growth.
column43:
Gatisheel has identified several challenges associated with scaling digital water infrastructure solutions. These include long government procurement cycles, integration with diverse legacy equipment, varying levels of digital readiness among customers, and the need to demonstrate measurable ROI before large-scale adoption. Connectivity limitations at remote irrigation sites and the availability of skilled personnel for deployment and maintenance are additional operational challenges.

We mitigate these risks through a hardware-agnostic architecture that integrates with existing systems, phased pilot deployments to demonstrate value, remote monitoring capabilities, and partnerships with government agencies, EPC companies, and local implementation partners. We also continuously strengthen cybersecurity, data reliability, and after-sales support to ensure dependable long-term operations.

Qualitatively, we collect feedback from farmers, irrigation departments, ULBs, and operators on ease of use, reliability, safety, reduced dependence on manual intervention, and improved decision-making. The innovation addresses the lack of real time operational intelligence, monitoring and accountability in solid waste management. Waste is often collected in mixed form because there is limited visibility into source segregation and waste movement, making downstream recycling and recovery less efficient and increasing dependence on landfills.

ECOWRAP addresses this gap by using its Waste Intelligence platform to monitor source segregation, track collection and waste movement, generate performance data, and support better operational decisions. This enables municipalities and waste operators to identify gaps, improve collection efficiency and ensure segregated waste reaches the appropriate recovery or processing facility.

ECOWRAP solves the information and accountability gap that prevents solid waste systems from achieving effective segregation, recovery and landfill diversion.
column37: Technology is the core enabler of ECOWRAPs innovation. Our in house Waste Intelligence platform combines AI based waste monitoring, real time data analytics and GPS based tracking to create visibility and accountability across the waste management process. The technology enables us to monitor source segregation, generate segregation performance ratings, track waste collection and movement, analyse waste generation patterns, forecast waste volumes and optimize collection routes and fleet operations. It also helps identify operational gaps and track the recovery and processing of segregated waste. By connecting households, waste workers, operators and municipalities through a single intelligence and accountability layer, ECOWRAP makes waste management more measurable, transparent, efficient and outcome driven.
column38: ECOWRAP addresses the need for a more accountable, data driven and efficient waste management system, particularly at the point where waste is generated. The key gap is poor source segregation and limited real time visibility into waste generation, collection and recovery. When waste is mixed at source, recyclable and organic materials become contaminated, reducing recovery efficiency and increasing dependence on landfills. The available alternatives are largely traditional municipal waste collection and contractor based systems, where waste is manually monitored and transported as mixed waste, along with standalone MRFs, recycling facilities, composting and other downstream processing solutions. ECOWRAP differentiates itself by combining source segregation, technology based monitoring, real time tracking, accountability and on ground operations into one integrated Waste Intelligence system, enabling waste to be managed and recovered more effectively before it reaches the landfill.

column36: Our innovation addresses the safe, efficient and economically viable recovery of faecal sludge-derived biosolids for climate-resilient agriculture. India currently has more than 1,034 FSTPs generating approximately 250 tonnes of biosolids daily, yet only 33 of FSTPs reuse biosolids and just 8 use co-composting. Biosolids often have high pathogen loads, variable quality and limited farmer acceptance, while the absence of consistent reuse standards further restricts agricultural utilisation. We addresses this gap through a specialized microbial consortium and controlled co-composting process using biosolids with green/agricultural residues. The technology is designed to accelerate stabilization, improve pathogen reduction and compost maturity, and convert sanitation waste into a safe, nutrient-rich organic soil amendment. This creates a practical link between urban sanitation, resource recovery and agriculture, reducing environmental risks while enabling municipalities to recover value from biosolids and providing farmers with locally produced organic inputs.

Our innovation addresses the critical need for safe, efficient and economically viable conversion of faecal sludge-derived biosolids into agricultural resources. Although India has more than 1,034 FSTPs producing approximately 250 tonnes of biosolids daily, only about 33 of facilities currently reuse biosolids and just 8 use co-composting. Major barriers include pathogen risks, inconsistent biosolids quality, limited testing and monitoring, lack of clear reuse standards, and low farmer acceptance. 
Available alternatives include direct land application/soil conditioning, conventional co-composting with agricultural residues or municipal organic waste, vermicomposting, pyrolysis/biochar production, and disposal or storage. These approaches can be useful, but their suitability depends on biosolids quality, infrastructure, cost and end-use requirements. Our differentiation is a biosolids-specific microbial consortium integrated with controlled co-composting, layer-wise inoculum application and systematic quality monitoring. Rather than replacing existing FSTP infrastructure, the technology is designed to enhance the biological process, improve consistency and accelerate conversion into a quality-controlled agricultural soil amendment. This directly addresses the gap between biosolids treatment and reliable agricultural reuse.
