Project Description:
GI CERI LAB Private Limited is seeking support to scale its microbial consortium-based faecal sludge biosolids co-composting technology from pilot validation to multi-location deployment. The solution addresses the growing challenge of safely managing faecal sludge-derived biosolids generated by Faecal Sludge Treatment Plants (FSTPs). Instead of treating biosolids as a waste requiring disposal, the technology converts them into a stable, nutrient-rich organic soil amendment for agriculture. The proposed process uses a 1:1 ratio of dewatered biosolids with green biomass/agricultural residues, with the microbial inoculum applied uniformly as a powder over successive layers. Controlled aerobic composting is then carried out with monitoring of temperature, moisture, pH, C:N ratio, pathogen reduction and compost maturity.

The innovation is designed to work with existing FSTP and composting infrastructure, thereby reducing the need for major capital investment. The microbial consortium is intended to accelerate organic matter degradation, improve process consistency, reduce odour and support faster stabilization. The project will also establish standardized SOPs, quality-control protocols and agricultural validation to demonstrate the safety and effectiveness of the final compost.

Scaling Opportunity:
India has rapidly expanded its FSTP infrastructure, creating a significant opportunity for biosolids resource recovery. However, biosolids reuse and co-composting remain limited. GI CERI LAB aims to address this gap by providing a low-infrastructure, scalable biotechnology solution that can be integrated into existing treatment facilities. The business model will follow a B2G and B2B approach, targeting Municipal Corporations, Urban Local Bodies (ULBs), FSTP operators, sanitation companies, compost producers and agricultural organizations. Downstream markets will include FPOs, organic farming networks, agri-input distributors and farmers.

The initial scale-up will focus on demonstrating the technology under different operating conditions and feedstock characteristics. Once validated, the model can be replicated across FSTPs in other cities and states through technology licensing, microbial consortium supply, technical service contracts, operator training and annual maintenance agreements.

Geography:
The immediate pilot and field-validation activity is proposed in Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala, in association with the Thiruvananthapuram Municipal Corporation. Kerala will serve as the initial demonstration geography because of the existing institutional engagement and FSSM ecosystem. Following successful validation, the project will expand to Karnataka, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, and subsequently to other states with operational FSTPs and demand for organic soil amendments.

Maharashtra is considered an important future scale-up geography because of its large network of ULBs and FSTPs. However, no pilot has yet been conducted by GI CERI LAB in Maharashtra; the first municipal deployment is being initiated in Kerala.

Timeline:
The proposed scale-up programme will be implemented over 18 months:

Months 1–3: Process optimization, baseline characterization, SOP finalization and pilot-site preparation.
Months 4–9: Field-scale demonstration at the Thiruvananthapuram FSTP, including multiple composting batches and process monitoring.
Months 7–12: Agricultural validation, compost quality assessment, pathogen testing and farmer/user acceptance studies.
Months 10–15: Replication demonstrations at additional FSTPs and development of standardized deployment protocols.
Months 15–18: Commercial readiness, partnerships with ULBs/FSTP operators, business-model validation and preparation for wider geographical expansion.

Funding Required:
GI CERI LAB proposes an estimated funding requirement of ?85 lakh for the scale-up programme. The proposed allocation is:

?20 lakh – Pilot deployment and process scale-up: FSTP implementation, composting infrastructure modifications and field operations.
?15 lakh – R&D and laboratory validation: microbial consortium optimisation, pathogen testing, nutrient analysis and compost quality assessment.
?15 lakh – Agricultural field trials: crop trials, soil testing, farmer demonstrations and product validation.
?15 lakh – Equipment and monitoring: temperature, moisture, pH, microbiological and process-monitoring equipment.
?10 lakh – Capacity building: operator training, SOP development, safety training and stakeholder workshops.
?10 lakh – Market development and project management: documentation, certification, stakeholder engagement and commercialisation activities.

Partnerships Associated:
The project benefits from existing institutional relationships and partnerships relevant to deployment. GI CERI LAB has an MoU/engagement with Thiruvananthapuram Municipal Corporation, which provides an important pathway for municipal-level field validation. The organization has also engaged with the Administrative Staff College of India (ASCI) within the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs ecosystem for capacity building and sanitation-sector engagement. GI CERI LAB is an associate incubatee at the CSIR–NIIST Innovation Centre, providing access to scientific expertise, innovation support and technology-development infrastructure.

Additional academic and technical collaborations provide opportunities for laboratory testing, research, manpower development and knowledge exchange. These partnerships will support the transition from laboratory/pilot validation to field-scale deployment and commercialisation.

Expected Impact:
The project is expected to generate measurable environmental, social and economic impacts. Environmentally, it will divert faecal sludge-derived biosolids and agricultural residues from disposal and convert them into a useful agricultural resource. The project targets approximately 25–30% reduction in composting time, improved pathogen reduction, reduced odour and improved compost maturity and quality. Batch-wise monitoring will quantify tonnes of biosolids treated, compost produced, agricultural residues recovered and nutrients recycled.

Socially, the project will strengthen the capacity of FSTP operators and sanitation workers through structured training and improve the availability of locally produced organic soil amendments for farmers. It will also create opportunities for employment in compost production, processing, testing, logistics and agricultural distribution. Farmer acceptance, operator feedback and community perceptions will be monitored as part of the impact assessment.

Economically, the solution will create a circular sanitation-to-agriculture business model. Municipalities can reduce biosolids management burdens, while FSTP operators can generate value from recovered resources. Farmers and agricultural networks can access locally produced organic inputs. GI CERI LAB will generate revenue through microbial consortium sales, per-tonne treatment services, technical consultancy, laboratory testing, operator training, annual maintenance contracts and compost sales/revenue sharing.

In the short term, the project will establish field evidence and validate the technology under real FSTP conditions. In the medium term, it will enable replication across multiple ULBs and establish commercial partnerships. In the long term, the objective is to develop a nationally replicable biotechnology-enabled sanitation-to-agriculture model, contributing to sustainable sanitation, resource recovery, circular economy, soil health and climate-resilient agriculture.

Overall, the proposed project represents an opportunity to move GI CERI LAB’s technology from pilot validation toward TRL 6–7 and commercial deployment, while demonstrating a practical pathway for transforming a sanitation challenge into an agricultural and economic opportunity.

column36:
Mumbai, Thane and Mira Bhayandar generate more wastewater than they treat, and treat it far from where it arises. Maharashtra treats about 47 percent of its sewage (CPCB, 2021). Thane treats 73 percent of its used water but reuses about 5 percent, against a 53 MLD supply deficit (TMC and CEEW, 2025). Mira Bhayandar supplies 190 MLD against 235 MLD of demand, and its Climate Action Plan asks large consumers to treat on site. Mumbai's seven new STPs will add 2,464 MLD by 2027, at the coast, after the water has crossed the city.
The gap sits at the source: hospitals, hostels, markets, laundries, housing clusters and small plants producing 10 to 500 KLD of variable, high-strength effluent with no land for a conventional plant. Biological treatment needs 6 or more hours of retention, civil tanks, chemical dosing and a skilled operator, and fails under shock loads, which CPCB cites as a leading cause of STP failure. The result: untreated discharge to nallas and creeks, no reuse, and no live record of what each plant does.
Our Water Battery treats this water in 50 seconds to 3 minutes inside a containerised unit needing up to 75 percent less space, with up to 50 percent less sludge, no chemicals and tolerance for 80 percent load swings. Lambert Sense reports flow, pH, ORP, conductivity and energy to a dashboard the ULB can open. That closes both gaps: treatment where water arises, and evidence that it works.
column37:
Technology is the product, in three layers.
Reactor. The Water Battery is a multi-process electrochemical reactor: one chamber runs electrocoagulation, electro-oxidation, electro-flotation, electro-Fenton and in-situ disinfection simultaneously, driven by a patented oscillating electrode. An external magnetic field induces micro-vibration at the electrode surface, suppressing passivation by up to 70 percent. Passivation is the failure mode that kept electrochemical treatment out of municipal service for decades. Removing it makes the reactor stable for years rather than months. Primary treatment takes 50 seconds to 3 minutes (field-validated), sludge is up to 50 percent lower and energy use is 0.8 to 1.1 kWh per KL for sewage.
Digital. Every unit ships with Lambert Sense, an on-board data-feedback module that reads flow, pH, ORP, conductivity and temperature at the inlet and adjusts power, residence time and electrode duty cycle live. The plant self-corrects to shock loads without an operator. It also streams flow, water quality, energy and alarm data to a cloud dashboard, so a municipal engineer sees every unit on one screen and an auditor can pull the record. This log makes pay-per-KL and BOOT contracts bankable: litres and quality are recorded, not claimed.
Manufacturing. Standardised 5 to 1000 KLD modules with quick-swap electrode cartridges, replaced in under 30 minutes, are built and installed in 4 to 8 weeks against 12 to 16 for a civil plant.
Under development: a machine-learning layer that predicts influent change from live data and tunes the reactor itself.
column38:
The need is compliant treatment and reuse at the point of generation, in a footprint a city site can spare, at a cost a ULB can sustain, with proof it works, without land, chemicals or a full-time operator.
Hospital and laundry effluent is the hard case. Laundry water carries surfactants, hypochlorite and quaternary ammonium disinfectants at high pH and temperature. Hospital effluent carries antibiotics, pharmaceutical residues, disinfectants and pathogens. These inhibit or kill the biomass a biological plant depends on, so it loses its biology or passes the compounds through untreated. Electrochemical treatment has no biomass to poison: Water battery generate flocs out surfactants and emulsified oils, and electro-oxidation with in-situ hydroxyl radicals and chlorine breaks down pharmaceutical residues and disinfects in the same chamber.
The alternatives:
MBBR, SBR and activated sludge, the ULB tender default: 6 or more hours of retention, 3 to 4 times our footprint, chemical dosing, shock-load failures and the biomass problem above. Nationally, only 20,235 of 31,841 MLD installed is treated (CPCB, 2021).
MBR and Johkasou-type units: the same biology, plus membranes that foul on surfactants.
Chemical ETPs: daily coagulant, the most sludge, no oxidation of pharmaceutical residues.
Hydroleap and Axine: static electrodes that passivate, no India service base, overseas pricing.
The Water Battery treats in seconds, needs no chemicals, and cuts operating cost about 35 percent as measured at deployed sites. It retrofits ahead of an existing biological plant, so a ULB upgrades without demolishing what it owns.

PROJECT TITLE
Chemical-free treatment and reuse of hospital laundry and effluent at a municipal hospital in Mumbai, Thane or Mira Bhayandar, with live digital compliance monitoring for the ULB, and a compact municipal STP as the alternate site.
SUMMARY
We will install and operate one 20 KLD containerised Water Battery unit for 12 months at a site agreed with the ULB in month 1. The primary site is a municipal hospital laundry, where we treat the laundry and associated effluent to the liquid waste limits of the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016, return 80 to 90 percent of it for non-potable reuse inside the hospital, and give the ULB a live Lambert Sense dashboard showing flow, water quality, energy and compliance. If no hospital clears permissions by the end of month 1, the same unit goes to the alternate site: a compact STP for an unsewered pocket whose sewage now reaches a nalla untreated. Same unit, same budget, same 12 months. Funding requested: Rs 40 lakh. At month 12 the ULB holds a working plant, a year of NABL-certified data, trained staff and a per-kilolitre price for replication.
1. PROJECT DESCRIPTION
Why hospital laundry effluent
Municipal hospitals are among the largest single-point water users a ULB operates, and their laundries produce the most difficult stream on the campus: hot, alkaline, surfactant-rich water with blood, organics and pathogens, at flows that swing with shifts. Under the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016, hospital liquid waste must meet pH 6.5 to 9.0, suspended solids 100 mg/L, oil and grease 10 mg/L, BOD 30 mg/L and COD 250 mg/L. In practice most public hospital effluent goes to the sewer or drain untreated, or through an undersized chemical ETP that generates sludge and needs daily dosing, while the hospital draws freshwater for flushing, gardening, cleaning and the laundry itself, inside cities with supply deficits of 565 MLD (Mumbai), 53 MLD (Thane) and about 45 MLD (Mira Bhayandar).
Biological treatment does not fit this stream. Laundry water carries surfactants, hypochlorite and quaternary ammonium disinfectants at high pH and temperature, and hospital effluent carries antibiotics, pharmaceutical residues and disinfectants. These inhibit or kill the biomass a biological plant depends on, so it loses its biology or passes the compounds through untreated, and it needs 6 or more hours of retention, civil tanks a hospital campus cannot spare and a skilled operator the ULB does not have. Electrochemical treatment has no biomass to poison: electrocoagulation flocs out surfactants and emulsified oils, and electro-oxidation with in-situ hydroxyl radicals and chlorine breaks down pharmaceutical residues and disinfects in the same chamber. We have already built an 80 KLD laundry effluent plant on this exact stream at The Westin Mumbai Garden City, Goregaon, for Oberoi Realty Limited, installed in 2026 under a 7-year maintenance contract. The T-MAP pilot moves that configuration from a hotel basement into a municipal hospital.
The alternate site: a compact municipal STP
Each of the three cities has pockets the sewer network has not reached, where septic tanks overflow or a small plant has failed and sewage reaches a nalla and then the creek. Mira Bhayandar's Climate Action Plan asks large consumers to treat on site, and Thane reuses about 5 percent of the water it treats. Our precedent is the 15 KLD skid-mounted municipal plant for a fishing community at Vizhinjam, delivered to Thiruvananthapuram Municipal Corporation, where an NABL laboratory recorded COD 1,080 to 40 mg/L, BOD 355 to 7 mg/L and TSS 1,681 to 9 mg/L. The same 20 KLD unit serves 300 to 1,000 residents, treats to CPCB norms on site, and returns water for flushing, gardening or road washing where the ULB has a taker.
What we will build
One containerised treatment unit, 20 KLD design capacity: the Water Battery electrochemical reactor with patented oscillating electrodes, which runs electrocoagulation, electro-oxidation, electro-flotation and in-situ disinfection in one chamber with primary treatment in 50 seconds to 3 minutes and no chemical dosing, a tube settler, media filtration, a disinfection stage, treated-water storage with pumps to the reuse points, and the Lambert Sense data-feedback module. The unit occupies about 40 square metres including tanks, three to four times less than an equivalent biological plant (design-basis), and arrives factory-built, so site work is limited to a foundation, power connection and piping.
The digital layer is part of the deliverable. Lambert Sense reads flow, pH, ORP, conductivity and temperature at the inlet, adjusts reactor power, residence time and electrode duty cycle live, and streams flow, water quality, energy and alarm data to a cloud dashboard. The site engineer and the ULB's engineering department each get a login, and every quarterly NABL report is uploaded against the same timeline, so the compliance record is one screen: litres treated, litres reused, kWh per KL and certified outlet quality. This is the record a ULB needs to specify decentralised treatment and to pay per kilolitre rather than per plant.
Performance commitments
Hospital site: outlet within the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016 liquid waste limits on every monthly NABL sample. Compact STP: outlet within the CPCB and MPCB norms for treated sewage on every monthly sample. Both: a reuse-stream target of BOD 10 mg/L, TSS 20 mg/L and COD 50 mg/L or better, which our Thiruvananthapuram and Bengaluru units already meet on NABL certificates, with microbiological parameters tested monthly. Reuse of 80 to 90 percent of treated water at the hospital for flushing, landscaping, floor and vehicle washing and, after microbiological validation by month 8, laundry pre-wash. No coagulant or biocide consumed. At least 50 percent less sludge than a chemical followed with biological plant. Uptime above 90 percent from month 5. Energy metered and reported: our sewage-strength baseline is 0.8 to 1.1 kWh per KL, and the pilot will establish the laundry-effluent figure.
What the ULB gets at month 12
A working plant and a trained municipal team, 12 months of NABL-certified inlet and outlet data and a continuous Lambert Sense log, an SOP and O&M manual, an impact assessment, a per-kilolitre cost model with three procurement routes (CAPEX purchase, annual maintenance contract, or pay-per-KL where the ULB pays only for litres treated to specification), and a replication proposal for the rest of the estate. The unit stays on site and is handed over to the ULB at the end of the pilot, with Lambert offering O&M at standard rates.
2. GEOGRAPHY
Mumbai Metropolitan Region, within one of the three T-MAP ULBs, finalised with Villgro and the ULB in month 1. We are already in talk with Kasturba hospital, Mumbai. 
Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation: four teaching hospitals (KEM, Sion, Nair, Cooper), six specialty and 16 peripheral hospitals, more than 12,000 beds. A peripheral hospital with a central laundry of 20 to 40 KLD is the ideal first site, with the teaching hospitals as replication targets. Thane Municipal Corporation: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Hospital, Kalwa, 500 beds. Mira Bhayandar Municipal Corporation: Bharat Ratna Indira Gandhi Hospital, Mira Road East, in the same locality as our operations office.
Hospital site criteria: laundry effluent of 15 KLD or more, about 40 square metres of ground or terrace space, three-phase power, reuse demand of at least 10 KLD and a ULB nodal engineer.
Compact STP candidates: an unsewered pocket, slum rehabilitation colony or municipal housing cluster of 300 to 1,000 residents identified by the ULB, where a septic tank overflow, failed small plant or drain can be intercepted at one point with 15 KLD or more, with the same space and power, and an agreed discharge or reuse point.
Our team is based in Mira Bhayandar and Thane and our fabrication partners in the Thane and Mumbai belt, so any site in the three cities is within a day's reach.
3. TIMELINES
12 months from sanction.
Month 1: site finalization with Villgro and the ULB, including the choice between the hospital and compact STP tracks, site survey, reuse audit, baseline inlet characterisation by an NABL laboratory (physico-chemical and microbiological), design freeze, permissions and power arrangement.
Months 2 to 3: fabrication and assembly at our facilty (standard delivery 4 to 8 weeks), sensor and gateway integration, factory acceptance test, dashboard configured with ULB and site logins.
Month 4: installation, commissioning, commissioning NABL test, operator and staff training, dashboard live.
Months 5 to 10: continuous operation, monthly NABL inlet and outlet testing, monthly review with the ULB nodal engineer on the dashboard record, optimisation against the site's load pattern, and at the hospital, microbiological validation of the laundry pre-wash loop by month 8.
Month 11: impact assessment, per-kilolitre cost model from metered energy, consumables and service data, replication proposal.
Month 12: handover to the ULB, closing workshop with Villgro and Cisco, final report, ULB decision on replication.
4. FUNDING AMOUNT REQUIRED
Rs 40,00,000 from the T-MAP pilot pool, identical for either track, allocated as follows.
Water Battery reactor and containerised treatment module, 20 KLD, including power module, tube settler, media filtration, disinfection stage, pumps, control panel and container: Rs 23,00,000.
Site works and integration: Tanks, treated-water storage, piping to reuse or discharge points, electrical connection, foundation and commissioning: Rs 6,00,000.
Lambert Sense monitoring and ULB dashboard: flow, pH, ORP, conductivity, temperature and energy instruments, gateway, 12 months of connectivity and hosting, dashboard and logins: Rs 3,00,000.
Third-party verification: baseline characterisation and monthly NABL inlet and outlet testing quarterly, including microbiological parameters: Rs 1,50,000.
Operations for 12 months: electrode cartridges and consumables, service visits, spares, operator and staff training: Rs 4,00,000.
Documentation and replication: baseline and impact reports, SOP and O&M manual, cost model, replication proposal, two workshops: Rs 1,50,000.
Contingency: Rs 1,00,000.
Lambert contributes process design, engineering, project management and the Lambert Sense software at no cost to the pool, and offers post-pilot O&M at standard rates. The ULB contributes the site, power connection, sampling access, a nodal engineer and permissions. 
5. PARTNERSHIPS
Urban local body: BMC, TMC or MBMC, through the hospital administration or the engineering department, as site owner, nodal partner and end user of the dashboard and the replication proposal. We will send a written pilot proposal to the shortlisted sites on selection and welcome Villgro's introduction to the ULB's decision makers.
Villgro and Cisco: programme partner, pilot funding, implementation support and convening the ULB relationship.
ICCW, International Centre for Clean Water at IIT Madras (our incubator since 2023): technical review of the pilot protocol and results.
NABL laboratory: Enviro Analysts and Engineers Private Limited, Mumbai (TC-8848) as one of a option, which certified our Kerala plant, for baseline and monthly testing.
Existing public sector relationships: Thiruvananthapuram Municipal Corporation and K-DISC (delivered municipal plant, Kerala), Bangalore Water Supply and Sewerage Board (active collaboration, Karnataka), and Social Alpha, DST and NITI Aayog (grant and programme support).
6. EXPECTED IMPACT
Pilot, 12 months: about 6 million litres treated (20 KLD over 300 operating days), up to 5 million litres of freshwater offset where a reuse taker exists, pathogen-laden effluent within the applicable limits on every monthly sample, at least 6 tonnes less dewatered sludge a year than a chemical followed with biological plant, no coagulant purchased, about 4 tonnes of CO2e avoided (design-basis, about 680 kg per million litres), two to three municipal staff trained, and a live compliance dashboard in a ULB engineer's hands for the first time.
Replication, 1 to 3 years: 10 units in year one and up to 50 by year three, averaging 30 KLD, across the hospital estates and unsewered pockets of the three ULBs would treat about 450 million litres a year, offset about 360 million litres of freshwater, avoid about 300 tonnes of CO2e and roughly 450 tonnes of dewatered sludge, and give the three cities a decentralised reuse model that supports Thane's reuse plan and Mira Bhayandar's Climate Action Plan. Across Lambert, the same module serves hotels, schools, hospitals and industrial effluent: a target operating fleet of about 2,500 KLD by March 2027, and 5 billion litres treated cumulatively by FY 2028-29, about 4 billion litres of freshwater offset and about 3,400 tonnes of CO2e avoided.
For Cisco and Villgro, the pilot produces something transferable: a documented model in which a ULB buys treatment as a measured outcome, litres and quality logged on a dashboard, rather than buying a plant and hoping it runs. That is what lets decentralised treatment scale across the 40 communities Cisco supports.
7. WHY LAMBERT CAN DELIVER
The technology is field-validated, patented (IN202531012468, First Examination Report received and response filed, second application pending) and built on electrochemistry the founder published in Chemosphere at CSIR-NEERI. The configuration already runs on laundry effluent in Mumbai and on municipal sewage in Kerala, and two independent NABL laboratories have certified our outlets in two states. The company has been profitable every year since incorporation and has delivered more than 200 KLD of Water Battery capacity across Maharashtra, Karnataka, Kerala and Haryana. The team of 5 comprises the founder (M.Tech in Water Engineering and Management, CSIR-NEERI, 8 years in industrial and municipal water), a Head of Manufacturing and Operations with 5 years in factory automation, a project manager with ETP and ZLD operations experience, a proposal engineer and a commissioning and laboratory engineer, advised part-time by a process and design specialist with 40 years in international water projects. We are registered on GeM, hold DPIIT and Udyam registration, and are setting up an in-house fabrication facility in Maharashtra next quarter that raises output about four times.
8. SCALING OPPORTUNITY
The pilot is sized to be replicated. The per-kilolitre price it produces lets a ULB procure decentralised treatment for hospitals, unsewered pockets, markets and small plants through a rate contract or pay-per-KL agreement, removing the capital decision that stalls most municipal technology adoption. Standardised modules, 4 to 8 week delivery, quick-swap electrodes and remote operation make a fleet of 50 small municipal units serviceable from one base. Beyond the three cities, the Maharashtra ULB reference is the document other Indian cities ask for, and it anchors our plan of more than 1,000 installed systems by 2030.

Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) face a growing challenge in managing organic/biodegradable waste, which forms a significant portion of municipal solid waste. A large volume of wet waste is still collected, transported over long distances and disposed of at centralized processing facilities or landfills. This creates high transportation and operational costs, increases pressure on existing waste infrastructure, generates odour and leachate, and contributes to greenhouse-gas emissions.

Decentralized processing is difficult because existing solutions can be slow, space-intensive, labour-dependent, odour-prone, and difficult to monitor and operate consistently. ULBs therefore need compact and reliable technologies that can be deployed closer to waste-generation points such as residential communities, markets, institutions and commercial establishments.

SOWPS addresses this gap by enabling rapid, decentralized processing of segregated organic waste at source, reducing the need for transportation and landfill disposal while recovering organic nutrients as a useful resource.
column37:
Technology is at the core of SOWPS (Smart Organic Waste Processing System), enabling rapid, decentralized, and consistent processing of organic waste. SOWPS integrates proprietary thermophilic microbial technology with automated shredding, mixing, controlled aeration, and optimized temperature and moisture conditions to accelerate biological decomposition and process organic waste within 18 hours.

The system uses PLC-based automation and sensors to continuously monitor and control critical operating parameters, reducing dependence on manual intervention and improving process consistency. IoT-enabled monitoring provides real-time operational data, remote supervision, alerts, performance tracking, and predictive maintenance, enabling ULBs and operators to manage multiple decentralized units efficiently.

A 6-stage air filtration and odor-control system helps address one of the major challenges in decentralized organic waste processingodour and air emissions. The modular engineering allows the technology to be configured from small community-level units to multi-tonne-per-day municipal applications.

By integrating biological processing, automation, sensing, digital monitoring, and odor management, SOWPS transforms conventional organic waste treatment into a smart, scalable, data-driven municipal waste management solution.
column38:
The key need is for compact, reliable, decentralized and technology-enabled organic waste processing that allows ULBs and waste generators to process wet waste closer to the point of generation. Current systems often depend on transporting organic waste to centralized facilities, resulting in high logistics costs, landfill dependency, odour, emissions, and loss of recoverable organic nutrients. There is also a need for solutions that require less manpower, occupy limited space, provide faster processing, and can be monitored and managed efficiently at multiple locations.

Available alternatives include traditional composting, windrow composting, vermicomposting, conventional mechanical composting/OWC machines, and anaerobic digestion/biogas plants. While these technologies have their applications, they can involve longer processing cycles, larger footprints, significant operational requirements, odour-management challenges, or higher infrastructure complexity.

SOWPS addresses this gap by combining rapid biological processing, automation, IoT monitoring, controlled aeration, and advanced odour management to process organic waste within 18 hours. This enables decentralized deployment, reduces transportation and disposal requirements, and converts waste into a valuable organic resource.
column42:
Ensect Farm operates a B2B and B2G technology-led business model, providing SOWPS (Smart Organic Waste Processing System) to Urban Local Bodies (ULBs), municipalities, Bulk Waste Generators, institutions, industries, hotels, hospitals, and residential communities. The business focuses on decentralized organic waste processing, enabling customers to process wet waste closer to the point of generation and reduce transportation, disposal, and operational costs.

Revenue is primarily generated through SOWPS system sales, installation and commissioning, followed by recurring revenues from Annual Maintenance Contracts (AMC), operation & maintenance services, proprietary microbial formulations, spare parts, and IoT-based monitoring and support. For large municipal deployments, Ensect Farm can also undertake O&M and technology-as-a-service contracts.

The model is designed to create long-term customer relationships through recurring service and consumable revenues while enabling scalable deployment across multiple ULBs. Additional value can be generated through the recovery and utilization/sale of organic manure, creating a circular revenue stream from processed waste.
column43:
The key challenges for SOWPS are customer adoption, waste segregation, technology scaling, municipal procurement cycles, and operational consistency. Decentralized organic waste processing requires proper source segregation contamination of wet waste with plastics or other non-biodegradable materials can affect processing performance. Customer adoption may also be influenced by initial capital costs and preference for conventional waste-disposal practices.

For ULB deployments, tendering, approvals, procurement timelines, site readiness, and coordination with multiple stakeholders can extend the sales and deployment cycle. Scaling the technology across different climatic conditions, waste compositions, and operating environments also requires continuous field validation and process optimization.

Operational risks include equipment downtime, maintenance requirements, availability of trained operators, and ensuring consistent output quality. There is also a market risk from low-cost conventional alternatives and varying awareness of decentralized processing.

Ensect Farm plans to mitigate these risks through modular system design, automation and IoT-based monitoring, preventive maintenance, operator training, standardized operating protocols, field pilots, and close engagement with ULBs and customers. This approach will help build confidence, demonstrate measurable outcomes, and support reliable large-scale deployment.

Ensect Farm is applying to T-MAP to pilot, validate and scale SOWPS™ (Smart Organic Waste Processing System) as a compact, decentralized and technology-enabled solution for organic/biodegradable waste management within Urban Local Bodies (ULBs).

SOWPS™ combines proprietary thermophilic microbial technology, automated shredding and mixing, controlled aeration, temperature and moisture management, PLC-based automation, sensor-driven process control, IoT-enabled remote monitoring, and a 6-stage air-filtration and odor-control system to process segregated organic waste into nutrient-rich organic manure within approximately 18 hours.

The project will demonstrate how decentralized processing can reduce the need to transport wet waste over long distances to centralized facilities, reduce landfill dependency, improve operational efficiency, and enable ULBs to recover value from organic waste.

Geography

The initial project will focus on Maharashtra, with priority for the T-MAP geographies of:

Mumbai
Thane
Mira-Bhayandar

Following successful validation, the model will be expanded to other ULBs across Maharashtra and subsequently replicated in other Indian cities.

Ensect Farm already has experience working in municipal waste-management environments in Tamil Nadu and intends to use this experience to establish effective municipal partnerships in Maharashtra.

Timelines

We propose an 18–24 month scaling programme, structured in phases:

Phase 1 – 0–3 months:
ULB engagement, site assessment, waste-characterization study, stakeholder consultations, technical planning and pilot-site selection.

Phase 2 – 4–9 months:
Installation and commissioning of SOWPS™ pilot systems and commencement of operations. Baseline and operational data will be collected.

Phase 3 – 10–15 months:
Performance validation under real municipal conditions, optimization of operating parameters, measurement of waste diversion, operational savings, environmental impact and output quality.

Phase 4 – 16–24 months:
Scale-up within participating ULBs, development of replication models, documentation of results and preparation for wider Maharashtra deployment.

Funding Required

We seek ?3 crore in cumulative pilot support through the T-MAP pilot pool, subject to the programme's funding structure and final project scope.

The funding will support pilot equipment deployment, installation and commissioning, site-level infrastructure, sensors and IoT integration, testing and validation, field operations, manpower and training, monitoring and impact measurement, maintenance, and documentation for replication.

The proposed funding will be deployed in a milestone-based manner linked to pilot installation, operational performance and measurable impact.

Partnerships

The project will be implemented through partnerships with relevant Urban Local Bodies, municipal corporations, government agencies and ecosystem partners in Maharashtra. ULB partners will support site identification, municipal coordination, waste-stream integration, local operational requirements and pilot validation.

Ensect Farm will provide the SOWPS™ technology, engineering, installation, commissioning, technical operations, IoT monitoring, training, maintenance and impact reporting.

We are particularly interested in establishing partnerships with ULBs in Mumbai, Thane and Mira-Bhayandar, while remaining open to additional municipal partners identified through T-MAP.

Expected Impact

The project is expected to demonstrate measurable improvements in decentralized organic waste management, including:

Increased tonnes of organic waste diverted from landfill
Reduced wet-waste transportation and associated costs
Reduced dependence on centralized processing infrastructure
Processing of organic waste within approximately 18 hours
Reduction in odor, pests and local sanitation issues
Improved working conditions and reduced manual handling for waste-management workers
Recovery of organic nutrients through production of organic manure
Real-time digital monitoring of decentralized processing operations
Generation of reliable performance data for ULB decision-making
Creation of a replicable municipal deployment model for Maharashtra

In the long term, the project aims to demonstrate that compact, automated and digitally monitored decentralized organic-waste processing can become an economically and operationally viable component of urban solid-waste management, enabling Maharashtra's ULBs to move from waste collection and disposal toward local processing, resource recovery and a circular economy.

column36:
India's water decisions are made without a shared evidence layer. Cities plan supply augmentation, agencies fund lake and river restoration, industries site plants, and listed companies report water risk, but the data behind each decision is scattered across dozens of portals and formats: India-WRIS, CGWB and IN-GRES assessments, IMD rainfall grids, state pollution control board monitoring, state GIS servers, audit annexures. Each source is authoritative individually, but they do not join: different geographies, different vintages, key tables in PDF, no common keys. So institutional memory fades between plans. Every new DPR, restoration project or disclosure exercise starts data collection from scratch, and baselines that were paid for once are rebuilt again and again.

Neer Vazhvu (neervazhvu.org) addresses exactly this gap: a maintained water intelligence layer for Indian cities and basins where every number is source-linked to a primary government record, standardized into one data model, kept current by automated pipelines, and published in both human form (dashboards, maps, atlases) and machine form (versioned open datasets). It is live today for 10 Indian cities plus a growing district atlas, with more than 1,000 versioned data artifacts, each carrying provenance and licence metadata.

The innovation is not another dashboard. It is the missing shared record: an evidence layer that governments, consultancies, researchers and companies can all build on instead of re-collecting, so that restoration money, planning effort and compliance work start from a common, current baseline.
column37:
Technology is what lets one engineer build and maintain a national water platform, and what makes the data trustworthy rather than merely aggregated.

1. Automated ingestion: scheduled scrapers and API pipelines pull daily from canonical sources (India-WRIS, IN-GRES, IMD, state pollution control boards, state GIS servers), so freshness does not depend on manual effort.

2. A standardized water data model: every published artifact carries machine-readable provenance, licence, geography and time-period metadata, enforced by automated conformance gates before anything ships. This is the difference between a data dump and an evidence layer.

3. Satellite analytics: Google Earth Engine pipelines over Sentinel-2 and Dynamic World fill gaps where ground monitoring is thin: water spread over time, built-up change around lakes and wetlands, vegetation proxies for canal health.

4. Freshness intelligence: a watch-and-alert registry monitors upstream sources and flags new editions, so published data never ages silently. Staleness is computed and shown in the product, not hidden.

5. A modern web platform: Next.js frontend, Python FastAPI services and Postgres serve verdict-first dashboards, interactive maps and exportable datasets.

The product is the curated, maintained corpus. Technology is what makes that curation reproducible, auditable and affordable at one-person cost, which is why the platform could reach 10 cities without a team.
column38:
The need: decision-grade water data that is current, local (city, basin and asset level), source-linked and maintained, for restoration programs, urban planning, technical assistance projects, corporate water disclosure and research.

Available alternatives and their limits:

1. Primary government portals (India-WRIS, IN-GRES, PCB monitoring, state GIS). Authoritative and improving, but designed as individual repositories: different formats and geographies, key tables in PDF, no cross-source joins. A user must be expert in ten portals at once.

2. One-off consulting studies and DPRs. Deep but snapshot-in-time and expensive the data typically lives in report annexures and is not reusable by the next project.

3. Global water-risk tools such as WRI Aqueduct. Useful screening layers, but coarse-resolution, not built on Indian primary sources, and not asset-level. SEBI's BRSR framework has no canonical list of water-stressed areas, so listed companies must self-classify; global tools do not resolve this.

4. In-house GIS cells in a few advanced cities. Valuable but city-bound and mandate-bound.

No alternative offers one maintained layer joining ground records, satellite evidence and published plans across cities and basins, with per-number provenance, machine-readable licences and computed freshness. The closest substitute is re-collecting data per project, which is exactly the waste the platform removes.
column42:
Neer Vazhvu is an infrastructure company with a services wedge. The open city platform is the commons layer: it builds trust and distribution and demonstrates depth (10 cities live). Revenue comes from what institutions need on top of it:

1. Commissioned deep dives: waterway, basin and corridor baselines built to decision grade. Validation to date: a canal baseline pilot requested by the Tamil Nadu Water Investment Company (TWIC) went from brief to live product in two days river dashboards co-built with Paani Earth Foundation (Bengaluru) a first international deliverable (UAE water profile brief).

2. Recurring maintenance: every delivered deep dive carries an annual maintenance subscription under which data is watched, refreshed and staleness-flagged. This line scales without scaling hours and converts one-off projects into recurring revenue.

3. Wedge customers: water-sector consultancies and multilateral technical assistance programs, whose data components match our contract sizes, buy faster than direct government procurement.

4. Regulatory products: BRSR Core water assurance reaches the top 500 listed companies this fiscal year and the top 1,000 next site-level water-stress evidence packs fill a gap companies currently self-classify around. CGWA's mandatory annual water audits for large groundwater abstractors are adjacent recurring demand.

Bottom-up, source-cited TAM is Rs 100-260 crore per year, with a serviceable market of Rs 30-60 crore. The design intent: services share declines by design as each service SKU hardens into a repeatable product.
column43:
1. Category monetization: no Indian water-data company has crossed roughly Rs 15 crore in revenue, and pure data-sales models have struggled. Mitigation: a services wedge with recurring maintenance attached, demand pulled by regulation (BRSR assurance, CGWA audits) rather than discretionary budgets, and global validation that the category matures (MSCI's 2026 acquisition of climate-risk data firm First Street).

2. Long sales cycles: government and multilateral procurement is slow. Mitigation: consultancies and technical assistance programs as faster first buyers, and pilots that convert the TWIC pilot was delivered in days, not quarters.

3. Key-person concentration: the platform is currently built and maintained by one founder. Automation and a standardized data model keep it one-person-operable, but scale requires a small team the funding plan phases in five hires against defined milestones. We're currently looking for a non-technical co-founder who'd walk this journey alongwith me.

4. Upstream source churn: portals get redesigned, feeds freeze, editions move. Mitigation: a watch-and-alert registry over every source, archived editions, multi-source redundancy, and honest staleness flags in the product itself.

5. "Free alternative" perception: buyers may assume government portals suffice. The counter is the product itself: joined, maintained, provenance-carrying, asset-level data that no single portal provides.

6. Licensing and data rights: managed proactively a dataset enters the corpus only with recorded provenance and licence, so commercial use stands on clean ground.
column44: Numbers first: how many people's water situation is publicly visible (the MMR, Pune, and Satara's 6.07 lakh rural households in Maharashtra alone), 1,467 Gram Panchayat briefs generated in Satara, equity indicators surfaced such as the per-capita supply spread across MMR corporations and tap-coverage gaps by block, requests answered (a village profile in a day), plus usage analytics. Qualitatively, the impact I care about is information equity: a village gets the same treatment as a metro, tanker registers are published as counts and never as addresses, and where data does not exist we say so.
column46:
The users range from a 718-household village to a metropolitan region, and I have tried to keep the depth the same at both ends.

In Maharashtra, the covered population is the nine corporations of the MMR, Pune city, and Satara district, where the atlas covers 6.7 lakh rural households across 1,502 Gram Panchayats, Marul Haveli among them. Ten cities are live nationally. So the mix runs from dense urban wards and informal settlements, whose supply gaps the MMR view documents, to agrarian Panchayats that depend on groundwater and tankers.

Who actually uses it: residents and resident welfare associations checking their own locality, journalists and researchers who need numbers they can cite, NGO and restoration workers, planners in ULBs and districts, students. It is free and open, no login, so nothing filters who gets to benefit. One limitation I will state plainly: the interface is English-first today. Marathi and Tamil are planned before outreach to rural audiences, and the data model already supports them.
column47:
None of these were commissioned pilots. I built them on my own time and cost, using only what the bodies themselves publish, and all of them run in production today on neervazhvu.org. The approach has been to show working product first and have conversations after.

1. Mumbai Metropolitan Region, live since 6 July 2026. I modelled the full MMR rather than Greater Mumbai alone, because the water system does not stop at the BMC boundary. Nine municipal corporations (Greater Mumbai, Thane, Kalyan-Dombivli, Navi Mumbai, Vasai-Virar, Mira-Bhayandar, Ulhasnagar, Bhiwandi-Nizampur, Panvel), each mapped to the sources that actually supply it: BMC's seven lakes, MIDC's Barvi on the eastern corridor, the MMRDA Surya scheme for Vasai-Virar and Mira-Bhayandar, Morbe for Navi Mumbai, Hetawane for Panvel. Reservoir storage updates daily from the Water Resources Department's Pravah bulletin, which covers 139 dams statewide. Looking at the region as one unit brings out the supply-equity picture: per-capita supply runs from 252 LPCD in Greater Mumbai to about 70 in Vasai-Virar, against the CPHEEO benchmark of 135. Every figure carries its citation.

2. Pune, live since 18 August 2026, built on PMC's own registers. The most useful finding came straight out of PMC's Environmental Status Report 2025-26 water budget: requirement 21.03 TMC against 16.36 TMC sanctioned, with non-revenue water at 32, or 6.73 TMC. So the recoverable loss is bigger than the 4.67 TMC shortfall everyone debates. Same table, different reading. Beyond that: 57,370 tanker deliveries digitised from PMC's daily dispatch registers (7 filling points, 1,956 vehicles), published as counts only the source files contain 54,235 addresses and 26,326 phone numbers and I republished none of them. 3,075 storm-water drain segments totalling 1,014 km from PMC's drainage layer, with my computed lengths matching PMC's own to within 0.4. Groundwater drilled down to taluka level across six IN-GRES editions, which shows Shirur at 95.71 extraction inside a district that reads safe at 63.73. And 791 water bodies mapped.

3. Marul Haveli village, Patan taluka, Satara, July 2026. The first village-level request the platform ever received. I turned around a three-page water profile within a day: 718 functional household tap connections (100, Har Ghar Jal certified), two habitations, two piped schemes, 19 water-quality samples with zero contamination, the taluka's groundwater safe at 65.4 extraction, and where the season's rainfall stood for its revenue circle. A small deliverable, but it proved the method works at village grain in Maharashtra, using JJM IMIS, Census and Maharain.

4. Satara district atlas, live 1 September 2026. The third full district on the platform and the first outside Tamil Nadu. Because the pipeline is shared, onboarding took days, not months. What it covers: 1,502 Gram Panchayats across 11 blocks JJM service registers read for all 1,742 villages, showing 93.0 of 6,07,637 rural households with tap connections groundwater for all 11 talukas (IN-GRES 2024-25, nine safe, two semi-critical) 3,756 water bodies and structures from the First Census of Water Bodies, 3,423 of them placed in their Gram Panchayats rainfall per Panchayat against normals village boundaries and the district Environment Plan's own figures with page citations, including 49.75 MLD of urban sewage generation against 21.5 MLD of installed treatment capacity, which puts a number on the treatment investment needed across the district's ULBs. Marul Haveli, the village that started all this, now carries a hand-reviewed brief in the atlas. A monthly automated job re-reads the registers so nothing goes stale quietly.

Between them, these four cover the whole ladder in one state: region, corporation, district, block, Gram Panchayat, village. They also forced me to learn the Maharashtra-specific sources properly (Pravah, Maharain, MPCB district plans, LGD, JJM's Maharashtra registers). Onboarding cost is now measured in days, which is why statewide coverage is a plan and not a wish.

column50:
Project Description

Neer Vazhvu (neervazhvu.org) is India's water intelligence platform. Every number on it is linked to a primary government record, standardised into one data model, refreshed by automated pipelines, and published both as readable pages and as versioned open datasets. It is live today for ten cities across eight states, and for three full districts down to the Gram Panchayat level. I have built and maintained all of it single-handedly since the first commit in March 2026.

The project I am applying with is the Maharashtra scale-up: take the platform's proven district and ULB pipeline statewide across Maharashtra, and convert what are today self-initiated deployments into working relationships with the state's institutions.

Maharashtra is already the platform's largest footprint outside Tamil Nadu, and the pipeline has been proven there end to end. The Mumbai Metropolitan Region went live in July 2026, modelled as one water system across nine municipal corporations with daily reservoir tracking through the Water Resources Department's Pravah bulletin. Pune went live in August 2026 on PMC's own registers, including its Environmental Status Report water budget and 57,370 digitised tanker dispatch records. In July 2026 the platform answered its first ever village-level request, from Marul Haveli in Patan taluka, with a verified water profile delivered within a day. That request led to the Satara district atlas, live since 1 September 2026: 1,502 Gram Panchayats, JJM service registers for all 1,742 villages, groundwater status for all 11 talukas, 3,756 water bodies from the First Census of Water Bodies, and the district Environment Plan's own figures served with page citations. Satara was onboarded in days, not months, because the pipeline is shared across every district.

The scale-up has five workstreams:

1. A district signal ledger for all 36 Maharashtra districts: a sourced per-district reading of groundwater status, tap coverage and water-quality sampling, pollution listings, and flood-proneness, drawn from national and state sources. This work has started. It decides where deep coverage goes first, so the sequence is evidence-led rather than intuition-led.

2. District onboarding: every district gets the thin tier of indicators; deep coverage (Panchayat-level registers, water bodies, boundaries, rainfall, briefs) rolls out in ledger priority order. The marginal cost per district is proven at roughly a day of focused work plus register runtime.

3, ULB deepening: ward-level layers for Mumbai and Pune, and the corporation-level view extended, so the urban side matches the district side in depth.

4. Marathi: the interface is English-first today. Marathi language keys ship before any outreach to Marathi-first audiences, and the data model already supports it.

5. Institutional adoption: converting the self-initiated pilots into official ones, with district administrations, ULBs, restoration NGOs and CSR programs using the atlas as their working baseline. This is where the program's support matters most, and it is the honest gap in what I can do alone from Chennai.

Geography

The project geography is Maharashtra, statewide: 36 districts and roughly 28,000 Gram Panchayats per the Local Government Directory. The existing Maharashtra footprint is the nine-corporation MMR, Pune city, Satara district, and Marul Haveli village. The platform as a whole serves ten cities across eight states, so Maharashtra work strengthens, and is strengthened by, a national system. Neer Vazhvu Technologies Pvt. Ltd. is based in Chennai; the platform is built remote-first on public data sources, with field validation trips planned into the project budget.

Timelines

An 18-month project in three phases.

1. Months 1 to 6: complete the 36-district signal ledger; onboard the next five to six districts chosen by it; ship Marathi interface keys; publish ward-level layers for Pune. Deliverable: a third of the state covered, with a public, evidence-led plan for the rest.

2. Months 7 to 12: all 36 districts live at the thin tier, with 12 to 15 carrying deep Panchayat-level coverage; Mumbai ward layers; first official pilots signed with at least two district administrations or ULBs. Deliverable: statewide baseline nobody in Maharashtra has to re-collect.

3. Months 13 to 18: deep coverage extended in ledger priority order; the monthly automated refresh chain, already proven in Satara, running for every live district; at least one recurring revenue engagement in the state (a maintained baseline or commissioned deep dive). Deliverable: a self-sustaining Maharashtra atlas with named institutional users.

These timelines are grounded in measured costs: Satara, the first district in a new state, took under a week of focused work including the Maharashtra-specific source adapters; the second district in a state falls to about a day. The adapters, once built, are paid for.

Funding amount required

Rs 1 crore over 18 months, indicative breakup:

1. One full-stack data engineer, 18 months: Rs 33 lakh
2. One water-sector analyst (register review, Marathi source verification, district research): Rs 24 lakh
3. Field validation and travel across districts, including ground-truthing satellite layers: Rs 10 lakh
3. Marathi localisation and native-speaker review: Rs 6 lakh
4. Infrastructure, satellite compute, data operations: Rs 8 lakh
5. Founder time, partnerships and program engagement, contingency: Rs 19 lakh
6. This project sits inside a larger platform plan (a Rs 3 crore, 24-month raise for a five-person team nationally), so program funding at any level accelerates a machine that already runs; it does not create one from scratch.

Partnerships associated

I will state the current position plainly rather than dress it up.

Delivered and live: a canal baseline pilot requested by the Tamil Nadu Water Investment Company (TWIC), taken from brief to live product in two days and now in production; ongoing co-built river dashboards with Paani Earth Foundation, a Bengaluru river-restoration nonprofit, including a paid scope of work on the Cauvery; active conversations with WELL Labs (a joint flood-pilot demo package in progress) and with the International Centre for Clean Water at IIT Madras; a partnership MoU drafted with the Water Parliament initiative (University of Maryland); and a first international deliverable, a UAE water profile brief.

In Maharashtra specifically: no formal partnerships yet. The Maharashtra work so far is built on the state's own public systems (WRD's Pravah, Maharain, MPCB district plans, LGD, JJM Maharashtra, MRSAC-adjacent sources), and it stands up to scrutiny, but it has been done without a counterpart on the other side of the table. That is precisely the scaling gap this application addresses: I can build the state's water atlas from public records alone, and have; converting it into something district administrations, ULBs and CSR programs formally use needs introductions and institutional standing that an incubation program provides and a solo founder in Chennai does not.

Expected impact description

Direct output: all 36 Maharashtra districts carrying a current, source-linked, publicly maintained water record, joined from groundwater assessments, service registers, water-body censuses, reservoir feeds, rainfall and district plans, with roughly 28,000 Gram Panchayats resolvable to their own brief. Urban side: the MMR and Pune covered to ward depth, with supply-equity differences documented from the bodies' own records.

What changes because of it: restoration programs, DPR preparers, district planners and CSR funders in Maharashtra stop paying for baseline re-collection, because a maintained citable baseline exists. Adoption is the primary impact metric and it is countable: programs that cite or build on the data, official pilots signed, requests answered. The Marul Haveli experience is the template; a village asked, and got a verified profile within a day. At scale that responsiveness becomes ordinary.

Environmental impact is tracked in the platform's own longitudinal record: taluka extraction stages across IN-GRES editions, water spread of restored water bodies across seasons, treatment capacity against documented sewage generation. Social impact is information equity: the same depth for a 718-household village as for a metropolitan region, privacy-first publication throughout, and gaps named honestly so absence of data is itself visible.

The long-term case: Maharashtra becomes the first state with a complete, living water atlas, and the working proof that this can be replicated state by state across India.

Short term, the first twelve months.

Twenty five kiosks live across South Mumbai, displacing 41.25 lakh single use plastic bottles, avoiding 402 tonnes of CO2e and 103 tonnes of plastic waste, and dispensing 16.5 lakh litres of certified drinking water at half the packaged retail price. Fifty seven direct jobs created and recruited locally. A working per container audit trail delivered to the Corporation, giving a Maharashtra ULB source level data on a waste stream currently measured only after disposal.

Medium term, years two to four.

Expansion within Greater Mumbai and the Metropolitan Region to suburban rail, metro hubs, beaches, markets and civic precincts, and replication into Ayodhya, Delhi and Bengaluru under the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs co location framework. Table top dispensers hosted at small shops create a dense corridor layer alongside mobile kiosks, multiplying touchpoints without proportionate capital. The clean circle programme extends a maintained 500 metre radius around each kiosk, reducing sweeping and drain clearing load for the ward.

At this stage the model shifts from a project to municipal infrastructure, self funding its own expansion from operations, with corporations sharing in net distributable profit rather than carrying cost.

Long term, five years and beyond.

Reuse becomes the default in Indian public space rather than the exception, in the same way that packaged water displaced the piau over the previous three decades. The measurement layer matters as much as the hardware: a validated methodology for reuse based packaging displacement would open carbon finance to the entire reuse sector, not only to this network.

For Maharashtra specifically, a replicable template that any urban local body with high footfall public space can adopt under an existing sanction model, contributing to Plastic Waste Management Rules compliance, Swachh Survekshan performance and measurable reduction in the plastic load reaching stormwater drains and coastal waters.
